docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Counterweight is an experimental text user interface (TUI) framework for Python, inspired by React and Tailwind CSS.

A TUI application built with Counterweight is a tree of declarative components, each of which represents some piece of the UI by bundling together a visual element along with its state and how that state should change due to events like user input.

As an application author, you define the components and their relationships as a tree of Python functions. You use hooks to manage state and side effects, and styles to change how the elements look.

Counterweight takes this declarative representation of the UI and renders it to the terminal, updating the UI when state changes in response to user input or side effects (by calling your function tree).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Counterweight is available on PyPI, and needs Python 3.15 or newer:

pip install counterweight

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This to-do list is a complete app. Save it as todo.py, or have counterweight examples copy todo write it there, and run it with python todo.py; Ctrl+C quits.

"""
To-do list

A to-do list, the app the quick start builds.

Type a task and press Enter to add it, Tab to move between the tasks, and Space or a click to mark one done.
"""

import asyncio
from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass
from dataclasses import replace
from functools import partial

from counterweight import app
from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.elements import Div
from counterweight.elements import Text
from counterweight.events import InputEvent
from counterweight.events import InputResponse
from counterweight.events import KeyPressed
from counterweight.events import Receiver
from counterweight.handlers import first
from counterweight.handlers import on_click
from counterweight.handlers import tab_focus
from counterweight.hooks import use_focus
from counterweight.hooks import use_state
from counterweight.keys import Key
from counterweight.styles.utilities import *
from counterweight.widgets import text_input


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Task:
    title: str
    is_done: bool = False


FIRST_TASKS: tuple[Task, ...] = (Task("Install Counterweight", is_done=True), Task("Write a component"))


@component
def root() -> Div:
    tasks, set_tasks = use_state(FIRST_TASKS)
    draft, set_draft = use_state("")

    def add_task(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter) if draft.strip():
                set_tasks(lambda tasks: (*tasks, Task(draft.strip())))
                set_draft("")
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    def toggle(index: int) -> None:
        set_tasks(
            lambda tasks: tuple(replace(t, is_done=not t.is_done) if i == index else t for i, t in enumerate(tasks))
        )

    left = sum(not task.is_done for task in tasks)
    return Div(
        style=col | width(44),
        on_input=first(add_task, tab_focus),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | gap(1) | border | border_lightrounded | border_color("slate", 500) | pad_x(1),
                children=(
                    Text(content=f"To do ({left} left)", style=text_color("amber", 400)),
                    Div(style=col, children=tuple(task_row(task, partial(toggle, i)) for i, task in enumerate(tasks))),
                    text_input(draft, set_draft, placeholder="What needs doing?", auto_focus=True),
                ),
            ),
            Text(
                content="enter: add  ·  tab: move  ·  space: done",
                style=text_justify_center | text_color("slate", 500),
            ),
        ),
    )


@component
def task_row(task: Task, toggle_done: Callable[[], None]) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus()

    def on_space(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Space):
                toggle_done()
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=f"{'✓' if task.is_done else '○'} {task.title}",
        style=(text_color("emerald", 400) if task.is_done else text_color("slate", 200))
        | (text_bg("slate", 700) if focus.is_focused else default),
        on_input=first(on_space, on_click(toggle_done)),
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(app(root()))

After adding "Read the docs", with "Ship it" typed but not yet added:

ScreenshotText 

╭──────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ To do (2 left)                           │
│                                          │
│ ✓ Install Counterweight                  │
│ ○ Write a component                      │
│ ○ Read the docs                          │
│                                          │
│ ╭──────────────────────────────────────╮ │
│ │ Ship it                              │ │
│ ╰──────────────────────────────────────╯ │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────╯
  enter: add  ·  tab: move  ·  space: done

Adding tasks, then moving to them with Tab and marking them done with Space:

What's in it:

  • root and task_row are components: functions decorated with @component that return elements, a Div that lays out its children and a Text that shows a string. Counterweight calls them again whenever their state changes.
  • use_state holds the tasks and the draft. Each setter takes a new value, or a function from the latest value to the next.
  • text_input is a widget, a text box built on a headless hook, which edits draft through set_draft.
  • Each on_input handler matches the events it cares about and returns () to claim them, or None to let them bubble up to the element's parent. Enter bubbles out of the text input to add_task on the root.
  • use_focus makes each row focusable, tab_focus moves focus with Tab, and on_click marks a task done when you click it.
  • The style utilities, such as col, border and text_color("amber", 400), merge with |, as Tailwind's classes combine.

docs.title: Showcase
docs.text: Counterweight ships with complete apps, each standing for a kind of app people build with it, beside the snippets these docs show. Run one with counterweight examples run <name>, such as counterweight examples run wordle, or browse them all, and run each in place, with counterweight examples gallery (see Examples).

docs.title: Running an App
docs.text:
app runs an application. Give it the root component, already called with its arguments, and run it on an event loop with asyncio.run:

import asyncio

from counterweight import app
from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.elements import Text


@component
def root(name: str) -> Text:
    return Text(content=f"Hello, {name}!")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(app(root("world")))

It switches the terminal to its alternate screen, reads input raw and turns on mouse reporting, then renders the root and handles input until something returns Quit, which by default Ctrl+C does. It restores the terminal before it returns, and before an error raised in a component, a handler or an effect propagates out of it.

docs.title: What else it takes
docs.text:
The rest of app's parameters each belong to a part of the framework, with its own page:

To Pass See Title the terminal window title SetTitle Change what Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z do, or give other keys defaults unclaimed_keys Keys the terminal would act on Read the time in another time zone, or freeze it clock use_clock Drive it without a person, or without a terminal autopilot, headless, dimensions Autopilot Record it as an asciicast recording Recording Catch components that go stale check_purity Performance Let garbage collection run in the middle of a frame collect_garbage_between_frames Performance See other libraries' debug logs in the devlog log_levels The devlog Match a font that isn't twice as tall as it is wide cell_aspect_ratio Gradients Draw on a terminal other than standard input and output input_stream, output_stream Running programs

docs.title: counterweight.app async
docs.text:
app(
    root: Component,
    output_stream: TextIO = stdout,
    input_stream: TextIO = stdin,
    headless: bool = False,
    dimensions: tuple[int, int] | None = None,
    autopilot: Iterable[AutopilotStep] = (),
    check_purity: bool = False,
    clock: Clock = SystemClock(),
    log_levels: Mapping[str, int] = frozendict(),
    title: str | None = None,
    unclaimed_keys: Mapping[
        str, AnyControl
    ] = DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_KEYS,
    cell_aspect_ratio: float = DEFAULT_CELL_ASPECT_RATIO,
    recording: Recording | None = None,
    clipboard_handler: Callable[
        [str], Awaitable[None] | None
    ]
    | None = None,
    collect_garbage_between_frames: bool = True,
) -> None
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION root

The root component of the application, already called with its arguments, such as app(root(path)).

TYPE: Component

output_stream

The stream to which the application will write its output. To draw on the terminal while standard output is a pipe, as a picker run in vim $(picker) does, pass /dev/tty opened for writing.

TYPE: TextIO DEFAULT: stdout

input_stream

The stream from which the application will read its input.

TYPE: TextIO DEFAULT: stdin

headless

If True, the application will not attempt to read from the input stream or write to the output stream. This is primarily useful when combined with the autopilot parameter.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

dimensions

The dimensions of the terminal window, in characters. If None, the size of the terminal output_stream writes to, read again on each resize, or 80 by 24 if it isn't a terminal. The COLUMNS and LINES environment variables are ignored.

TYPE: tuple[int, int] | None DEFAULT: None

autopilot

An iterable of events and controls to be processed by the application, and of Wait and WaitFor, which hold the rest back until real time has passed or the screen shows something. This is primarily useful for testing or generating screenshots and recordings programmatically. Each step is handled once the renders the last one caused are painted, and the effects they started have run up to where each first waits on something, as a person's next key press would be. An app that never settles, such as one showing a program that prints without pause, holds a step back for at most SETTLE_LIMIT passes of the render loop, after which the autopilot takes it anyway. A Wait or WaitFor is checked on every pass, settled or not, so a WaitFor times out on time. Note that the autopilot will not be processed until after the initial render cycle, and that using the autopilot does not automatically cause the application to quit!

TYPE: Iterable[AutopilotStep] DEFAULT: ()

check_purity

If True, check that components are pure: that their output depends only on their arguments and their hooks. A render keeps the previous output of every component it doesn't re-run (because its state didn't change and its parent didn't re-run, or because it's a memo component whose arguments didn't change), so an impure one goes stale. With this on, each render is followed by a second one that re-runs every component against copies of its hooks, and if that builds a different tree, the application raises ImpureComponent, naming the first component whose output differs. Elements are compared with ==, and where that fails, piece by piece, so handlers are compared by their code and the values they captured, since a re-run builds new ones. The second run also raises InconsistentHookExecution for a component that calls a different number of hooks, and computes each use_memo that keeps its cached value again, raising StaleMemo if the result differs, naming the component and the hook. It costs as much as a render that re-runs everything, so turn it on in tests rather than in production.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

clock

Where use_clock reads the time, once per render. The SystemClock reads the time in UTC unless it's given a timezone. Pass a FrozenClock to make output that doesn't depend on when the application runs, such as a screenshot, and move it with the AdvanceClock control.

TYPE: Clock DEFAULT: SystemClock()

log_levels

Levels by logger name, with "" the root logger, as in logging.config, for the records the devlog captures while the app runs. They're merged over a base that captures counterweight's records and the app's own at every level, and everyone else's from INFO up, where the app's own are those of the top-level package of the module that defines root's function (__main__ for an app run as a script). Pass {"some_library": logging.DEBUG} to see a library's debug records too, or {"my_app": logging.INFO} to hide the app's own. An app that runs while another has the devlog open, such as one run headless in another's handler, writes its records into that devlog, at the levels the other app set.

TYPE: Mapping[str, int] DEFAULT: frozendict()

title

The title to give the terminal window when the application starts, as SetTitle would, before the first frame is drawn. If None, the terminal keeps the title it has.

TYPE: str | None DEFAULT: None

unclaimed_keys

What a key press does when no handler claims it, by its key, as a browser takes a key's default action unless a listener prevents it. The application reads the terminal raw, so every key reaches it as a key press, including Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z, which a terminal otherwise turns into signals, and the defaults, DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_KEYS, give those two what they'd do there: Ctrl+C returns Quit, and Ctrl+Z Suspend.to_shell(). A handler that claims one of those keys, such as one that passes keys on to a program, keeps it from taking its default. Pass {} to give unclaimed keys no defaults, or merge onto the defaults to change some, as in DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_KEYS | {Key.ControlQ: Quit()}.

TYPE: Mapping[str, AnyControl] DEFAULT: DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_KEYS

cell_aspect_ratio

How many times taller than it is wide a cell of the terminal's font is, which gradients compute their angles and circles with, so that a 45 degree gradient or a circle looks like one. Most terminal fonts are about 2.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: DEFAULT_CELL_ASPECT_RATIO

recording

Where and how to record the application as an asciicast, which asciinema-player plays back, whether it's headless or not. If None, the application isn't recorded.

TYPE: Recording | None DEFAULT: None

clipboard_handler

What a CopyToClipboard without a handler of its own does with its text, awaited if it returns an awaitable, such as copied.append in a test, which can't reach the controls the app's handlers return. If None, the text goes to the terminal's clipboard over OSC 52, or nowhere when headless. An error it raises is logged rather than stopping the app.

TYPE: Callable[[str], Awaitable[None] | None] | None DEFAULT: None

collect_garbage_between_frames

If True, the default, Python's cyclic garbage collector doesn't run while a frame is generated, from re-running components to writing the frame to the terminal, and runs once after the frame is written instead, if the objects the frame allocated and didn't free call for it, as a browser schedules garbage collection in the idle time between frames. The temporary objects a frame frees before it ends then never trigger a collection, a frame that keeps enough for several triggers one, and the older generations, collected once every so many collections of the youngest, are collected less often, so cyclic garbage is freed later than it would be. Nothing frees the cyclic garbage a frame makes until the frame is written, so memory grows with every cycle a frame drops. The collector is paused for every thread of the process, not just the app's, and isn't touched by a frame that starts with it disabled, such as by gc.disable(), though a frame that paused it enables it again once it's written, even if another thread disabled it meanwhile. Pass False to let it run whenever it would, as an app whose frames make and drop a lot of cyclic garbage should (see When not to pause it).

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: True

docs.title: Autopilot and Recording
docs.text: An autopilot drives an app without a person at the keyboard: it feeds the app events and controls, as tests and these docs' screenshots do. A recording saves what an app draws, with its timing, as an asciicast file that asciinema-player and asciinema play play back, whether a person or an autopilot is driving. This page covers both, and how they combine to record a demo that comes out the same on every run.

docs.title: Driving an app
docs.text:
app's autopilot is an iterable of events and controls, which the app handles in order, starting after its first frame. Each step waits for what the last one set off, as a person's next key press would: the renders it caused, and the effects those renders started, up to where each first waits on something. An app that never goes quiet, such as one showing a program that prints without pause, holds a step back for at most SETTLE_LIMIT passes of its render loop, as React stops a cascade of updates after 50, and then the autopilot takes the step anyway. It doesn't quit the app when it runs out, so end it with Quit(). With headless=True the app neither reads the terminal nor draws on it, and dimensions gives it a screen size:

await app(
    search(),
    headless=True,
    dimensions=(30, 8),
    autopilot=[
        KeyPressed(key="a"),
        KeyPressed(key="n"),
        Screenshot.to_file(Path("typed.svg")),
        Quit(),
    ],
)

search is the fruit search from use_text_input. The screenshot it writes is the frame after both keys, with the list narrowed to the fruits that contain "an":

ScreenshotText 

search: an                    

banana                        
mango                         
orange

typed gives the key presses that type some text, one per grapheme cluster, as Playwright's keyboard.type does, so typed("an") is the two key presses above.

docs.title: Composing steps
docs.text: An autopilot's steps are plain values, so build one with plain Python: list literals, * unpacking, and the iterable combinators of itertools and more-itertools, which counterweight depends on, so it's already installed. Counterweight's helpers, such as typed, give lists of steps to compose that way, rather than taking options for pacing or repeating them, and its one combinator, paced, only adds the type that interleave can't infer.

docs.title: Controlling time
docs.text:
An app reads the time from its clock, the system's by default. A FrozenClock reads the same time until the autopilot moves it on, with AdvanceClock or by waiting, so an autopilot can show a minute of a clock-driven app in milliseconds, and show the same thing on every run. To pace an autopilot, put an AdvanceClock before each of its steps with paced, and one more after the last, so a recording that loops lingers where it ends:

pause = AdvanceClock(by=timedelta(milliseconds=300))

await app(
    search(),
    headless=True,
    dimensions=(30, 8),
    clock=FrozenClock(datetime(2026, 3, 14, tzinfo=UTC)),
    autopilot=[*paced(typed("mango"), pause=pause), AdvanceClock(by=timedelta(seconds=2)), Quit()],
)

Its recording plays a key every 300 milliseconds, though the autopilot ran in only as long as the app took to render:

paced(steps, pause) is more_itertools.interleave(itertools.repeat(pause), steps), typed as steps. Passed straight to interleave, a list of steps of different kinds, such as clicks and key presses, has nothing to say what type it is, so mypy settles on a base class they share, which isn't a step, and rejects the autopilot. For other shapes, reach for more-itertools: intersperse(pause, steps) pauses only between steps, and intersperse(pause, steps, n=3) after every third. Give a list of mixed kinds that goes to one of them the type list[AutopilotStep].

A single AdvanceClock jumps straight to the time it names, so an animation jumps to that frame. advance moves the clock the same distance a step at a time, one frame of the animation hooks unless it's given another step, so a recording shows the animation play out, as Playwright's clock.runFor fires each timer due along the way:

autopilot = [KeyPressed(key=Key.Space), *advance(timedelta(seconds=2)), Quit()]

docs.title: Waiting for real work
docs.text:
An autopilot runs ahead of anything the app does in the background, such as an effect waiting on a subprocess or a command, since it hands the app its next step once the renders the last one caused are painted, not once the work they started is done. Two steps hold it back while the app keeps handling events and rendering:

  • WaitFor waits until a condition is true of the frame on screen, and fails with AutopilotTimedOut if it's still false after its timeout. It's the one to reach for, as Playwright's assertions are, since it waits exactly as long as the work takes.
  • Wait waits for a duration of real time.
await app(
    test_runner(),
    headless=True,
    dimensions=(60, 20),
    autopilot=[
        KeyPressed(key="r"),
        WaitFor(lambda frame: "passed" in frame.text(ansi=False), timeout=timedelta(seconds=30)),
        Screenshot.to_file(Path("passed.svg")),
        Quit(),
    ],
)

showing is that WaitFor, waiting for some text to be on screen, so the step above is showing("passed"). A program on a pseudo-terminal echoes each key it's sent, so to type into one, pace the keys typed gives with a Wait, as when pacing a recording, which gives the program real time to echo each key before the next arrives, then wait for what it prints:

autopilot = [showing("$ "), *paced(typed("ls\n"), pause=Wait(timedelta(milliseconds=90))), showing("README.md"), Quit()]

Both wait in real time, and a FrozenClock runs in real time while they do, so a component that reads the clock, such as a spinner, keeps moving while the work goes on. Each step of an autopilot can pick its own kind of time: an AdvanceClock skips ahead at once, and a wait lets the time the work really takes pass. A Wait moves the clock on by exactly its duration, and a WaitFor by however long its condition took to hold.

Waiting brings real time into a frozen clock

An app under an autopilot that waits doesn't come out the same on every run, even with a FrozenClock. The frames it renders during a wait are timed by when the event loop wakes, and a WaitFor moves the clock on by however long the work took, which shifts everything the app shows of the time from then on. For screenshots and recordings that must not change between runs, such as ones checked into a repository, pace the autopilot with AdvanceClock alone.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text:
Pass app a Recording to record it to a file:

await app(search(), recording=Recording(Path("search.cast"), title="Search"))

The recording holds what the app draws on its terminal, as it draws it: the first frame in full, and each later frame as the cells that changed, which a player applies to the screen it already shows, as a terminal does. Each frame is timed by the app's clock. With the system's clock, run the app on a terminal and use it, and it records itself, with no asciinema rec around it. With a FrozenClock and an autopilot, its timing is the autopilot's AdvanceClocks and waits, so with no waits it records as fast as the app renders and comes out the same on every run, as this one, from the spinner recipe, does:

The recording also holds the screen's size when it changes, and how the app exited: 0 once it quits, and 1 if it stops with an error. While the app is suspended, the recording can't see what the program it hands the terminal to draws, so the time it spends suspended is cut out, and a suspended marker shows where.

Recording input records everything typed

Recording(input=True) records every key press, paste and mouse event the app handles, which asciinema-player can show as they're typed (its keystrokeOverlay option). That includes passwords and tokens typed into the app, in a file that's made to be shared, so it's off by default, under an autopilot too. Turn it on when you know what will be typed, as for an autopilot's demo.

docs.title: Marking chapters
docs.text:
The Marker control marks a point in the recording with a label, which asciinema-player shows on its progress bar as a chapter to jump to. An autopilot can mark each step of a demo, and a handler can return one too, such as to mark each view the user opens. An app that isn't recording ignores it. This demo of the fruit search starts each chapter with a marker, and pauses between its keys:

PAUSE = AdvanceClock(by=timedelta(milliseconds=400))


def chapter(label: str, steps: Iterable[AutopilotStep]) -> list[AutopilotStep]:
    return [Marker(label), *paced(steps, pause=PAUSE), PAUSE]


DEMO = [
    *chapter("Scroll the results", [KeyPressed(key=Key.Down)] * 2),
    *chapter("Search", [KeyPressed(key="a"), KeyPressed(key="n")]),
    *chapter("Clear the search", [KeyPressed(key=Key.Backspace)] * 2),
]


async def record_demo() -> None:
    await app(
        search(),
        headless=True,
        dimensions=(30, 8),
        clock=FrozenClock(datetime(2026, 3, 14, tzinfo=UTC)),
        recording=Recording(Path("search.cast"), input=True),
        autopilot=[*DEMO, Quit()],
    )

Notice the chapters on the player's progress bar, one for each marker, which jump to the start of their step.

docs.title: counterweight.autopilot.AutopilotStep module-attribute
docs.text:
AutopilotStep = AnyEvent | AnyControl | Wait | WaitFor

What an autopilot feeds an app: events, controls, and the steps that wait.

docs.title: counterweight.autopilot.Wait dataclass
docs.text:
Wait(duration: timedelta)

Hold the autopilot back for duration of real time, while the app keeps handling events and rendering, so work like a subprocess can make progress.

A FrozenClock runs in real time while the autopilot waits, and ends the wait exactly duration later, however late the event loop wakes from it. The frames the app renders during the wait are timed by when the event loop wakes, so a recording with them comes out a little different on every run.

To wait for work to finish, prefer WaitFor, which doesn't have to guess how long the work takes.

docs.title: duration instance-attribute
docs.text: duration: timedelta

docs.title: counterweight.autopilot.WaitFor dataclass
docs.text:
WaitFor(
    condition: Callable[[Frame], bool], timeout: timedelta
)

Hold the autopilot back until condition is true of the frame on screen, checked after each render, while the app keeps handling events and rendering, as Playwright's assertions wait for the page.

The condition receives the whole screen as a Frame, so it can look for text with frame.text(ansi=False).

A FrozenClock runs in real time while the autopilot waits, so it moves on by however long the condition took to hold, which is different on every run, as is everything the app shows of the time from then on.

RAISES DESCRIPTION AutopilotTimedOut

From app, if the condition is still false after timeout of real time.

docs.title: counterweight.autopilot.AutopilotTimedOut

docs.title: counterweight.autopilot.SETTLE_LIMIT module-attribute
docs.text:
SETTLE_LIMIT = 50

How many passes of the render loop in a row the autopilot holds its next step back while the app has work queued, before it takes the step anyway, so an app that never goes quiet, such as one streaming a program's output, doesn't stall it, as React stops a cascade of updates after 50.

AnyEvent = (
    TerminalResized
    | KeyPressed
    | Pasted
    | StateSet

    | Dummy

Any event the app handles, which an autopilot can send it beside controls.

docs.title: counterweight.events.TerminalResized dataclass
docs.text:
TerminalResized(dimensions: tuple[int, int] | None = None)

The terminal changed size, so the app lays out and draws the whole screen again. The app sends itself one when the terminal reports a resize, and an autopilot can send one to resize a headless app.

docs.title: dimensions class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
dimensions: tuple[int, int] | None = None

The new size, as (width, height) in cells, or None for the size the app was given as its dimensions, or else the terminal's size.

docs.title: counterweight.autopilot.typed
docs.text:
typed(text: str) -> list[KeyPressed]

The key presses that type text, one per grapheme cluster, as Playwright's keyboard.type does, with a newline ("\n" or "\r\n") pressing Enter, and any other control character pressing the key a terminal sends it as, such as Tab for a tab.

The keys arrive one after another. They're plain steps, so pace them, or combine them with others, with paced or iterable combinators such as more_itertools's.

docs.title: counterweight.autopilot.showing
docs.text:
showing(
    text: str, timeout: timedelta = timedelta(seconds=30)
) -> WaitFor

Waits until text is on screen, such as a program's prompt, as Playwright's toContainText does.

RAISES DESCRIPTION AutopilotTimedOut

From app, if text still isn't on screen after timeout of real time.

docs.title: counterweight.autopilot.advance
docs.text:
advance(
    by: timedelta, step: timedelta = FRAME_INTERVAL
) -> list[AdvanceClock]

Moves the app's clock on by by, step at a time, the last step taking whatever is left, so each step renders a frame and an animation plays out in a recording rather than jumping to its end, as Playwright's clock.runFor fires the timers due along the way. The default step is the interval the animation hooks read the clock at, so each step draws one of their frames.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

If by is negative, or step isn't positive.

docs.title: counterweight.autopilot.paced
docs.text:
paced(
    steps: Iterable[AutopilotStep], pause: AutopilotStep
) -> list[AutopilotStep]

steps with pause before each one: interleave(repeat(pause), steps), with the type of its steps.

Written with the combinators directly, a list of steps of different kinds, such as clicks and key presses, has nothing to say what type it is, so mypy settles on a base class its steps share, which isn't a step; passed to paced, it's checked as steps. The pause is usually an AdvanceClock, to pace a recording, or a Wait, to give a program on a pseudo-terminal real time to echo each key.

docs.title: counterweight.asciicast.Recording dataclass
docs.text:
Recording(
    path: Path,
    title: str | None = None,
    idle_time_limit: timedelta | None = None,
    theme: Theme | None = None,
    input: bool = False,
)

Record the app, as app's recording, to an asciicast v3 file at path, whether it's headless or not, which asciinema-player and asciinema play play back.

The recording holds what the app draws, as it draws it on a terminal, with each frame's time as the app's clock reads it: with a SystemClock that's real time, and with a FrozenClock only the autopilot moves it, so an autopilot can record a minute of an app in milliseconds, the same on every run unless it waits in real time. Marker marks a point in it that players can jump to.

While the app is suspended, the recording can't see what the program it hands the terminal to draws, so the time it spends suspended is cut out, and a suspended marker shows where.

Recording input records everything typed

With input, the recording holds every key press, paste and mouse event the app handles, including passwords and tokens typed into it, in a file that's made to be shared. That's why it's off by default, and stays off under an autopilot, whose input is safe to share: turn it on yourself when you know what will be typed.
