TYPE: Style DEFAULT: default

styles

How the box, the cursor and the placeholder are drawn.

TYPE: TextFieldStyles DEFAULT: TextFieldStyles()

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Counterweight uses "hooks", inspired by React hooks, to manage state and side effects in components. The headless components, such as use_text_input, are hooks too, built on these, that give a component a common control's behavior.

A component MUST call the same hooks in the same order on every render, because each hook finds its state by its position in that order. Don't call a hook inside a condition, a loop whose length can change, or after an early return. A render that calls a different hook at some position, or a different number of hooks than the previous render, raises InconsistentHookExecution.

When a component seems to need a hook only some of the time, or one hook per item, move that hook down into a child component that owns it. A parent can't conditionally call a hook, but it can conditionally render a component, and each component has its own hooks.

from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.elements import Div
from counterweight.hooks import use_state


@component
def settings() -> Div:
    is_advanced, set_advanced = use_state(False)
    if is_advanced:
        level, set_level = use_state(3)  # wrong: raises when is_advanced changes
    ...

Here the hook moves into an advanced_settings component, which settings renders only when it's needed:

@component
def advanced_settings() -> Text:
    use_focus(auto_focus=True)
    level, set_level = use_state(3)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key="+"):
                set_level(lambda level: level + 1)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(content=f"Level: {level} (+ raises it)", style=text_color("amber", 400), on_input=on_input)


@component
def settings() -> Div:
    is_advanced, set_advanced = use_state(False)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key="a"):
                set_advanced(toggle)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Text(content=f"[{'x' if is_advanced else ' '}] Advanced (a toggles it)"),
            *((advanced_settings(),) if is_advanced else ()),
        ),
    )

advanced_settings takes focus as it mounts, so it receives +, and a, which it doesn't handle, bubbles up from it to settings.

ScreenshotText 

╭──────────────────────────────╮
│ [x] Advanced (a toggles it)  │
│ Level: 5 (+ raises it)       │
╰──────────────────────────────╯

Showing advanced_settings mounts it with fresh state, and hiding it unmounts it, which discards that state. Here the level is raised to 5, and hiding and showing the advanced settings starts it over at 3:

If the state should outlive the child, keep it in the parent and pass it down instead.

The same move handles a hook per item: render a component per item, rather than calling the hook in a loop over the items. See Components for how to key those components so each one's state follows its item.

docs.title: Animation
docs.text:
Two hooks built on use_clock give a component an animation's progress, a number from 0 to 1 it draws whatever it likes from: use_progress plays once and holds at its end, and use_loop repeats. counterweight.animation holds the pure half: CSS's easing functions, which shape how an animation moves, and between, which picks one phase out of an animation, as a keyframe does.

A browser animates a property for you, given a CSS animation or transition. Here the component computes each frame itself, from the progress the hook returns, so anything it can compute from a number can move: a bar's length, a character's position, a gradient's angle.

docs.title: Playing once
docs.text:
use_progress(duration) rises from 0 when the component mounts to 1 once duration has passed, and holds there, as a CSS animation that plays once and fills forwards does:

@component
def filling_bar(plays: int) -> Text:
    # Starts again from 0 each time `plays` changes, and stops reading the clock once it's full.
    progress = use_progress(timedelta(seconds=2), deps=(plays,))
    return Text(content=bar(ease_in_out(progress)), style=text_color("teal", 400))


@component
def replayable() -> Div:
    plays, set_plays = use_state(0)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Space):
                set_plays(lambda plays: plays + 1)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1),
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(filling_bar(plays), Text(content="Space plays it again", style=text_color("slate", 400))),
    )
ScreenshotText 

████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░

Space plays it again

It starts again whenever one of its deps changes, compared with == as use_effect's are, so a component that stays mounted can play it more than once. Giving the component a new key, which remounts it, starts it again too.

Once it reaches 1, it stops reading the clock, so a finished animation re-runs its component only once more, at the next frame, and costs nothing after that. A duration of zero is at 1 at once, so a component can skip its animation, as a thumbnail that shows only the last frame would.

docs.title: Easing
docs.text:
The progress rises at a steady rate. Pass it through an Easing to shape the motion, as the bar above does with ease_in_out. These are CSS's:

  • linear, a steady rate, and piecewise_linear, straight lines between stops, as CSS's linear() function draws.
  • cubic_bezier, a curve through two control points, as CSS's cubic-bezier(), and the curves CSS names: ease, ease_in, ease_out and ease_in_out. A control point's y outside 0 to 1 overshoots, going past the end and coming back.
  • steps, which moves in equal jumps, as CSS's steps(), and step_start and step_end, which jump once.

An easing is any function from a float to a float, so a curve CSS doesn't name, such as lambda t: t**3, is one too.

Here one progress moves a dot along each track, through a different easing on each row:

EASINGS: tuple[tuple[str, Easing], ...] = (
    ("linear", linear),
    ("ease", ease),
    ("ease_in", ease_in),
    ("ease_out", ease_out),
    ("ease_in_out", ease_in_out),
    ("cubic_bezier", cubic_bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1)),  # Overshoots the end, then comes back.
    ("piecewise", piecewise_linear(0, (1, 0.6), (0.8, 0.8), 1)),  # Reaches the end early and bounces once.
    ("steps(4)", steps(4)),
    ("step_start", step_start),
    ("step_end", step_end),
)
END = WIDTH - 4  # Room past the end of the track for an easing that overshoots it.


def track(eased: float) -> str:
    position = min(max(round(eased * END), 0), WIDTH - 1)
    return "".join("●" if x == position else "·" if x <= END else " " for x in range(WIDTH))


@component
def easings() -> Div:
    plays, set_plays = use_state(0)
    # One progress, eased a different way on each row.
    progress = use_progress(timedelta(seconds=2), deps=(plays,))

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Space):
                set_plays(lambda plays: plays + 1)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col,
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            *(
                Div(
                    style=row | gap(1),
                    children=(
                        Text(content=f"{name:>12}", style=text_color("slate", 400)),
                        Text(content=track(easing(progress)), style=text_color("sky", 400)),
                    ),
                )
                for name, easing in EASINGS
            ),
            Text(content="Space plays it again", style=margin_top(1) | text_color("slate", 400)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

      linear ··········●··········   
        ease ················●····   
     ease_in ······●··············   
    ease_out ··············●······   
 ease_in_out ··········●··········   
cubic_bezier ····················· ● 
   piecewise ·················●···   
    steps(4) ··········●··········   
  step_start ····················●   
    step_end ●····················   

Space plays it again

Halfway through, linear and ease_in_out are halfway along, ease and ease_out are ahead and ease_in behind, the overshooting cubic_bezier is already past the end of its track, and the step easings are wherever their last jump left them. An easing's output isn't clamped, so the component decides what a value past 0 or 1 draws as: this one keeps room past the end of each track for the overshoot.

Something moving whole, such as a box sliding into place, usually looks best eased in and out. Something that happens at a steady rate, such as typing or a sweep, usually looks best not eased at all, since its pace is part of what it shows.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
One animation can run several motions one after another, or overlapping. between(progress, start, stop) is how far progress is through the part from start to stop: 0 before it, 1 after it, as a CSS keyframe's offsets pick out a phase. Each phase can take its own easing:

@component
def staggered() -> Div:
    progress = use_progress(timedelta(seconds=3))
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=tuple(
            # Each bar fills in its own half of the animation, a quarter after the one above it.
            Text(content=bar(ease_out(between(progress, start, start + 0.5))), style=text_color("amber", 300))
            for start in (0, 0.25, 0.5)
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

████████████████████████
███████████████████████░
████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░

docs.title: Looping
docs.text:
use_loop(period) is where in an animation that repeats every period the component is, from 0 up to 1, as a CSS animation whose iteration count is infinite is. For one that goes there and back, as animation-direction: alternate does, fold the loop's progress in half:

@component
def bouncing() -> Div:
    is_playing, set_playing = use_state(True)
    there_and_back = 1 - abs(2 * use_loop(timedelta(seconds=2), is_playing=is_playing) - 1)
    position = round(ease_in_out(there_and_back) * (WIDTH - 1))

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Space):
                set_playing(lambda is_playing: not is_playing)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1),
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Text(content="·" * position + "●" + "·" * (WIDTH - 1 - position), style=text_color("rose", 400)),
            Text(content="Space pauses and plays", style=text_color("slate", 400)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

···············●········

Space pauses and plays

With is_playing=False, the loop stops reading the clock and holds where it is. Unlike a paused CSS animation, it doesn't resume from where it stopped: it carries on from wherever the time since it started puts it, so the dot here jumps ahead when it plays again. Like use_progress, it starts again from 0 whenever one of its deps changes. A loop that starts while it isn't playing, as it mounts or as its deps change, holds at 0 and starts when it plays, as a CSS animation that starts paused does.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
While an animation moves, its hook reads the clock every interval, FRAME_INTERVAL unless it's given another, which is 20 frames a second. Each frame re-runs the component that calls the hook, and nothing else, so call it in the component that draws the animation, not in one that also renders things that don't change with it (see Performance).

Every animation counts from when it started, on the app's clock, so on a FrozenClock it moves only when an autopilot moves the clock. advance moves it on a frame at a time, so a recording or a test shows each frame rather than jumping to the end, as the recordings on this page do (see Autopilot and Recording).

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.use_progress
docs.text:
use_progress(
    duration: timedelta,
    deps: tuple[object, ...] = (),
    *,
    interval: timedelta = FRAME_INTERVAL,
) -> float

How far through an animation duration long the calling component is, from 0 when it starts, rising to 1, where it holds, as a CSS animation that plays once and fills forwards does. Shape the motion by passing the result to an easing function.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION duration

How long the animation takes. Zero ends it as soon as it starts, at 1.

TYPE: timedelta

deps

The values the animation depends on. It starts when the component mounts, and again whenever any of them change (compared with ==), as use_effect runs again, so a component that stays mounted can play it more than once.

TYPE: tuple[object, ...] DEFAULT: ()

interval

How often it reads the clock while it moves. Once it reaches 1 it stops reading the clock, so a finished animation re-runs its component only once more, at the next interval, and never after that.

TYPE: timedelta DEFAULT: FRAME_INTERVAL

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

If duration is negative.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.use_loop
docs.text:
use_loop(
    period: timedelta,
    deps: tuple[object, ...] = (),
    *,
    is_playing: bool = True,
    interval: timedelta = FRAME_INTERVAL,
) -> float

Where in an animation that repeats every period the calling component is, from 0 up to (but not including) 1, as a CSS animation whose iteration count is infinite is.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION period

How long one time through the animation takes.

TYPE: timedelta

deps

The values the animation depends on. It starts when the component mounts, and again from 0 whenever any of them change (compared with ==).

TYPE: tuple[object, ...] DEFAULT: ()

is_playing

Whether it moves. While it doesn't, it stops reading the clock, holding where it is. One that starts while it isn't playing, as it mounts or as its deps change, holds at 0 and starts when it plays. Unlike a paused CSS animation, one paused partway doesn't resume from there: it carries on from wherever the time since it started puts it.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: True

interval

How often it reads the clock while it plays.

TYPE: timedelta DEFAULT: FRAME_INTERVAL

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

If period isn't positive.

docs.text:
piecewise_linear(
    *stops: float
    | tuple[float, float]
    | tuple[float, float, float],
) -> Easing

Moves in straight lines between stops, as CSS's linear() function does.

Each stop is an output alone, an (output, input) pair, or an (output, start, end) triple, which holds the output from the input start to end, as linear(0, 0.25 75%, 1) is piecewise_linear(0, (0.25, 0.75), 1). As in CSS, the first stop's input defaults to 0 and the last's to 1, an input less than an earlier stop's is raised to it, and stops without inputs are spread evenly between the stops on either side that have them.

If there are fewer than two stops.

docs.title: use_clock
docs.text:
use_clock gives a component the time, so it can show a clock, an uptime, or a timer while staying pure. A component that reads the time any other way, such as with datetime.now(), keeps showing the time from whenever it last ran.

@component
def wall_clock() -> Text:
    tick = use_clock(timedelta(minutes=1))
    return Text(content=f"{tick.now:%H:%M %Z}", style=text_color("amber", 400))


@component
def uptime() -> Text:
    tick = use_clock(timedelta(seconds=1))
    seconds = tick.since_start // timedelta(seconds=1)
    return Text(content=f"Up {seconds // 3600}:{seconds // 60 % 60:02}:{seconds % 60:02}")


@component
def status_bar() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | justify_children_space_between | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
        children=(uptime(), wall_clock()),
    )
ScreenshotText 

╭──────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Up 1:02:05                 16:11 UTC │
╰──────────────────────────────────────╯

docs.title: Ticks
docs.text:
Each call reads the clock every interval. A component takes a reading when it mounts, and again on its first render after each new tick starts, re-running then if nothing else made it. Every render in between gets the same reading, so re-running the component for any other reason doesn't change what it shows.

Ticks start at whole multiples of interval on the wall clock, so wall_clock re-runs as the minute turns, along with uptime, rather than a minute after the app started. Components that take a reading in the same frame get the same one, so two clocks on screen never disagree.

Each tick re-runs the components that read the clock and nothing else, so call use_clock in the component that shows the time, not in one that also renders things that don't change with it. See Performance.

docs.title: Time zones
docs.text:
The app's clock reads the wall-clock time in UTC, so an app shows the same time wherever it runs unless it asks for another zone. Give app a SystemClock with a timezone to read the time in that zone instead:

await app(status_bar(), clock=SystemClock(timezone=ZoneInfo("America/New_York")))

Ticks follow the clock's zone too, so an interval of a day ticks at that zone's midnight. Converting a UTC reading with tick.now.astimezone(zone) shows the right time, but its ticks still start on UTC's boundaries: a day-long tick at UTC's midnight rather than the zone's, and an hour-long tick off the zone's hour where it's offset by a fraction of one, such as India's.

docs.title: Timing from an event
docs.text:
since_mount is how long the component has been mounted. To time something from an event, such as a key press, render a component that reads the clock and give it a new key when the event happens, which remounts it and starts its since_mount again from zero:

@component
def lap_time() -> Text:
    elapsed = use_clock(timedelta(seconds=1)).since_mount
    return Text(content=f"{elapsed // timedelta(seconds=1)} s")


@component
def lap_timer() -> Div:
    laps, set_laps = use_state(1)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Space):
                set_laps(lambda laps: laps + 1)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=row | gap(1),
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Text(content=f"Lap {laps}:", style=text_color("slate", 400)),
            # A new key each lap remounts lap_time, so its time since mounting starts again from zero.
            lap_time().with_key(str(laps)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

Lap 2: 42 s

Each press of Space starts the next lap from zero:

A handler sees the reading from the latest tick, so a time it records, such as the lap time when a lap ends, is up to one interval early. Choose an interval as fine as the precision the time needs. A timer that can be paused and resumed loses up to that much on each pause, since it carries the time recorded at the pause into the next run.

docs.title: Pausing
docs.text: An interval of None stops the component reading the clock, as a null delay pauses React's useInterval: every render returns the last reading, and the clock never re-runs the component. The render that gives it an interval again takes a fresh reading, so a component that stops reading the clock for an hour doesn't show the time from an hour ago when it starts again. Pause a clock a component reads only while something is moving, such as an animation that has finished, so it costs nothing while nothing moves. The animation hooks pause their clocks that way.

docs.title: Why compute from elapsed time?
docs.text:
Compute whatever changes over time, such as an animation frame or a countdown, from since_mount or since_start. Don't keep a running total in state and add to it each tick:

@component
def spinner() -> Text:
    frame, set_frame = use_state(0)

    async def step() -> None:
        while True:
            await sleep(0.1)
            set_frame(lambda frame: frame + 1)  # wrong: falls further behind each step

    use_effect(step, deps=())

    return Text(content="|/-\\"[frame % 4])

Each step counts a full interval, but takes longer: sleep wakes up late, and a render and any other work run before the next step starts. The total falls behind the real elapsed time by a little more each step, and the gap only grows. Measured on an otherwise idle event loop, steps of 10 ms counted 2 seconds when 2.05 had passed. Adding up the real time between steps instead fixes the drift, but anything that misses a step or repeats one, such as an effect that restarts, still breaks the total.

Elapsed time from use_clock is the difference between two readings of a monotonic clock, so a value computed from it can't drift, however long the component runs:

@component
def spinner() -> Text:
    frame = use_clock(timedelta(milliseconds=100)).since_mount // timedelta(milliseconds=100)
    return Text(content="|/-\\"[frame % 4])

It also needs no state or effect, so a tick re-renders once instead of twice.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Pass a FrozenClock to app to fix the time, and move it on with AdvanceClock in the autopilot, so a test or a screenshot doesn't depend on when it runs or how long it takes:

async def test_the_lap_timer_counts_from_the_last_lap() -> None:
    await app(
        lap_timer(),
        headless=True,
        clock=FrozenClock(datetime(2026, 3, 14, 15, 9, 26, tzinfo=UTC)),
        autopilot=[
            AdvanceClock(by=timedelta(seconds=75)),
            KeyPressed(key=Key.Space),
            AdvanceClock(by=timedelta(seconds=42)),
            Screenshot.to_file(Path("lap-timer.txt")),
            Quit(),
        ],
        check_purity=True,
    )

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.use_clock
docs.text:
use_clock(interval: timedelta | None) -> Tick
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION interval

How often the component reads the clock. Ticks start at whole multiples of interval past midnight on the wall clock, in the clock's timezone (for an interval that divides a day), so components reading the clock every second and every minute both re-run as the minute turns. None stops reading it, as a null delay pauses React's useInterval: every render returns the last reading, and the clock never re-runs the component, until a render gives it an interval again, which takes a fresh reading.

TYPE: timedelta | None

RETURNS DESCRIPTION Tick

A reading of the app's clock, taken when the component mounts, and again on the first render after each new tick starts, with the component re-running then if nothing else made it. Between those, every render returns the same reading, so the component's output stays a function of its arguments and hooks. Components that take a reading in the same frame get the same one, whatever their intervals.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

If interval isn't positive.

docs.title: use_controls
docs.text:
An input handler acts on the app by returning controls, but an effect, or a callback that a program or a timer calls, has no event to return them for. use_controls gives a component a sender that hands the app a control from anywhere. Here an effect scrolls a test run's first failure into view once the log has rendered, as a React effect calls scrollIntoView on an element through a ref:

@component
def results_log(lines: tuple[str, ...] = LOG) -> Div:
    first_failure, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)
    send_control = use_controls()
    failure_index = next((i for i, line in enumerate(lines) if line.startswith("FAIL")), None)

    async def show_first_failure() -> None:
        if failure_index is not None:
            send_control(ScrollIntoView(first_failure, block="center"))

    use_effect(show_first_failure, deps=(failure_index,))

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1) | size(42, 7) | overflow_y_scroll,
        on_input=scroll_on_wheel(),
        children=tuple(
            Text(
                content=line,
                style=text_color("red" if line.startswith("FAIL") else "slate", 400),
                handle=first_failure if i == failure_index else None,
            )
            for i, line in enumerate(lines)
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ ok   tests/test_geometry.py            │
│ ok   tests/test_hooks.py               │
│ FAIL tests/test_layout.py::test_wraps  │
│      expected 3 lines, got 4           │
│ ok   tests/test_output.py              │
╰────────────────────────────────────────╯

The log opens with its failure in the middle of the view, rather than at its start, where the failure would be out of sight. The effect depends on failure_index, so it scrolls again only when a different line is the first failure, and leaves the log where the reader scrolled it otherwise.

The multiplexer example sends Quit when its last pane's shell exits, and moves focus with FocusNext when the focused pane's shell exits.

The app handles a sent control as it handles one a handler returns, after the events already waiting, so state set just before sending it changes the same frame the control does. Every render returns an equal sender, so it can be left out of an effect's deps.

docs.title: use_effect
docs.text:
use_effect runs an async function, the effect's setup, alongside a component: it starts after the frame that mounts the component is painted, and starts again whenever its dependencies change. Effects are for work that takes time or reaches outside the tree, such as fetching data, subscribing to something, or running a program, so that rendering stays pure. An effect usually ends by setting state, which renders what it found.

FOREDEMOS = {
    "Lisbon": "Sunny, 24°C",
    "Oslo": "Light snow, -3°C",
    "Lima": "Overcast, 18°C",
}


async def fetch_forecast(city: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)  # Stands in for a request to a weather service.
    return FOREDEMOS[city]


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Fetched:
    city: str
    summary: str


@component
def forecast(city: str) -> Text:
    fetched, set_fetched = use_state(Fetched(city="", summary=""))

    async def fetch() -> None:
        set_fetched(Fetched(city=city, summary=await fetch_forecast(city)))

    use_effect(fetch, deps=(city,))

    if fetched.city != city:
        return Text(content=f"Fetching {city}...", style=text_color("slate", 400))

    return Text(content=fetched.summary, style=text_color("amber", 400))


@component
def weather() -> Div:
    cities = tuple(FOREDEMOS)
    selected, set_selected = use_state(0)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Right):
                set_selected(lambda i: (i + 1) % len(cities))
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Left):
                set_selected(lambda i: (i - 1) % len(cities))
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | gap(2),
                children=tuple(
                    Text(content=city, style=text_bg("sky", 800) if i == selected else text_color("slate", 400))
                    for i, city in enumerate(cities)
                ),
            ),
            forecast(cities[selected]),
        ),
    )
FetchedFetching, after Right ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────╮
│ Lisbon  Oslo  Lima         │
│ Sunny, 24°C                │
╰────────────────────────────╯
ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────╮
│ Lisbon  Oslo  Lima         │
│ Fetching Oslo...           │
╰────────────────────────────╯

forecast fetches the forecast for its city when it mounts, and again each time city changes, since city is in its deps. It keeps the city each summary is for, so right after Right selects Oslo, it shows that Oslo's forecast is on its way, rather than Lisbon's forecast under Oslo's name.

A change of city also cancels the fetch already in flight, so pressing Right twice quickly never shows Oslo's forecast once Lima is selected, however late Oslo's answer would have arrived. React's effects need an ignore flag set in their cleanup function for that; here, the cancelled fetch never reaches its set_fetched.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
deps says when the effect starts again:

  • A tuple of values starts it again on each render where any of them changed, compared with ==. List every value the effect reads that can change between renders: arguments, state, and anything computed from them. An effect that reads a value left out keeps using the value from the render that started it.
  • () starts it once, when the component mounts, and keeps it running until the component unmounts.
  • None, the default, starts it again on every render of the component.

A setter from use_state and the sender from use_controls are the same on every render, so they can be left out. An effect that runs for a long time and updates state from its previous value should pass the setter a function, since the state it closed over doesn't change (see An effect that outlives its render).

To do something on a schedule, such as animating or counting down, read the time with use_clock instead of sleeping in a loop in an effect (see Why compute from elapsed time?).

docs.title: Cleaning up
docs.text:
Where a React effect returns a cleanup function, a Counterweight effect is cancelled: it runs as an asyncio.Task, which is cancelled when its component unmounts or its dependencies change (see Effect Cancellation). The cancellation raises CancelledError at whatever await the effect is waiting on, so cleanup goes in a finally block:

@component
def service_status(url: str) -> Text:
    status, set_status = use_state("connecting")

    async def watch() -> None:
        connection = await connect(url)
        try:
            while True:
                set_status(await connection.status())
                await asyncio.sleep(5)
        finally:
            await connection.close()

    use_effect(watch, deps=(url,))

    return Text(content=status)

The next frame waits for every cancelled effect to finish, so keep cleanup quick, and don't catch CancelledError without raising it again: an effect that swallows its cancellation and returns fails the app with a RuntimeError, and one that keeps going holds up every frame after it.

docs.title: Effect Cancellation
docs.text:
Effects are canceled by the framework when one of the following conditions is met:

  • The component that created the effect is unmounted.
  • The effect's dependencies change and the effect's setup function is going to be re-run.

Effect cancellation is synchronous

Note that the effect is synchronously cancelled (i.e., the Task that represents the effect is cancelled and then awaited; see this discussion) before the next render cycle starts. Assuming that you do not mess with the cancellation yourself from inside the effect setup function, the effect will definitely stop running before the next frame is rendered.

Within a render, every effect that is being cancelled is cancelled concurrently, and all of them finish before any effect's setup function starts, so an effect that holds something exclusive (a subscription, a terminal mode) releases it before its own re-run or a sibling's effect can acquire it.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: An autopilot hands the app its next step as soon as the last one has rendered, without waiting for effects. To check what an effect shows, wait for it with WaitFor, as the screenshots above wait for Sunny to appear on screen (see Waiting for real work).

TYPE: Setup

docs.title: use_focus
docs.text:
Each key press goes to one element: the focused one. A component becomes focusable by calling use_focus, and when it's focused, its top-level element, the one it returns, receives every key press first. The key then bubbles to that element's ancestors, until a handler returns something other than None. When nothing is focused, key presses go to the root component's element alone.

This page covers making components focusable and moving focus between them. How a key press travels once it reaches the focused element is on the Events page.

docs.title: Making a component focusable
docs.text:
@component
def counter() -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(auto_focus=True)
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Up):
                set_count(lambda count: count + 1)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=str(count),
        style=text_bg("indigo", 700) if focus.is_focused else default,
        on_input=on_input,
    )

focus.is_focused says whether the component is focused, so it can draw a focus ring, and auto_focus=True focuses it when it mounts while nothing else is focused.

Put a focusable component's key handler on the element it returns. Elements inside that one never receive key presses, since they're descendants of the focused element rather than ancestors. For the same reason, a component deep in the tree can't own a global shortcut: a help overlay toggled with ? puts that binding on the root component's element, or on an ancestor of whatever is focused, which every key press bubbles through unless a handler below it stops it.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
This order form uses every way focus moves. Its fields take keys rather than text: the size and the wrapping paper cycle with Left and Right, the quantity steps with Up and Down, and gift wrap toggles with Space.

SIZES = ("Small", "Medium", "Large")
PAPERS = ("Stripes", "Dots", "Plain")
TIPS = ("Enter moves to the next field", "Press a label to focus its field", "Tab stays inside the dialog")


def marked(focus: Focus, content: str) -> str:
    return f"{'▸' if focus.is_focused else ' '} {content}"


def field_style(focus: Focus, is_focusable: bool = True) -> Style:
    if not is_focusable:
        return text_color("slate", 600)
    return text_bg("indigo", 700) | text_color("slate", 50) if focus.is_focused else text_color("slate", 300)


@component
def choice_field(
    options: tuple[str, ...], handle: FocusHandle, auto_focus: bool = False, is_focusable: bool = True
) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(auto_focus=auto_focus, handle=handle, is_focusable=is_focusable)
    index, set_index = use_state(0)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Left):
                set_index(lambda i: (i - 1) % len(options))
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Right):
                set_index(lambda i: (i + 1) % len(options))
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=marked(focus, f"< {options[index]} >"),
        style=field_style(focus, is_focusable),
        on_input=first(on_input, focus_receiver_on_press),
    )


@component
def quantity_field(handle: FocusHandle) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(handle=handle)
    quantity, set_quantity = use_state(1)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Up):
                set_quantity(lambda q: q + 1)
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Down):
                set_quantity(lambda q: max(q - 1, 1))
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=marked(focus, f"{quantity} ▴▾"),
        style=field_style(focus),
        on_input=first(on_input, focus_receiver_on_press),
    )


@component
def toggle_field(is_on: bool, set_on: Setter[bool], handle: FocusHandle) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(handle=handle)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Space):
                set_on(toggle)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=marked(focus, "[x]" if is_on else "[ ]"),
        style=field_style(focus),
        on_input=first(on_input, focus_receiver_on_press),
    )


@component
def help_panel() -> Div:
    # A press focuses it, but Enter and Tab never stop on it.
    focus = use_focus(in_focus_order=False)
    page, set_page = use_state(0)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Left):
                set_page(lambda p: (p - 1) % len(TIPS))
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Right):
                set_page(lambda p: (p + 1) % len(TIPS))
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=border
        | border_lightrounded
        | pad_x(1)
        | (border_color("indigo", 400) if focus.is_focused else border_color("slate", 600)),
        on_input=first(on_input, focus_receiver_on_press),
        children=(
            Text(
                style=position_absolute | inset_left(1) | inset_top(-1) | clip_to_border,
                content=f" {marked(focus, f'Tip {page + 1}/{len(TIPS)}')} ",
            ),
            Text(content=TIPS[page], style=text_color("slate", 400)),
        ),
    )


@component
def button(
    label: str, action: Callable[[], InputResponse], auto_focus: bool = False, handle: FocusHandle | None = None
) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(auto_focus=auto_focus, handle=handle)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
                return action()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=marked(focus, label),
        style=pad_x(1) | border | border_lightrounded | field_style(focus),
        on_input=first(on_input, each(on_click(action), focus_receiver_on_press)),
    )


dialog_box = position_absolute | inset(0) | margin_auto | fit_content_width | fit_content_height


@component
def confirmation(close: Callable[[], None], return_to: FocusHandle) -> Div:
    def close_and_return() -> InputResponse:
        close()
        return FocusOn(return_to)

    return Div(
        style=dialog_box | col | align_children_center | border | border_double | pad_x(2),
        # Tab from either button reaches this element before the form's, and cycles between the two.
        on_input=tab_focus,
        children=(
            Text(content="Place this order?"),
            Div(
                style=row | gap(1),
                children=(
                    button("Confirm", close_and_return),
                    button("Cancel", close_and_return, auto_focus=True),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )


@component
def labelled(label: str, handle: FocusHandle, field: Component) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(1),
        children=(Text(content=f"{label:<10}", on_input=focus_on_press(handle)), field),
    )


@component
def order_form() -> Div:
    size, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    quantity, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    gift_wrap, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    paper, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    submit, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    is_wrapped, set_wrapped = use_state(False)
    is_confirming, set_confirming = use_state(False)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
                return FocusNext(within=receiver.subtree)
            case _:
                return None

    def open_confirmation() -> InputResponse:
        set_confirming(True)
        # With nothing focused, the dialog's Cancel button takes focus as it mounts.
        return ClearFocus()

    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1) | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
        on_input=first(on_input, tab_focus),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col,
                children=(
                    labelled("Size", size, choice_field(SIZES, size, auto_focus=True)),
                    labelled("Quantity", quantity, quantity_field(quantity)),
                    labelled("Gift wrap", gift_wrap, toggle_field(is_wrapped, set_wrapped, gift_wrap)),
                    labelled("Paper", paper, choice_field(PAPERS, paper, is_focusable=is_wrapped)),
                ),
            ),
            help_panel(),
            Div(style=row, children=(button("Submit", open_confirmation, handle=submit),)),
            *([confirmation(close=lambda: set_confirming(False), return_to=submit)] if is_confirming else []),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Moving focus
docs.text:
Focus moves only through controls, auto_focus, and the focused component going away. No key or press does anything to focus unless a handler on its path returns a control that does:

  • FocusNext and FocusPrevious move to the next or previous component in the focus order, which is tree order, wrapping at the ends.
  • FocusOn focuses the component with a given focus handle, including one that mounts in the render its handler causes.
  • ClearFocus clears focus, so key presses go to the root component's element.

The library handlers return these for the common bindings: tab_focus for Tab and Shift+Tab, focus_receiver_on_press and focus_on_press for a press, and clear_focus for a press that should blur. An app without tab_focus on some element has no Tab navigation, and a focusable component without focus_receiver_on_press doesn't take focus when it's clicked. An app that wants Escape to clear focus binds it to ClearFocus() on its root.

Focus also changes when a render leaves the focused component unable to keep it. Unmounting it, hiding it, or making it unfocusable clears focus, rather than moving it to whichever component took the departed one's place. A component that mounts with auto_focus=True in the same render can then take focus.

Wherever focus moves, the newly focused component's element is scrolled into view in any scroll container it's in, by as little as it takes, as browsers do.

docs.title: Focusing a component you render
docs.text:
A FocusHandle names a focusable component for FocusOn. use_focus creates one on the component's first render and keeps it, but a parent that needs to focus a child it renders creates the handle itself, before the child mounts, and passes it down:

@component
def labelled_input(label: str) -> Div:
    input_handle, _ = use_state(FocusHandle)
    value, set_value = use_state("")
    return Div(
        children=(
            Text(content=label, on_input=focus_on_press(input_handle)),
            text_input(value, set_value, handle=input_handle),
        ),
    )

A child that can be focused from outside takes a handle: FocusHandle | None = None parameter and passes it on to use_focus, as text_input and the headless components do. Keep the handle in use_state: one built with FocusHandle() on every render makes use_focus raise ChangedFocusHandle on the second. Two mounted components given the same handle raise DuplicateFocusHandle. The handle never changes while the component is mounted, so it's safe in an effect's deps.

docs.title: Focusing a component as it mounts
docs.text:
A handler that adds a component can focus it too: it creates the new component's handle, keeps it in state with whatever else describes the component, and returns FocusOn with it:

@component
def notes() -> Div:
    handles, set_handles = use_state(tuple[FocusHandle, ...]())

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.ControlN):
                handle = FocusHandle()
                set_handles(lambda handles: (*handles, handle))
                return FocusOn(handle)
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(on_input=on_input, children=tuple(note(handle) for handle in handles))

The note doesn't exist until the next render, so FocusOn waits for it: a FocusOn whose handle names no component that can take focus yet focuses that component in the next render, before the frame is drawn, so the new note is focused in the first frame that shows it. It's how a browser's <dialog> focuses a field inside it as showModal() opens it. A control that moves focus after it, in the same handler or a later one before that render, wins, and a FocusOn whose component doesn't take focus in that render does nothing.

docs.title: Moving focus within part of the tree
docs.text:
FocusNext and FocusPrevious take within, a Subtree that limits them to the focusable components inside one element, including the element itself. A handler gets its own element's from its receiver, as receiver.subtree. From focus outside the subtree, they go to its first or last focusable component.

tab_focus passes its receiver's subtree, so on the root component's element it moves through the whole tree, and on a dialog's element, which Tab from a field inside the dialog bubbles to first, it keeps Tab inside the dialog. A form that moves to its next field on Enter does the same thing for Enter, from its own element's handler.

A dialog traps Tab and nothing else. A press beside it still reaches whatever is drawn there, and if focus clears while the dialog is open, because its focused field unmounted, key presses go to the root, whose tab_focus can move focus out of the dialog.

docs.title: Taking a component out of focus
docs.text:
Two parameters take a mounted, visible component partly or wholly out of focus, each like a browser attribute:

  • is_focusable=False makes it unfocusable, like disabled, for a field that's disabled until another is filled in. Nothing can focus it, and if it's focused, focus clears. It still receives the mouse events routed to it, so a press on it is still claimed by its focus_receiver_on_press, which then does nothing.
  • in_focus_order=False takes it out of the focus order only, like tabindex="-1", for a component that should take focus when it's pressed or named, but isn't a Tab stop. FocusNext and FocusPrevious skip it, while FocusOn, auto_focus and a press still focus it, and it keeps focus once it has it. From it, FocusNext and FocusPrevious move to its neighbors in tree order.

Either way the component keeps its focus handle and its place in tree order, so it's back in the focus order where it was when the parameter flips back, though making a component focusable again doesn't focus it. They're parameters, rather than a use_focus call to skip, because a component can't call a hook conditionally.

docs.title: When focus changes
docs.text:
Every key press in a batch of input is routed with the focus as it is when it arrives, so a Tab followed by a letter delivers the letter to the newly focused component. A key press that mounts an auto_focus component, or that mounts one and returns FocusOn for it, doesn't send the next key press in its batch there, since the component doesn't exist until the next render.

A control that moves focus re-renders the components that gained and lost focus, as a state change would, so is_focused is current on the next frame. When a render moves focus itself, to an auto_focus component that mounted or to the component a FocusOn waited for, or away from a focused component that unmounted, hid, or became unfocusable, the components that gained and lost focus re-render before the frame is drawn, so an auto_focus component is focused in the first frame that shows it. An auto_focus component that hides itself because it gained focus would move focus again, so it raises UnsettledFocus instead, and so does one that a waiting FocusOn focuses. One that a control focuses and that hides itself because it gained focus loses focus in the same render, like any focused component that hides, and is drawn unfocused.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.use_focus
docs.text:
use_focus(
    auto_focus: bool = False,
    handle: FocusHandle | None = None,
    is_focusable: bool = True,
    in_focus_order: bool = True,
) -> Focus

Makes the calling component focusable. Its top-level element, the one it returns, is the one that's focused, so a component that handles key presses puts its handler on that element. A component can call it only once.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION auto_focus

Whether the component takes focus when it mounts visible and focusable while nothing is focused, or inside the focused component while that one is out of the focus order, as an element with autofocus takes focus from a document's body, which no Tab reaches either. When several mount in the same render, the first in tree order takes focus. A component that mounts hidden or unfocusable doesn't take focus when it's shown or made focusable later.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

handle

The handle that names the component, which a parent creates with use_state(FocusHandle) to focus a child it renders with FocusOn. If None, use_focus creates one on the first render and keeps it. Every render MUST pass the same handle as the first, or use_focus raises ChangedFocusHandle, and two mounted components given the same handle raise DuplicateFocusHandle.

TYPE: FocusHandle | None DEFAULT: None

is_focusable

Whether the component can be focused, like a browser's disabled attribute when False. Nothing can focus an unfocusable component, and making the focused component unfocusable clears focus. It still receives the mouse events routed to it.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: True

in_focus_order

Whether FocusNext and FocusPrevious stop on the component, like a browser's tabindex="-1" when False. A component out of the focus order can still be focused with FocusOn, auto_focus, or a press, and keeps focus once it has it, until an auto_focus component mounts inside it.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: True

RETURNS DESCRIPTION Focus

Whether the component is focused, and its handle, which is the same object on every render.

FocusHandle()

An opaque token that names one focusable component, for FocusOn.

It's an identity token, equal only to itself, so it can exist before the component it names has mounted: a parent creates one with use_state(FocusHandle) and passes it to the child's use_focus.

docs.title: counterweight.focus.Subtree dataclass
docs.text:
Subtree(key: NodeKey = next_node_key())

An opaque name for an element and its descendants, which FocusNext and FocusPrevious take to move focus only among the focusable components inside it. ScrollTo, ScrollBy, ScrollIntoView, page_down and page_up take one in place of an ElementHandle, to name the element itself, so a handler can scroll its own element without a handle. A handler gets its own element's from its Receiver.

Subtree() names nothing mounted, as a fresh FocusHandle does until a component takes it, so a test can build a Receiver to call a handler with directly; a control naming it moves nothing.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.DuplicateUseFocus
docs.text: Raised when a component calls use_focus more than once, since every call would name the same node.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.ChangedFocusHandle
docs.text: Raised when a component passes use_focus a different handle from the one its first run passed, usually because its parent builds a new FocusHandle() on every render rather than keeping one in use_state.

docs.title: counterweight.focus.DuplicateFocusHandle
docs.text: Raised when two mounted components are given the same FocusHandle, which leaves it naming neither.

docs.title: counterweight.focus.UnsettledFocus
docs.text: Raised when re-rendering the components whose focus a render changed changes focus again, which only a component that hides itself because it gained focus can cause: one that lost focus already rendered unfocused if it became unfocusable, and draws nothing if it's hidden.

docs.title: use_hovered
docs.text:
use_hovered tells a component whether the mouse is over the element it returns, as CSS's :hover does, so it can highlight itself under the pointer:

@component
def menu_item(label: str) -> Text:
    hovered = use_hovered()

    return Text(
        content=f"{'>' if hovered.border else ' '} {label}",
        style=pad_right(1) | (text_bg("sky", 800) if hovered.border else text_color("slate", 300)),
    )


@component
def menu() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | fit_content_width,
        children=tuple(menu_item(label) for label in ("New file", "Open...", "Save", "Save as...", "Quit")),
    )
ScreenshotText 

╭─────────────╮         
│  New file   │         
│  Open...    │         
│> Save       │         
│  Save as... │         
│  Quit       │         
╰─────────────╯

The highlight follows the pointer down the menu, and goes away when the pointer leaves it:

docs.title: Which box the mouse is in
docs.text:
Hovered reports each of the element's boxes, from its content box out to its margin box, so a component can tell the mouse over its border from the mouse over its content. Each box holds the ones inside it, so the mouse in the content box is in all four:

@component
def boxes() -> Div:
    hovered = use_hovered()

    return Div(
        style=col
        | margin(1)
        | margin_color("slate", 800)
        | border
        | border_lightrounded
        | (border_color("amber", 400) if hovered.border else None)
        | pad(1)
        | padding_color("slate", 700)
        | content_color("slate", 900)
        | fit_content_width,
        children=tuple(
            Text(
                content=f"{name:<7} {'yes' if is_hovered else 'no'}",
                style=text_color("emerald" if is_hovered else "slate", 400),
            )
            for name, is_hovered in (
                ("content", hovered.content),
                ("padding", hovered.padding),
                ("border", hovered.border),
                ("margin", hovered.margin),
            )
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

 ╭─────────────╮        
 │             │        
 │ content no  │        
 │ padding yes │        
 │ border  yes │        
 │ margin  yes │        
 │             │        
 ╰─────────────╯

Here the pointer crosses the margin, the border and the padding into the content, then leaves through the bottom:

Only the parts of the element that are painted count: the mouse over a part of it that an ancestor clips away, such as a row scrolled out of a scroll container, is outside all four boxes (see Clipping and the mouse).

docs.title: When it renders again
docs.text: use_hovered is built on use_mouse and use_rects, so a component that calls it renders again on every move of the mouse, wherever it is on the screen, and whenever its boxes move. It reports where the boxes were in the previous frame, as use_rects does, so the mouse over a box that just moved is checked against where it was drawn.

docs.title: use_memo
docs.text:
use_memo keeps a value from one render to the next, computing it again only when its dependencies change. Use it for:

  • An expensive value derived from arguments or state, such as a sorted or filtered list.
  • An unchanging part of a component's output. A component that returns the same element object as last render keeps the components inside it from re-running.
  • A handler passed to a memo component. A handler defined inline is a new object every render, so the memo component's arguments never equal last render's.
@component
def file_list(paths: tuple[str, ...]) -> Div:
    use_focus(auto_focus=True)
    descending, set_descending = use_state(False)

    ordered = use_memo(lambda: sorted(paths, reverse=descending), deps=(paths, descending))

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key="r"):
                set_descending(toggle)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col,
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Text(content=f"{'Z to A' if descending else 'A to Z'} (r reverses)", style=text_color("slate", 400)),
            *(Text(content=path) for path in ordered),
        ),
    )


@component
def browser() -> Div:
    tick = use_clock(timedelta(seconds=1))
    seconds = tick.since_mount // timedelta(seconds=1)

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
        children=(
            Text(content=f"Open for {seconds} s", style=text_color("amber", 400)),
            file_list(PATHS),
        ),
    )

browser re-runs every second to show how long it's been open, and each of those renders re-runs file_list with it (see Which components run in a frame?). file_list sorts paths again only when paths or descending changes, as pressing r did above, not on every render its parent causes.

A handler to keep stable is use_memo(lambda: handler, deps).

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
deps has to list every value compute reads that can change between renders: arguments, state, and anything computed from them. A value left out keeps the cached result from updating when it changes. For a cached handler, that means the handler keeps acting on the value it captured when it was cached. When a handler only needs the latest state to compute the next state, pass a function to the setter (set_count(lambda count: count + 1)), which needs no dependency on count.

Since hooks are found by their position, use_memo can't be called once per item in a loop whose length can change. To cache something per item, render a component per item and call use_memo in it, or declare that component memo.

Passing check_purity=True to app in tests catches a missing dependency: each use_memo whose deps didn't change also calls compute, and raises StaleMemo if the result differs from the cached value. Handlers are compared by their code and the values they captured, as in Keeping components pure.

docs.title: use_memo or functools.lru_cache?
docs.text:
Both cache a computed value, but they differ in who owns it. A use_memo value belongs to one mounted component. An lru_cache value belongs to a function, and every caller in the process shares it. So cache a pure function of its arguments with lru_cache, and use use_memo for a value that belongs to the component.

use_memo lru_cache Shared by One component instance Every caller, across instances, renders and apps Keeps One value, for the latest deps Up to maxsize values, keyed by arguments Freed When the component unmounts When evicted, or never with maxsize=None Hits when deps equal last render's (==) The arguments equal a cached call's (hash, then ==) Goes stale when compute reads a value missing from deps The function reads something besides its arguments Defined Inside the component At module level

Prefer lru_cache when:

  • The computation reads only its arguments. Its key is its dependency list, so that list can't be incomplete.
  • Many components compute the same thing, such as rows formatting the same column widths. They all share one cache.
  • The inputs alternate, such as a sort order toggled back and forth. lru_cache keeps both results, while use_memo keeps one and recomputes on every toggle.

The file_list above, rewritten that way:

from functools import lru_cache


@lru_cache(maxsize=64)
def sorted_paths(paths: tuple[str, ...], descending: bool) -> tuple[str, ...]:
    return tuple(sorted(paths, reverse=descending))


@component
def file_list(paths: tuple[str, ...]) -> Div:
    use_focus(auto_focus=True)
    descending, set_descending = use_state(False)

    ordered = sorted_paths(paths, descending)
    ...

Prefer use_memo when:

  • The value captures the component's state or setters, as a handler does.
  • The inputs can't be hashed, such as lists, dicts and most mutable objects.
  • The value should go away with the component. A module-level cache keeps every argument and result it holds alive until they're evicted, and carries them between tests and between apps run in the same process.
  • The value is part of the component's output, such as an element whose children shouldn't re-run. That's meant for one instance, not for every instance that happens to pass equal arguments.
  • Each instance computes from its own input, such as a document per message in a transcript. A render with more instances than the cache's maxsize asks for more keys than it holds, in the same order every render, so each key is evicted before it's asked for again and nothing hits. use_memo keeps one value per instance, however many instances there are.

Don't put lru_cache on a function defined inside a component: every render defines a new function with an empty cache, so it never hits.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.use_memo
docs.text:
use_memo(
    compute: Getter[T], deps: tuple[object, ...]
) -> T
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION compute

A zero-argument function that computes the value. It runs while the component renders: on the first render, and on every render whose deps changed.

TYPE: Getter[T]

deps

The values compute depends on. If any of them change (compared with ==), compute runs again. () computes the value once, when the component mounts. Unlike use_effect's, these can't be None: to compute on every render, don't use this hook.

TYPE: tuple[object, ...]

RETURNS DESCRIPTION T

The value compute returned when deps last changed. It is the same object on every render until then, so an element returned from it keeps the components below it from re-running, and a handler returned from it can be passed to a memo component without making it re-run. The cached value MUST depend only on deps; check_purity on counterweight._app.app catches a value that goes stale.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.StaleMemo
docs.text: Raised when check_purity is on and a use_memo whose deps didn't change computes something different from the value it cached, so the computation depends on something missing from its deps and the cached value is stale.

docs.title: use_mouse
docs.text:
use_mouse gives a component the state of the mouse wherever it is on the screen: where it is, how far it just moved, and which button is held. Each mouse move or press renders the component again with the new state.

@component
def pointer() -> Div:
    mouse = use_mouse()
    is_on_screen = mouse.absolute.x >= 0

    return Div(
        style=full,
        children=(
            Text(
                content=(
                    f"At {mouse.absolute.x},{mouse.absolute.y}"
                    f", moved {mouse.motion.x:+},{mouse.motion.y:+}"
                    f", button {mouse.button}"
                ),
                style=text_color("slate", 400),
            ),
            *(
                (
                    Text(
                        content="●" if mouse.button is not None else "◆",
                        style=position_absolute
                        | inset_left(mouse.absolute.x)
                        | inset_top(mouse.absolute.y)
                        | text_color("red" if mouse.button is not None else "amber", 400),
                    ),
                )
                if is_on_screen
                else ()
            ),
        ),
    )
MovingWith a button held ScreenshotText 

At 12,4, moved +2,+1, button None       



            ◆
ScreenshotText 

At 13,5, moved +3,+2, button 1          




             ●

The marker follows the pointer, and turns into a dot while a button is held:

absolute counts cells from the top-left corner of the screen, whatever component reads it. To find the mouse within an element, subtract the element's position from use_rects, as in mouse.absolute - rects.content.top_left. Until the mouse first moves over the app, absolute is Position(-1, -1), off the screen, which is why pointer checks is_on_screen before drawing the marker.

Every component that calls use_mouse renders again on every move of the mouse, wherever it is, so call it in the small component that shows the mouse, not in one that renders much else. To know only whether the mouse is over a component, use use_hovered.

use_mouse vs. on_input

use_mouse and an element's on_input handler both see the mouse, but use_mouse is a hook and on_input is an event handler. use_mouse is more efficient when a component depends only on the current state of the mouse (e.g., the current position, or whether a button is currently pressed), while on_input is more convenient when a component needs to respond to changes in the mouse state, (e.g., a button release (MouseUp). use_mouse sees every change, while a handler sees only the events routed to its element. See the draggable components recipe for a handler that follows the mouse.

docs.title: use_rects
docs.text:
use_rects tells a component where the element it returns is on the screen, as Rects: the regions of its content, padding, border and margin boxes, and how much of it its ancestors' clips leave visible. A component can fit what it shows to the space layout gives it, as a CSS container query does. Here each label shortens a path to fit its own width:

def shortened(path: str, width: int) -> str:
    """`path` with as many leading directories as it takes to fit in `width` cells replaced by `…`."""
    parts = path.split("/")
    for start in range(len(parts)):
        candidate = "/".join(("…", *parts[start:]) if start else parts)
        if len(candidate) <= width:
            return candidate
    return parts[-1][:width]


@component
def path_label(path: str) -> Text:
    width = use_rects().content.width
    return Text(
        content=shortened(path, width), style=full_width | min_width(0) | text_wrap_none | text_color("amber", 400)
    )


@component
def split() -> Div:
    left_width, set_left_width = use_state(24)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Left):
                set_left_width(lambda width: max(width - 4, 8))
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Right):
                set_left_width(lambda width: min(width + 4, 40))
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    pane = border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1)

    return Div(
        style=row,
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Div(style=pane | width(left_width), children=(path_label(PATH),)),
            Div(style=pane | fill(1), children=(path_label(PATH),)),
        ),
    )

╭──────────────────────────────────╮╭──────────╮
│ src/counterweight/focus.py       ││ focus.py │
╰──────────────────────────────────╯╰──────────╯

Left and Right move the border between the panes, and each label follows its pane's width:

The label's width comes from its pane, never from its text, so the path it shows can't change the width it reads. full_width stretches it across its pane, and min_width(0) lets it be narrower than its text (see Content sets a minimum size).

Use use_hovered for detecting hover state

use_rects is a low-level hook. For the common use case of detecting whether the mouse is hovering over an element, use the higher-level use_hovered hook instead.

docs.title: Measuring another element
docs.text: Given an ElementHandle, use_rects reports the rectangles of the element with that handle instead of the calling component's own top-level element, as a React component measures an element through a ref and a ResizeObserver. That's how a component measures an element a child component draws, such as the viewport of a scroll_area it passes the handle to as viewport. The handle comes from use_state(ElementHandle), so it's the same on every render. A handle that named no visible element in the previous render reports empty rectangles, as the first render does.

docs.title: When it renders again
docs.text: use_rects reports the previous frame's rectangles, and a component that calls it renders again as soon as any of the rectangles it read move, whether its own state changed or something else, such as a sibling growing, moved them. In the example, a key press moves the border between the panes in one frame, and the labels fit their new widths in the next. A component whose size depends on the rectangles it reads should settle: one that grows whenever it reads its own size renders without end.

docs.title: use_ref
docs.text: use_ref keeps a mutable box, a Ref, for as long as the component is mounted. Changing ref.current doesn't render anything, which is what sets a ref apart from state: it holds what the component needs to remember but doesn't show.

docs.title: Using a ref outside of rendering
docs.text:
Read and write current in handlers and effects, which run after a render, not while rendering.

@component
def line_entry() -> Text:
    use_focus(auto_focus=True)
    typed = use_ref(list[str]())
    line, set_line = use_state("")

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
                set_line("".join(typed.current))
                typed.current.clear()
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=key) if len(key) == 1:
                typed.current.append(key)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=f"Last line: {line}",
        style=border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1) | text_color("amber", 400),
        on_input=on_input,
    )
ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────╮
│ Last line: hello           │
╰────────────────────────────╯

line_entry collects keys without rendering, and renders only when Enter sets line. Rendering reads line, never typed, so the screen above still shows hello with wor typed since. Typing changes nothing on screen until Enter:

line_entry shows a ref, not how to take text: it has no cursor or Backspace, and drops pastes. For a field, use use_text_input.

Refs fit:

  • Values a handler builds up before it sets state, as typed does above.
  • Values a later event needs before the next render, such as where a drag began: a handler sees the state of the render that built it, so an event handled in the same batch as the one that set the state doesn't see the new value.
  • Objects outside the tree, such as a task or a client, that a handler or an effect uses.
  • Something expensive to build once, with a function as the initial value: use_ref(lambda: build_index()) calls build_index only on the first render.

docs.title: Not reading or writing a ref while rendering
docs.text:
A component has to be pure: given the same arguments and hook state, it returns the same element. A ref changes without a render, so it isn't part of that state, and a render can skip a component and keep its previous output.

Writing a ref while rendering happens once per run, and which renders run a component depends on what else changed:

@component
def counts_renders() -> Text:
    renders = use_ref(0)
    renders.current += 1
    return Text(content=f"rendered {renders.current} times")

The count goes up only on the renders that re-run counts_renders, so it says nothing reliable. Count something you can name instead, such as the events a handler saw, in state.

Reading a ref while rendering shows whatever it held when the component last ran:

@component
def shows_change(value: int) -> Text:
    previous = use_ref(value)
    text = f"{previous.current} -> {value}"
    previous.current = value
    return Text(content=text)

Once previous holds value, running shows_change again shows value -> value. Keep the previous value in state, and set it together with the current one.

Reading current once to start with, such as passing use_ref(lambda: build_index()).current to a child, is fine as long as nothing changes it afterward.

With check_purity on, the second run of every component gets copies of its refs, so assigning current there leaves the component's refs alone, and a component whose output depends on what a ref held raises ImpureComponent. The copies hold the same objects, so changing the object current holds, such as appending to a list, still reaches the component's ref.

docs.title: use_scroll
docs.text:
use_scroll tells a component how far a scroll container is scrolled, how far it can be, and how much of its content is in view, as a Scroll, which holds what the web's scrollTop, scrollHeight and clientHeight say. Counterweight draws no scrollbars, so this is how a component shows the reader where they are. Here the title counts the lines in view, and the bottom border counts the lines below them:

@component
def document(lines: tuple[str, ...] = LINES) -> Div:
    body, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)
    scroll = use_scroll(body)

    first = scroll.offset.y + 1
    last = min(scroll.offset.y + scroll.view_height, len(lines))
    percent = 100 * scroll.offset.y // scroll.max_offset.y if scroll.max_offset.y else 100

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(30, 9),
        children=(
            Text(
                content=f" Lines {first}-{last} of {len(lines)} ({percent}%) ",
                style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border | text_color("amber", 400),
            ),
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | col | pad_x(1) | overflow_y_scroll,
                handle=body,
                on_input=scroll_on_wheel(),
                children=tuple(Text(content=line) for line in lines),
            ),
            Text(
                content=f" ↓ {len(lines) - last} more " if last < len(lines) else "",
                style=position_absolute | inset_bottom(-1) | inset_right(1) | clip_to_border | text_color("slate", 400),
            ),
        ),
    )

│  9 GET /items/333 200      │
│ 10 GET /items/370 200      │
│ 11 GET /items/407 200      │

As the wheel scrolls the log down and back up, the counts follow:

The labels sit on the box around the log, not in the log itself, since a scroll container moves everything inside it by its offset. So document gives the log an ElementHandle and reads its scroll with use_scroll(body). Called without a handle, use_scroll reports on the calling component's own top-level element.

max_offset is how far the content reaches past the view, so it's 0 when everything fits, which is why percent checks it before dividing.

use_scroll reports the previous frame's scroll, and a component that calls it renders again as soon as that scroll changes, so the counts catch up in the frame after the one the wheel scrolled. See Scrolling for an example that renders only the rows in view, and Jumping to the end for a button that appears once the reader scrolls back.
