docs.title: use_state
docs.text:
use_state gives a component a value that persists across renders, and a setter that changes it. Setting a different value re-renders the component.

@component
def counter() -> Div:
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key="+"):
                set_count(lambda count: count + 1)
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key="-"):
                set_count(lambda count: count - 1)
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key="0"):
                set_count(0)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Text(content=f"Count: {count}", style=text_color("amber", 400)),
            Text(content="+ and - count, 0 resets", style=text_color("slate", 400)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────╮
│ Count: 3                   │
│ + and - count, 0 resets    │
╰────────────────────────────╯

Each key press sets the count, which renders counter again with the new value:

+ and - pass the setter a function, since the new count depends on the old one (see below), and 0 passes it a value, since the reset doesn't.

docs.title: Updating state from its previous value
docs.text:
When the new state depends on the old, pass the setter a function

count is the value as of the render that built the handler, and nothing updates it until the next render. A setter given a value replaces the state with it, so every update computed from count before the next render starts from the same stale count, and only the last one survives. No error is raised: the other updates just vanish.

Given a function, the setter calls it right away with the latest state, updates included, and stores what it returns:

set_count(count + 1)            # wrong: loses updates made since this render
set_count(lambda c: c + 1)      # right: builds on the latest state

Several updates can land before the next render in ways that are easy to miss, because each looks like one update when you read the code.

Two updates in one handler. Each by_value + 1 is computed from the same by_value, while each function builds on what the one before it returned:

@component
def plus_two() -> Div:
    by_value, set_by_value = use_state(0)
    by_function, set_by_function = use_state(0)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key="+"):
                set_by_value(by_value + 1)
                set_by_value(by_value + 1)
                set_by_function(lambda n: n + 1)
                set_by_function(lambda n: n + 1)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Text(content=f"By value:    {by_value}", style=text_color("red", 400)),
            Text(content=f"By function: {by_function}", style=text_color("emerald", 400)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────╮
│ By value:    3             │
│ By function: 6             │
╰────────────────────────────╯

After three presses of +, by_value has gone up by one a press, and by_function by two.

Key presses that arrive together. Counterweight routes every event it has read before rendering again, and a terminal delivers keys together whenever they come faster than one per frame: fast typing, a held key repeating, or text pasted into a terminal without bracketed paste. Each key press's handler sees the same text:

text, set_text = use_state("")


def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case KeyPressed(key=key) if len(key) == 1:
            set_text(text + key)  # "abc" typed in one burst leaves text as "c"
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

This one hides from tests: an autopilot renders after each event it sends, so every key press there sees the latest text, and so does slow typing by hand. Write set_text(lambda t: t + key). For a text field, use_text_input does this for you, along with the cursor, the editing keys and pastes.

An effect that outlives its render. An effect closes over the values from the render that started it, and one with deps=() keeps them for as long as the component is mounted:

count, set_count = use_state(0)


async def tick() -> None:
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        set_count(count + 1)  # count stays at 1, since this count is always 0


use_effect(tick, deps=())

Pass a value only when the new state doesn't depend on the old, as in set_query("") to clear a field or set_selected(item.id) to select an item. Toggling a flag depends on it, so it takes a function too: toggle, as in set_open(toggle).

The setter is the same object on every render, so a handler that updates state only through functions captures nothing that goes stale, and can be built once with use_memo or passed to a memo component.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.use_state
docs.text:
use_state(
    initial_value: Getter[T],
) -> tuple[T, Setter[T]]

use_state(initial_value: T) -> tuple[T, Setter[T]]

use_state(
    initial_value: Getter[T] | T,
) -> tuple[T, Setter[T]]
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION initial_value

The initial value of the state. It can either be the initial value itself, or a zero-argument function that returns the initial value.

TYPE: Getter[T] | T

RETURNS DESCRIPTION T

The current value of the state (i.e., for the current render cycle).

Setter[T]

A function that can be called to update the value of the state (e.g., in an event handler). It can either be called with the new value of the state, or a function that takes the current value of the state and returns the new value of the state. When the new value depends on the current one, pass a function: a value computed from the state a render saw loses every update made since, such as from other key presses read before the next render (see Updating state from its previous value). If the value is not equal to the current of the state, Counterweight will trigger a render cycle. It is the same object on every render, so it can be left out of an effect's deps, and including it never reruns the effect. Once the component unmounts, calling it does nothing.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.toggle
docs.text:
toggle(value: bool) -> bool

Flips a flag: pass it to a use_state setter, as set_open(toggle), so each toggle flips the latest value, even when several land before the next render. It takes only a bool, so a type checker rejects it for state of any other type, where operator.not_ would quietly turn the state into one.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.Getter
docs.text:
Getter = Callable[[], T]

A function that computes a value, such as the initial state use_state computes only on the first render.

docs.title: counterweight.hooks.Setter
docs.text:
Setter = Callable[[Callable[[T], T] | T], None]

What use_state returns to set its state: given a value, the next state, or given a function, the next state computed from the latest one.

docs.title: Input Handling
docs.text:
Counterweight reads the terminal's input as events: a KeyPressed for each key, a Pasted for each paste, and a mouse event for each change of the mouse. It delivers each one to an element's on_input handler, a function of the event and a receiver that describes the element, whose return value says whether it handled the event and what the app should do about it.

This page is an overview of how an event travels and what a handler does with it. The pages below it cover each part in detail:

  • Events: what each event holds, and how events are routed to handlers.
  • Handlers: the library handlers for clicks, focus and scrolling, and first and each, which compose them.
  • Controls: what a handler returns to act on the app, such as Quit().

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
These light switches turn on and off with the 1, 2 and 3 keys, or with a click:

ROOMS = ("Kitchen", "Hall", "Porch")


@component
def switch(room: str, is_on: bool, toggle: Callable[[], None]) -> Text:
    return Text(
        content=f"{'●' if is_on else '○'} {room}",
        style=border
        | border_lightrounded
        | pad_x(1)
        | (border_color("amber", 400) | text_color("amber", 300) if is_on else border_color("slate", 600)),
        on_input=on_click(toggle),
    )


@component
def root() -> Div:
    lit, set_lit = use_state(frozenset[str]())

    def toggle(room: str) -> None:
        set_lit(lambda lit: lit ^ {room})

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key="1" | "2" | "3" as key):
                toggle(ROOMS[int(key) - 1])
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key="0"):
                set_lit(frozenset())
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | align_children_center | justify_children_center | full,
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Div(style=row | gap(1), children=tuple(switch(room, room in lit, partial(toggle, room)) for room in ROOMS)),
            Text(content="Press 1, 2 or 3, or click a switch. 0 turns them all off.", style=text_color("slate", 400)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

            ╭───────────╮ ╭────────╮ ╭─────────╮            
            │ ● Kitchen │ │ ● Hall │ │ ● Porch │            
            ╰───────────╯ ╰────────╯ ╰─────────╯            
  Press 1, 2 or 3, or click a switch. 0 turns them all off.

The root component's element handles the keys, and each switch handles its own clicks with on_click. Here it turns on the kitchen and the hall with 1 and 2, clicks the porch on and the kitchen off, turns the hall off with 2, and everything off with 0:

docs.title: Where events go
docs.text:
Each event has one target element, which depends on the kind of event:

  • A key press or a paste goes to the focused element, or to the root component's element when nothing is focused, as it is in the switches.
  • A mouse event goes to the element drawn on top under the pointer, such as one of the switches.

Counterweight calls the target's handler first, then its parent's, and so on up to the root component's element, until one returns something other than None. That's bubbling, as in the DOM: a text field doesn't handle Enter, so Enter pressed in a field reaches the handler of a form around it, which can submit on it. See Routing Input Events for the rules, including how a press and drag stay with the element they began on.

docs.title: What handlers return
docs.text:
A handler returns None for an event it doesn't handle, so the event bubbles on. Anything else stops the event: a control for Counterweight to apply, such as the FocusNext() that tab_focus returns for Tab, a tuple of controls, or () when there's nothing more to do than what the handler already did, such as setting state.

Nothing happens to an event that no handler handles, except for a few keys with defaults, such as Ctrl+C, which quits (see Keys the terminal would act on). Tab doesn't move focus and the wheel doesn't scroll unless a handler on the event's path returns a control that does, so an app composes in the library handlers for the behaviors it wants.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Controls are objects that can be returned from an element's on_input handler to instruct Counterweight to take some action during the render loop, such as gracefully quitting the application or playing the terminal "bell" sound.

A handler returns one control (return Quit()), or a tuple of controls, which Counterweight applies in order (return Bell(), Screenshot.to_file(path)), skipping any None in it, as merge skips None styles. Returning (), a tuple of no controls, says the handler handled the event with nothing more to do, and returning any control or tuple stops the event, as () does (see Events). Code outside a handler, such as an effect, sends controls with use_controls.

docs.title: Returning controls
docs.text:
This app sets the terminal window's title to what's typed in its field when Enter is pressed:

@component
def title_editor() -> Div:
    draft, set_draft = use_state("")
    title, set_title = use_state("")

    def edited(outcome: EditOutcome) -> None:
        match outcome:
            case Edited(text=text):
                set_draft(text.strip())
            case _:
                pass

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
                if not draft:
                    return Bell()
                set_title(draft)
                return SetTitle(draft)
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Escape):
                set_title("")
                return RestoreTitle()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.ControlO):
                return Suspend.to_edit_text(draft, on_edit=edited)
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | width(60),
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            text_input(draft, set_draft, placeholder="Window title", auto_focus=True),
            Text(content=f"Window title: {title or "the terminal's own"}"),
            Text(
                content="Enter: set · Escape: restore · Ctrl+O: edit",
                style=text_color("slate", 400),
            ),
        ),
    )

Each key it binds returns a different control:

  • Enter returns SetTitle with the field's text, or Bell() to complain when the field is empty.
  • Escape returns RestoreTitle(), which puts back the title the window had before the app started.
  • Ctrl+O returns a Suspend that hands the terminal to the user's editor to edit the title in, and calls edited when the editor exits.

The text field handles typing, and passes Enter, Escape and the Ctrl keys it doesn't edit with on to the Div around it. A screenshot can't show the window's title, so the app shows the title it set below the field:

ScreenshotText 

╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮  
│ Build logs                                               │  
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯  
Window title: Build logs                                      
Enter: set · Escape: restore · Ctrl+O: edit

Other pages show the rest of the controls at work:

  • The focus controls move focus through the order form and the prefix keys recipe.
  • The scroll controls scroll a log to its end and a document to a section, in Scrolling from a handler and Scrolling an element into view.
  • Suspend runs a pager and the user's editor in Running Programs on the App's Terminal.
  • ToggleBorderHealing turns border healing off and on.
  • Screenshot, AdvanceClock and Marker drive and record an app from an autopilot.
  • CopyToClipboard copies a command from a list, below.

docs.title: Copying to the clipboard
docs.text:
CopyToClipboard copies text to the system clipboard, as a browser's navigator.clipboard.writeText does, for an app's own "copy" buttons and keys. Here Up and Down move through a list of commands, and Enter or a click copies one:

COMMANDS = (
    "git status",
    "git log --oneline --graph",
    "uv run pytest -x",
    "just docs-serve",
)


@component
def command_list() -> Div:
    selected, set_selected = use_state(0)
    copied, set_copied = use_state("")

    def copy(index: int) -> CopyToClipboard:
        set_selected(index)
        set_copied(COMMANDS[index])
        return CopyToClipboard(COMMANDS[index])

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Up):
                set_selected(lambda index: clamp(0, index - 1, len(COMMANDS) - 1))
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Down):
                set_selected(lambda index: clamp(0, index + 1, len(COMMANDS) - 1))
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
                return copy(selected)
            case _:
                return None

    def command_row(index: int) -> Text:
        return Text(
            content=f"$ {COMMANDS[index]}",
            style=pad_x(1) | (text_bg("sky", 800) if index == selected else text_color("slate", 300)),
            on_input=on_click(lambda: copy(index)),
        )

    return Div(
        style=col | width(40),
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | border | border_lightrounded,
                children=tuple(command_row(index) for index in range(len(COMMANDS))),
            ),
            Text(
                content=f"Copied: {copied}" if copied else "Enter or click to copy",
                style=pad_x(1) | text_color("emerald" if copied else "slate", 400),
            ),
        ),
    )

The handler that copies also sets state, so the app can say what it copied, since nothing else shows that the copy happened:

ScreenshotText 

╭──────────────────────────────────────╮  
│ $ git status                         │  
│ $ git log --oneline --graph          │  
│ $ uv run pytest -x                   │  
│ $ just docs-serve                    │  
╰──────────────────────────────────────╯  
 Copied: git log --oneline --graph

The app asks the terminal to set the clipboard with OSC 52, so it works only where the terminal supports that, and the app can't tell whether it did. Some terminals turn it off, or ask before letting a program set the clipboard, and tmux passes it on only with set -g set-clipboard on. A headless app copies nothing, and a recording leaves the copy out, since playing it back in a terminal would set the viewer's clipboard.

To send copies somewhere else, such as to a list a test checks or to the system clipboard through a library, give app a clipboard_handler, which takes the text of every copy, headless or not, in place of the terminal's clipboard:

copied: list[str] = []
await app(command_list(), headless=True, autopilot=[KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter), Quit()], clipboard_handler=copied.append)

A CopyToClipboard given a handler of its own sends its text there instead, whatever app was given, as a Screenshot's handler chooses where its frame goes.

Quit()

Cause the application to quit.

The quit occurs at the beginning of the next render cycle, so all other events that are due to be processed in the current cycle will be processed before the application exits.

Bell()

Cause the terminal to emit a bell sound.

The bell occurs at the beginning of the next render cycle, so all other events that are due to be processed in the current cycle will be processed before the sound is played.

docs.title: counterweight.controls.SetTitle dataclass
docs.text:
SetTitle(title: str)

Set the title of the terminal window. To set it when the application starts, pass title to counterweight._app.app.

The title is set at the beginning of the next render cycle, so all other events that are due to be processed in the current cycle will be processed before it changes. Line breaks in the title show as spaces, and other control characters as symbols, such as ␛ for an escape.

The application saves the title it started with, and restores it when it quits and while it's suspended, on terminals that support xterm's title stack (those that don't keep the last title set). RestoreTitle restores it while the application runs.

RestoreTitle()

Restore the title the terminal window had when the application started, undoing any SetTitle, on terminals that support xterm's title stack.

The title is restored at the beginning of the next render cycle, so all other events that are due to be processed in the current cycle will be processed before it changes.

docs.title: counterweight.controls.CopyToClipboard dataclass
docs.text:
CopyToClipboard(
    text: str,
    handler: Callable[[str], Awaitable[None] | None]
    | None = None,
)

Copy text to the system clipboard, as a browser's navigator.clipboard.writeText does, for an app's own "copy" buttons and key bindings.

The text is copied at the beginning of the next render cycle, so all other events that are due to be processed in the current cycle will be processed before it's copied, and the last copy in a cycle wins. Copying "" empties the clipboard.

The app asks the terminal to set the clipboard with OSC 52, so it works only where the terminal supports it, and the app can't tell whether it did. A terminal may turn it off, or ask before letting a program set the clipboard, and tmux passes it on only with set -g set-clipboard on (its default, external, ignores applications' requests). A headless app copies nothing, and a recording doesn't record the copy, since replaying it in a terminal would set the viewer's clipboard.

A handler takes the text in place of the terminal's clipboard, headless or not, as a Screenshot's handler chooses where its frame goes, and is awaited if it returns an awaitable; without one, app's clipboard_handler takes it, if it was given one. Either way nothing is written to the terminal, and an error the handler raises is logged rather than stopping the app.

docs.title: counterweight.controls.FocusNext dataclass
docs.text:
FocusNext(within: ElementHandle | Subtree | None = None)

Move focus to the next visible component in the focus order, in tree order, wrapping from the last to the first. From nothing focused, or from focus outside within, it focuses the first. From a focused component that's out of the focus order (see in_focus_order on use_focus), it moves from that component's place in tree order. It does nothing if within has unmounted or holds no visible component in the focus order.

docs.title: Scrolling
docs.text: These controls scroll a scroll container. scroll_on_wheel returns ScrollBy for the wheel, and scroll_on_keys returns ScrollBy for the keys that scroll by a step or a page, and ScrollTo for Home and End. ScrollIntoView brings an element into view in every container above it: moving focus applies it to the newly focused element, use_text_area's handler returns it for the cursor's row, and the autocomplete recipe returns it for the highlighted match.

ScrollTo(
    target: ElementHandle | Subtree,
    x: int | None = None,
    y: int | None = None,
)

It applies to the layout of the next render, before that render paints, after anchoring and sticking to the end, and in order with the other scroll controls returned since the last render, so a handler that returns it beside a state change scrolls the content that change lays out. It does nothing if target names no mounted, visible scroll container then.

ScrollIntoView(
    target: ElementHandle | Subtree,
    block: ScrollAlignment = "start",
    inline: ScrollAlignment = "nearest",

Scroll each scroll container above the element target names so the element's border box is in view, from the innermost container out, as the web's scrollIntoView does, aligning it as block says vertically and as inline says horizontally, with the web's defaults. On each axis, "start" puts the element's start edge at the start edge of the container's view, "center" its center at the view's center, and "end" its end edge at the view's end edge. "nearest" does whichever of "start" and "end" scrolls least, and doesn't scroll at all if the element is already wholly in view, or covers the whole view. Each offset is clamped to the range its container scrolls through.

It applies as ScrollTo does, to the layout of the next render, so a handler that returns it beside a state change, such as moving a highlight through a long list, shows the scroll in the same frame as the change. The element target names is the one with that element handle in the next render, so an element handle moved onto a newly highlighted element names the new one. It does nothing if target names no mounted, visible element then, and it stops at an element with clip_to_screen, since no container above that element clips it.

docs.title: Handling Input
docs.text:
Div and Text elements take an on_input handler, which Counterweight calls with key presses, pastes, and mouse events, along with a Receiver describing the element the event is delivered to. A handler matches on the event, so one case can cover a key and a mouse event alike:

def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case KeyPressed(key=Key.Space) | MouseDown(button=1):
            set_is_open(toggle)
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

The library handlers cover the common cases, such as on_click for a press released inside the element, and scroll_on_wheel and scroll_on_keys for a scroll container.

A handler's return value says whether the event was its to handle:

  • None means it wasn't, and the event bubbles on to the element's parent.
  • Anything else means it was, and the event stops there. That is a control for Counterweight to apply (return Quit()), a tuple of controls applied in order (return Bell(), Screenshot.to_file(path)), or (), a tuple of no controls, when there's nothing else to do. A None inside a tuple is skipped, so a control can be conditional (return Bell() if is_full else None, Screenshot.to_file(path)), and a tuple still stops the event when every item in it is None.

Return () (or the controls) from every case that does something, so an ancestor that handles the same event doesn't act on it too.

Don't chain handlers with or

() is falsy, so handler_a(event, receiver) or handler_b(event, receiver) calls handler_b even when handler_a handled the event. Compose handlers with first and each instead.

A handler that only cares about keys still receives mouse events, including every movement of the pointer over its element. One that matches many keys can return early on anything else, which keeps its cases about keys alone:

def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    if not isinstance(event, KeyPressed):
        return None

    match event.key:
        case Key.ControlC:
            return Quit()
        case Key.Tab:
            set_tab(lambda t: (t + 1) % len(TABS))
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

The receiver describes the element the event is delivered to. Its rectangles tell a handler where in the element a mouse event landed:

def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case MouseDown(absolute=position, button=1):
            set_clicked(receiver.relative(position))
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

Its is_focused, focus_handle and subtree serve the focus handlers: whether the element is focused, the focus handle that names its component if the component is focusable, and the element and its descendants, for moving focus among them. The subtree also names the element for the scroll controls, and scroll says how far the element is scrolled if it's a scroll container, which scroll_on_keys reads to tell how far a page is and whether it's reached an end.

A handler that calls another, as the autocomplete recipe calls a text field's, reads what it returned with response_controls, which turns any response into a tuple of controls, or None if the inner handler didn't handle the event.

docs.title: Routing Input Events
docs.text:
Each input event has one target element. Counterweight calls the target's on_input handler, then each of its ancestors' in turn, up to the root component's element, until one returns something other than None. The ancestors are the element tree's, not the screen's, so an absolutely positioned child bubbles to its parent even where it's drawn outside it. Each element receives the same event, with its own receiver: a parent's rects are its own, and its is_target is False.

In this example, every element on an event's path writes down whether it handles the event or passes it on, so each line of the log is one event's trip up the tree. Field A handles a, field B handles b, the panel around them handles p, and the root handles every typed character, and every press:

Trace = Callable[[InputEvent, str], None]


def traced(name: str, handles: Callable[[InputEvent], bool], trace: Trace) -> InputHandler:
    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        if not isinstance(event, KeyPressed | MouseDown):
            return None
        is_handled = handles(event)
        trace(event, f"{name} {'handles' if is_handled else 'passes'}")
        return () if is_handled else None

    return on_input


@component
def field(name: str, letter: str, trace: Trace) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus(auto_focus=name == "A")

    return Text(
        content=f"{'▸' if focus.is_focused else ' '} field {name}: {letter}",
        style=border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1) | text_bg("indigo", 700 if focus.is_focused else 900),
        on_input=traced(f"field {name}", lambda event: event == KeyPressed(key=letter), trace),
    )


def is_character_or_press(event: InputEvent) -> bool:
    return isinstance(event, MouseDown) or (isinstance(event, KeyPressed) and len(event.key) == 1)


@component
def routing() -> Div:
    lines, set_lines = use_state(tuple[str, ...]())
    last_event: Ref[InputEvent | None] = use_ref(None)

    def trace(event: InputEvent, step: str) -> None:
        # Every handler on an event's path receives the same event object, so a new one starts a new line.
        if event is last_event.current:
            set_lines(lambda lines: (*lines[:-1], f"{lines[-1]}, {step}"))
            return
        last_event.current = event
        label = repr(event.key) if isinstance(event, KeyPressed) else "press"
        set_lines(lambda lines: (*lines, f"{label}: {step}")[-LINES:])

    return Div(
        style=col | full | border | border_heavy | pad_x(1),
        on_input=traced("root", is_character_or_press, trace),
        children=(
            Text(content="root: every character, and presses"),
            Div(
                style=col | border | border_light | pad_x(1),
                on_input=traced("panel", lambda event: event == KeyPressed(key="p"), trace),
                children=(
                    Text(content="panel: p"),
                    Div(style=row | gap(2), children=(field("A", "a", trace), field("B", "b", trace))),
                ),
            ),
            *(Text(content=line) for line in lines),
        ),
    )

Field A is focused, so each key press starts there. a stops at field A, p bubbles one step to the panel, and x bubbles all the way to the root. b bubbles to the root too, though field B handles it, because field B is a sibling of the focused field, not an ancestor. A press on field B starts at field B, where the pointer is, though field A is focused. A press on the panel's label starts at the label, which has no handler, so the panel's handler is the first to see it.

Every handler on an event's path receives the same event object, so trace tells the next step of one event's trip from the start of another's by identity, with is, since two presses of one key are equal events. It keeps the last event in a ref, because the handlers of one batch of input all see the state of the render before it.

docs.title: Key Presses
docs.text:
The target of a key press is the focused element, or the root component's element when nothing is focused. A key press bubbles from the focused element through its ancestors, and never reaches its siblings, so two components that handle the same keys don't both act on one press. When nothing is focused, only the root component's handler receives key presses, and its receiver's is_target is True, though its is_focused is False.

A focusable component's key handler goes on the element the component returns, which is the one that's focused. Handlers on the elements inside it never receive key presses, and a component deep in the tree can't own a global shortcut: put the shortcut on the root component's element, which every key press bubbles to unless a handler on the way stops it.

docs.title: Mouse Events
docs.text: The target of a mouse event is the element drawn on top at the pointer: the last element in paint order whose border box contains it. An element's margin isn't part of it, so a press in a margin reaches whatever lies beneath. A pointer over none of the root component's elements, when the root's element is smaller than the terminal, targets the root's element, though its rectangles don't contain the pointer.

docs.title: Presses
docs.text:
A press runs from the first mouse button going down to the last one coming up, as in the web's Pointer Events. Its first MouseDown is routed like any mouse event, and the element whose handler stops it captures the press: the press's later events, each MouseMoved with a button held and each MouseDown and MouseUp of the buttons pressed and released while it lasts, go to that element alone, as their target, wherever the pointer is, and stop there whatever its handler returns. A second button pressed during a press joins it rather than starting a new one, so a handler that acts on one button matches on button, as on_click does for button 1. So a drag keeps reaching the element it started on however fast the pointer moves, and a release outside the element still reaches it, which a handler can tell from its receiver's rectangles.

The rest of a press that nothing stopped, or whose element has since unmounted, reaches no handler, and neither does a MouseUp for a button the press doesn't hold, so an element never receives the end of a press it didn't see begin: a release over a button after a press somewhere else doesn't click it. A handler that wants a press's moves stops its MouseDown, even with nothing to do for it:

def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case MouseDown(button=1):
            return ()
        case MouseMoved(absolute=position, button=1):
            set_end(receiver.relative(position))
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

A slider is one line of text that the pointer drags along. Its handler stops the press's MouseDown, so it receives every move of the drag, and sets the volume from where the pointer is across the slider, clamped to its ends:

WIDTH = 20


@component
def slider() -> Div:
    volume, set_volume = use_state(5)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case MouseDown(absolute=position, button=1) | MouseMoved(absolute=position, button=1):
                set_volume(clamp(0, receiver.relative(position).x, WIDTH - 1))
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | full | pad_x(1),
        children=(
            Text(content=f"Volume: {volume}"),
            Text(
                content="━" * volume + "●" + "─" * (WIDTH - 1 - volume),
                style=width(WIDTH) | text_color("indigo", 300),
                on_input=on_input,
            ),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

 Volume: 19                             
 ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━●

The drag above ended three rows below the slider and past its right end, outside it, and the moves kept reaching the slider all the way, so it's at its highest volume. If the press weren't captured, the moves past the slider's edge would go to whatever is under the pointer instead.

A MouseMoved with no button held ends a press whose release the terminal never reported, such as when focus moves to another window mid-drag, and so does a MouseDown for a button the press already holds. Both are routed by the pointer's position, and the MouseDown starts a new press. Scroll wheel events aren't part of a press, so they always target the element under the pointer, even mid-drag.

Since the press goes to whichever element stops its MouseDown, the innermost element with a handler for presses owns the whole press: a press on a button inside a draggable panel clicks the button and doesn't drag the panel. on_click builds a handler for the commonest case.

docs.title: Handling Keyboard Events
docs.text:
Each time a key is pressed, Counterweight emits a KeyPressed event that holds which key was pressed, and routes it to the focused element. This inspector writes down every event its element receives, much as counterweight check-input prints them. Nothing in it is focusable, so its root element receives every key press and paste:

LINES = 8


def concise(event: InputEvent) -> str:
    """The event's repr, without the fields that hold their defaults, such as modifier keys that weren't held."""
    shown = ", ".join(
        f"{field.name}={value!r}" for field in fields(event) if (value := getattr(event, field.name)) != field.default
    )
    return f"{type(event).__name__}({shown})"


@component
def inspector() -> Div:
    lines, set_lines = use_state(tuple[str, ...]())

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        set_lines(lambda lines: (*lines, concise(event))[-LINES:])
        match event:
            case MouseDown():
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | full | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Text(content="Press keys, paste, or use the mouse. Ctrl+C quits.", style=text_color("slate", 400)),
            *(Text(content=line) for line in lines),
        ),
    )

Its handler returns None for everything but a MouseDown, so the keys with defaults keep them, and Ctrl+C still quits. It stops each MouseDown so that it receives the rest of the press.

A key that types text, such as a or é, is that text, and any other key is a Key from counterweight.keys, such as Key.Enter, Key.Up or Key.ControlS. A handler matches either kind with a KeyPressed(key=...) pattern, such as KeyPressed(key="a") or KeyPressed(key=Key.Up). Enter and Ctrl+J are different keys, Key.Enter and Key.ControlJ, so a text area can insert a line break on Ctrl+J while Enter submits a form.

KeyPressed(key: str)

A key press, which goes to the focused element, or the root component's element when nothing is focused.

docs.title: key instance-attribute
docs.text:
key: str

The Key for a control or special key (Key.Enter, Key.Up, Key.F1), or for one pressed with Alt (Key.AltEnter, Key.AltUp, Key.ControlAltA), the text typed: one grapheme cluster, such as "a", "é" or "👩‍💻", or alt+ and the text, for text typed with Alt, such as "alt+b" or "alt+B" (Alt with Shift and B). Text pasted in a terminal without bracketed paste arrives as a key press per grapheme cluster; in one with it, the text arrives as one Pasted.

docs.title: Keys pressed with Alt
docs.text:
Terminals send a key pressed with Alt as ESC followed by what the key sends on its own (xterm's metaSendsEscape, which most terminals do by default), and Counterweight reads the two as one key press: Key.AltEnter for Alt+Enter, Key.AltBackspace for Alt+Backspace, Key.ControlAltA for Ctrl+Alt+A, and "alt+b" for Alt+B, which is alt+ and the text the key types, so Alt+Shift+B is "alt+B". Arrow, navigation and function keys pressed with Alt are Key.AltUp, Key.AltPageDown, Key.AltF1 and so on, whether the terminal sends Alt in their escape sequence, as xterm does, or as an ESC before it, as rxvt does. The inspector shows them:

ScreenshotText 

╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Press keys, paste, or use the mouse. Ctrl+C quits.                   │
│ KeyPressed(key=Key.AltEnter)                                         │
│ KeyPressed(key='alt+b')                                              │
│ KeyPressed(key='alt+B')                                              │
│ KeyPressed(key=Key.ControlAltA)                                      │
│ KeyPressed(key=Key.AltUp)                                            │
│                                                                      │
│                                                                      │
│                                                                      │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

A handler matches a key pressed with Alt as it matches any other key:

def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
            send()
            return ()
        case KeyPressed(key="alt+n"):
            start_new_chat()
            return ()
        case _:
            return None

The DOM's KeyboardEvent reports Alt in altKey, beside a key that doesn't change, as Counterweight's mouse events report it in is_alt_held. A key press names Alt in its key instead, as it names Control and Shift (Key.ControlLeft, Key.ShiftUp), so a handler that matches Key.Enter doesn't also take Alt+Enter, and a text field never types the b of Alt+B, since text is always one grapheme cluster, and "alt+b" isn't.

An Escape pressed on its own and then a key sends the same bytes as Alt with the key, so Counterweight tells them apart by time, as terminal programs do: an ESC at the end of the input that has arrived waits up to 50 milliseconds for more, as it waits for the rest of an escape sequence, and is Alt with the key that arrives in that time, or the Escape key once it passes. Two ESCs are two presses of Escape rather than Alt+Escape, so pressing Escape twice quickly is never lost. ESC [ and ESC O also begin escape sequences, so Alt+[ and Alt+Shift+O arrive as "alt+[" and "alt+O" only when no key follows them within that time.

A terminal that doesn't send Alt as an escape never sends these keys. One that sets the high bit of the byte for Alt instead (xterm with metaSendsEscape off and eightBitInput on) sends another character, as does macOS's Option key, which types characters such as ∫ for Option+B unless the terminal is set to send it as Meta (Terminal.app's "Use Option as Meta key", or iTerm2's "Esc+" for the Option key). Run counterweight check-input to see which events a terminal's keys arrive as.

docs.title: Keys the terminal would act on
docs.text:
A terminal acts on a few Ctrl keys itself unless the program reading it asks otherwise: Ctrl+C and Ctrl+\ send signals that interrupt and kill the program, Ctrl+Z one that stops it, and Ctrl+S and Ctrl+Q pause and resume its output. Counterweight asks otherwise, as tmux does: it reads the terminal raw, so every one of those keys arrives as a key press (Key.ControlC, Key.ControlBackslash, Key.ControlZ, Key.ControlS and Key.ControlQ), and an editor can save on Ctrl+S, or an app can pass Ctrl+C on to a program it runs.

A key press that no handler on its path claims then takes its default from app's unclaimed_keys, as a browser takes a key's default action unless a listener prevents it. DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_KEYS gives Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z what they'd do in a terminal: Ctrl+C quits, and Ctrl+Z suspends the app as a shell job, with Suspend.to_shell(), until the shell resumes it with fg. A handler that claims one of them keeps it from taking its default, and unclaimed_keys changes the defaults for the whole app:

# No defaults: Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z do nothing unless a handler handles them.
asyncio.run(app(root(), unclaimed_keys={}))

# Ctrl+Q quits too, as well as Ctrl+C.
asyncio.run(app(root(), unclaimed_keys=DEFAULT_UNCLAIMED_KEYS | {Key.ControlQ: Quit()}))

A key the terminal would turn into a signal only does something once the app reads it, so an app whose render loop is stuck, such as in a handler that never returns, can't be quit with Ctrl+C. Stop it from outside with kill: the first interrupt quits it as Ctrl+C would, and a second one goes to whatever handled interrupts before the app started. A focused component that claims every key, such as one that passes keys on to a program, takes Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z too, so an app that has one needs another way to quit, such as a key that it doesn't claim.

docs.title: Handling Pastes
docs.text:
Counterweight turns on the terminal's bracketed paste mode, so text pasted into the terminal arrives as one Pasted event holding all of it, rather than as a key press per character, and it's routed to the focused element, as a key press is. A handler that only matches key presses never sees it, so a paste can't trigger a binding by holding the binding's key. use_text_input and use_text_area insert it in one edit. Terminals without bracketed paste send pasted text as typed keys, with its line breaks as Enter, or as Ctrl+J from a terminal that sends them as line feeds.

In the inspector, typing h and i makes two key presses, while pasting two lines makes one event, with the line break inside its text:

│ Press keys, paste, or use the mouse. Ctrl+C quits.                   │
│ KeyPressed(key='h')                                                  │
│ KeyPressed(key='i')                                                  │
│ Pasted(text='first line\nsecond line')                               │

docs.title: Handling Mouse Events
docs.text:
Each time the state of the mouse changes, Counterweight emits a single mouse event, one of MouseMoved, MouseDown, MouseUp, MouseScrolledDown, MouseScrolledUp, MouseScrolledLeft, or MouseScrolledRight.

Each mouse event says which modifier keys were held, as the DOM's MouseEvent does, in is_shift_held, is_alt_held and is_control_held, so a handler can match a modified press or turn of the wheel. In this list, a press selects one item, and a press with Control held adds an item to the selection, or takes it out:

ITEMS = ("apples", "bread", "cheese", "dates")


@component
def shopping_list() -> Div:
    selected, set_selected = use_state(frozenset[str]())

    def row(item: str) -> Text:
        def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
            match event:
                case MouseDown(button=1, is_control_held=True):
                    set_selected(lambda selected: selected ^ {item})
                    return ()
                case MouseDown(button=1):
                    set_selected(frozenset({item}))
                    return ()
                case _:
                    return None

        is_selected = item in selected
        return Text(
            content=f"{'●' if is_selected else '○'} {item}",
            style=pad_x(1) | (text_bg("indigo", 700) if is_selected else default),
            on_input=on_input,
        )

    return Div(style=col | full, children=tuple(row(item) for item in ITEMS))

The case with is_control_held=True comes first, since a MouseDown(button=1) pattern matches a press whatever modifiers were held. After a press on bread and a press with Control on dates, both are selected:

ScreenshotText 

 ○ apples           
 ● bread            
 ○ cheese           
 ● dates

Terminals keep some combinations for themselves and never report them to the app: most select text for Shift with a press, even while the app tracks the mouse, and some scroll their own scrollback for Shift with the wheel or open links for Control with a press. So a modifier works best as a shortcut for something the app offers another way too. counterweight check-input --mouse shows the events a terminal reports.

For example, consider the following series of mouse actions and corresponding events:

Action Event Mouse starts at position (0, 0) No event emitted Mouse moves to position (1, 0) MouseMoved(absolute=Position(x=1, y=0), button=None) Mouse button 1 is pressed MouseDown(absolute=Position(x=1, y=0), button=1) Mouse moves to position (1, 1) MouseMoved(absolute=Position(x=1, y=1), button=1) Mouse button 1 is released MouseUp(absolute=Position(x=1, y=1), button=1) Mouse button 3 is pressed MouseDown(absolute=Position(x=1, y=1), button=3) Mouse moves to position (2, 2) and mouse button 3 is released simultaneously MouseUp(absolute=Position(x=2, y=2), button=3)

The inspector receives that series as the table lists it, followed by a turn of the wheel with Control held. It receives the presses' moves and releases because it stops each MouseDown:

ScreenshotText 

╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Press keys, paste, or use the mouse. Ctrl+C quits.                   │
│ MouseMoved(absolute=Position(x=1, y=0), button=None)                 │
│ MouseDown(absolute=Position(x=1, y=0), button=1)                     │
│ MouseMoved(absolute=Position(x=1, y=1), button=1)                    │
│ MouseUp(absolute=Position(x=1, y=1), button=1)                       │
│ MouseDown(absolute=Position(x=1, y=1), button=3)                     │
│ MouseUp(absolute=Position(x=2, y=2), button=3)                       │
│ MouseScrolledDown(absolute=Position(x=2, y=2), is_control_held=True) │
│                                                                      │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

Mouse Button Identifiers

Mouse buttons are identified by numbers instead of names (e.g., "left", "middle", "right") because the button numbers are the same regardless of whether the mouse is configured for left-handed or right-handed use.

Number Button for Right-Handed Mouse Button for Left-Handed Mouse 1 Left Right 2 Middle Middle 3 Right Left 8 Back Back 9 Forward Forward

You should always use the numbers instead of names to refer to mouse buttons to ensure that your application works as expected for both left-handed and right-handed users.

use_mouse vs. on_input

use_mouse and an element's on_input handler both see the mouse, but use_mouse is a hook and on_input is an event handler. use_mouse is more efficient when a component depends only on the current state of the mouse (e.g., the current position, or whether a button is currently pressed), while on_input is more convenient when a component needs to respond to changes in the mouse state, (e.g., a button release MouseUp). use_mouse sees every change, while a handler sees only the events routed to its element.

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text:
counterweight.handlers holds handlers for common behaviors, and combinators that compose several handlers into the one an element's on_input takes. Nothing happens to an input event unless a handler on its path does it, so a behavior an element should have is a handler composed onto it.

Each library handler is a pure function of the event and the receiver, so it can be tested by calling it, without running an app.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
This basket has a button for each fruit, which adds one to the basket when it's clicked, or when Enter is pressed while it's focused, and a button that empties the basket:

FRUITS = ("Apples", "Pears", "Plums")


def button_style(is_focused: bool) -> Style:
    ring = border_color("amber", 400) | text_color("amber", 200) if is_focused else border_color("slate", 600)
    return border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1) | ring


@component
def fruit_button(fruit: str, add: Callable[[], None]) -> Text:
    focus = use_focus()

    def add_on_enter(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Enter):
                add()
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Text(
        content=fruit,
        style=button_style(focus.is_focused),
        on_input=first(add_on_enter, each(on_click(add), focus_receiver_on_press)),
    )


@component
def basket() -> Div:
    counts, set_counts = use_state(lambda: dict.fromkeys(FRUITS, 0))

    def add(fruit: str) -> None:
        set_counts(lambda counts: {**counts, fruit: counts[fruit] + 1})

    def empty() -> None:
        set_counts(dict.fromkeys(FRUITS, 0))

    def shortcuts(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Backspace):
                empty()
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | full | pad_x(1),
        on_input=first(shortcuts, tab_focus, clear_focus),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | gap(1),
                children=(
                    *(fruit_button(fruit, partial(add, fruit)) for fruit in FRUITS),
                    Text(content="Empty", style=button_style(False), on_input=each(on_click(empty), clear_focus)),
                ),
            ),
            Text(content=" · ".join(f"{fruit}: {counts[fruit]}" for fruit in FRUITS)),
            Text(
                content="Tab moves focus, Enter adds the focused fruit, Backspace empties the basket",
                style=text_color("slate", 400),
            ),
        ),
    )

Each fruit button composes three handlers: its own add_on_enter for Enter, then, for presses, on_click and focus_receiver_on_press. The Empty button isn't focusable, and composes clear_focus with its on_click instead. The root's element composes the app's shortcuts, Tab navigation with tab_focus, and clear_focus for a press that lands on no button.

Tab from nothing focused focuses Apples, and the second Tab focuses Pears, which handles Enter itself, so the two Enters add two pears. A press on Plums both focuses it and adds a plum, since each runs both press handlers. A press on Apples that's released below it focuses Apples, which happens on the MouseDown, but adds no apple, since on_click acts only on a release over its element. A press beside the buttons reaches only the root's element, whose clear_focus clears focus, and a press on Empty empties the basket and clears focus too.

docs.title: Composing Handlers
docs.text: first tries handlers in order and stops at the first that handles the event, so the order states their precedence. In first(on_click(open_menu), drag_panel), drag_panel never sees a button 1 press, which on_click handles. each runs every handler and combines their controls, which is how two handlers that both act on a MouseDown share one element: only the element that stops a press's first MouseDown receives the rest of it, so they can't sit on an element and its parent. In the basket, on_click and focus_receiver_on_press both claim a press's MouseDown, so each runs them both, where first would run only on_click, and the press would never move focus.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.first
docs.text:
first(*handlers: InputHandler) -> InputHandler

A handler that calls each of handlers in turn with the same event and receiver, and returns the first response that isn't None, () included, without calling the rest. It returns None if none of them responds.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.each
docs.text:
each(*handlers: InputHandler) -> InputHandler

A handler that calls every one of handlers with the same event and receiver. If any responds with something other than None, it returns a tuple of every control they returned, in the order of handlers, which is () if every response was (). It returns None if none of them responds.

docs.title: Headless Components
docs.text:
A headless component returns its behavior as a handler, on_input, for the component to put on the element it returns, composed with any others:

field = use_text_input(value, set_value)
Text(content=..., on_input=first(field.on_input, submit_on_enter, focus_receiver_on_press))

The hook's handler returns None for the keys it doesn't edit with, such as Enter and Tab, so a handler after it in first, or on an ancestor, gets them.

docs.title: Clicks
docs.text: on_click makes a button: it claims a press's MouseDown, so the rest of the press comes to its element, and calls its action on the press's MouseUp, if the pointer is still over the element. As on the web, a press that's dragged off a button before it's released doesn't click it, which is how a user backs out of a click they've started.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.on_click
docs.text:
on_click(
    action: Callable[[], InputResponse],
) -> InputHandler

A handler that claims a button 1 MouseDown, and so every later event of the press, and on the press's MouseUp, calls action if the release is over the element: inside its border box, and inside its clip, where it's painted. It returns the controls action returns, or () if action returns None. It returns None for anything else, such as a key or a pointer move with no button held.

docs.title: Focus
docs.text:
Nothing moves focus unless a handler returns a control that does, so Tab navigation and click-to-focus are handlers an app composes in, as the basket does. focus_on_press focuses some other component, by its focus handle, as the labels of the order form focus their fields.

tab_focus moves within the element it's attached to, so on the root component's element it moves through the whole tree, and on a dialog's element it keeps Tab inside the dialog. A focused component that wants Tab for itself, such as a code editor that indents with it, handles it and returns (), so it never bubbles to tab_focus. The headless text components don't: they pass Tab on, so it moves focus out of them.

Every handler here that acts on a press claims its MouseDown, so of nested elements with press handlers, the innermost takes the press: with focus_receiver_on_press on nested focusable components, a press focuses the innermost one under the pointer. A press on a non-focusable element that claims presses, such as a button made with on_click, leaves focus where it was, unless the element composes clear_focus in too, as the basket's Empty button does.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.tab_focus
docs.text:
tab_focus(
    event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver
) -> InputResponse

A handler that moves focus to the next focusable component inside its element for Tab, and to the previous one for Shift+Tab, wrapping at the ends. On the root component's element it moves through the whole tree; on a modal's, it keeps Tab inside the modal. It returns None for anything else.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.focus_receiver_on_press
docs.text:
focus_receiver_on_press(
    event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver
) -> InputResponse

A handler that claims a MouseDown and focuses the component whose element received it. It goes on the element a focusable component returns, the one whose receiver carries its focus_handle. It returns None for anything else.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

For a MouseDown whose receiver has no focus_handle, because the component never called use_focus, or the handler is on an inner element.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.focus_on_press
docs.text:
focus_on_press(handle: FocusHandle) -> InputHandler

A handler that claims a MouseDown and focuses the component with handle, such as a label focusing the input beside it, whatever element received the press. It returns None for anything else.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.clear_focus
docs.text:
clear_focus(
    event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver
) -> InputResponse

A handler that claims a MouseDown and clears focus. On the root component's element it blurs on a press nothing below it claimed; composed into a non-focusable element's own press handler, it blurs on the presses that element claims. It returns None for anything else.

docs.title: Scrolling
docs.text:
Nothing scrolls a scroll container unless a handler returns a control that does, so a container the wheel scrolls composes scroll_on_wheel in, and one the keyboard scrolls composes scroll_on_keys in, on a focusable component's element:

from counterweight.handlers import first, scroll_on_keys, scroll_on_wheel

use_focus()
Div(style=fill(1) | col | overflow_y_scroll, on_input=first(scroll_on_keys(), scroll_on_wheel()), children=...)

Scrolling shows them at work, and binds paging to other keys with page_down and page_up.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.scroll_on_wheel
docs.text:
scroll_on_wheel(lines: int = 3) -> InputHandler

A handler that scrolls the scroll container it's on by lines toward the wheel's direction for each MouseScrolledUp, MouseScrolledDown, MouseScrolledLeft and MouseScrolledRight, which is three lines by default, as desktop platforms scroll for each notch of the wheel. With Shift held, the vertical wheel scrolls sideways, as browsers on Windows and Linux do: up scrolls left and down scrolls right. It returns None for a wheel event that would move the container past the end of its range, so the event bubbles to the next scroll container out, as the web chains scrolling, and for anything else.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

For a wheel event whose receiver isn't a scroll container.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.scroll_on_keys
docs.text:
scroll_on_keys(page: float = PAGE_FRACTION) -> InputHandler

A handler that scrolls the scroll container it's on for the keys that scroll a page in a browser: Up and Down by a row, Left and Right by a column, PageUp and PageDown by page times the height of the view (see page_down), and Home and End to the start and the end of the content. A key press reaches it while the container, or an element inside it, is focused, so the container is usually the top-level element of a component that calls use_focus, and a focused element inside that handles a key itself stops it first. It returns None for a key that would move the container past the end of its range, so the key bubbles to the next scroll container out, as scroll_on_wheel does with the wheel, and for anything else.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

If page isn't positive, and for one of those keys when its receiver isn't a scroll container.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.page_down
docs.text:
page_down(
    target: ElementHandle | Subtree,
    scroll: Scroll,
    fraction: float = PAGE_FRACTION,
) -> ScrollBy

The ScrollBy that scrolls the scroll container target names, scrolled as scroll says, down by fraction of the height of its view, rounded down, and at least one row.

The default is Chrome's, so on a 24-row view a page is 21 rows, and 3 stay in view. fraction=0.5 is less's half page for d, and fraction=1.0 its whole page for Space, with nothing kept.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

If fraction isn't positive.

docs.title: counterweight.handlers.page_up
docs.text:
page_up(
    target: ElementHandle | Subtree,
    scroll: Scroll,
    fraction: float = PAGE_FRACTION,
) -> ScrollBy

The ScrollBy that scrolls the scroll container target names up by a page, as page_down scrolls it down.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

If fraction isn't positive.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
These pages show how to get each layout effect, with every technique that achieves it, shown as code beside its screenshot. Where a technique has a well-known failure, the failure is shown too.

Each example labels its boxes with the styles that produced them. The examples are components; they all assume these imports:

import waxy

from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.elements import Div, Text
from counterweight.styles.utilities import *

waxy provides the values that styles are built from, for the cases no utility covers.

To run one, call the component and pass the result to counterweight.app, as in app(root()).

Start with Choosing a layout model, which says when to reach for flexbox and when for grid. Then read How layout sizes things: the defaults it describes explain most surprises in the other pages.

docs.title: Alignment and Distribution
docs.text:
A container places its children along two axes. The justify_children_* utilities distribute them along the main axis (across a row, down a col), and the align_children_* utilities place them on the cross axis. A child can override its parent's cross-axis alignment for itself with align_self_*. In a grid, justify_items_* and justify_self_* place items within their cells along the row.

The examples on this page title each panel with this helper, which draws its text over the top border:

def title(content: str) -> Text:
    return Text(content=f" {content} ", style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border)

docs.title: Distributing children along the main axis
docs.text:
The justify_children_* utilities share out the free space a row or column has left over after its children take their sizes. Children that grow leave no free space, so these only matter when nothing claims it.

@component
def justify() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=row | justify | border,
                children=(
                    title(name),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="a"),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="bb"),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="ccc"),
                ),
            )
            for name, justify in (
                ("justify_children_start", justify_children_start),
                ("justify_children_center", justify_children_center),
                ("justify_children_end", justify_children_end),
                ("justify_children_space_between", justify_children_space_between),
                ("justify_children_space_around", justify_children_space_around),
                ("justify_children_space_evenly", justify_children_space_evenly),
            )
        ),
    )

docs.title: Aligning children on the cross axis
docs.text:
The default, align_children_stretch, fills the cross axis; the others keep each child at its content size and place it.

@component
def align() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=row | align | fill(1) | border,
                children=(
                    title(name),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="a"),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="b\nb"),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="c\nc\nc"),
                ),
            )
            for name, align in (
                ("align_children_start", align_children_start),
                ("align_children_center", align_children_center),
                ("align_children_end", align_children_end),
                ("align_children_stretch", align_children_stretch),
            )
        ),

docs.title: Reversing the main axis
docs.text:
row_reverse and col_reverse lay children out right to left and bottom to top, as CSS's flex-direction: row-reverse and column-reverse do, so the first child ends up last on screen without reordering the children themselves. They reverse the main axis too, so with no justify_children_* the children pack against the main axis's new start, the right edge or the bottom.

justify_children_start and justify_children_end are CSS's start and end, not flex-start and flex-end: they name the container's own edges, left and top or right and bottom, whichever way its children run. So row_reverse | justify_children_start keeps the reversed order and packs it against the left edge, as a toolbar whose newest item goes first would.

@component
def reverse() -> Div:
    def items() -> tuple[Text, ...]:
        return tuple(Text(style=border | border_heavy, content=content) for content in ("1", "22", "333"))

    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            *(
                Div(style=direction | border, children=(title(name), *items()))
                for name, direction in (
                    ("row", row),
                    ("row_reverse", row_reverse),
                    ("row_reverse | justify_children_start", row_reverse | justify_children_start),
                )
            ),
            Div(
                style=row,
                children=tuple(
                    Div(
                        style=direction | align_children_start | height(13) | fill(1) | border,
                        children=(title(name), *items()),
                    )
                    for name, direction in (
                        ("col", col),
                        ("col_reverse", col_reverse),
                        ("… | justify_children_start", col_reverse | justify_children_start),
                    )
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Centering a box
docs.text:
Center a box on both axes with center_children, which is justify_children_center | align_children_center. It works in a grid too: there it centers the grid's tracks, and a grid with no template sizes its one track to fit its lone child. To center a box over other content rather than among it, see A dialog centered over the app.

@component
def center() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | center_children | fill(1) | border,
                children=(title("flexbox"), Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="centered")),
            ),
            Div(
                style=display_grid | center_children | fill(1) | border,
                children=(title("grid"), Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="centered")),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Aligning grid items in their cells
docs.text:
In a grid, each item sits in a cell, which can be wider than the item. justify_items_* on the grid places every item within its cell along the row, as CSS's justify-items does, and align_children_* places them down the column, as on a flex container. The default, justify_items_stretch, fills the cell's width; the others keep each item at its content width and place it. Flexbox has no cells, so these do nothing there, as in CSS.

@component
def grid_items() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1)) | justify | fill(1) | border,
                children=(
                    title(name),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="a"),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="bb"),
                    Text(style=border | border_heavy, content="ccc"),
                ),
            )
            for name, justify in (
                ("justify_items_start", justify_items_start),
                ("justify_items_center", justify_items_center),
                ("justify_items_end", justify_items_end),
                ("justify_items_stretch", justify_items_stretch),
            )
        ),
    )

docs.title: Content larger than its container
docs.text:
The *_center and *_end utilities are CSS's safe alignments: content too large for its container starts at the container's start edge and overflows only past the end, so its beginning stays in view. Each has an *_unsafe counterpart with CSS's default behavior, which centers or end-aligns the content anyway and overflows past the start edge too. These containers are fill(1) items, which clip what overflows them, so the unsafe one cuts off the content's beginning as well as its end.

@component
def overflow() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=col | justify | fill(1) | border,
                children=(title(name), Text(content=TALL)),
            )
            for name, justify in (
                ("justify_children_center", justify_children_center),
                ("justify_children_center_unsafe", justify_children_center_unsafe),
            )
        ),
    )

docs.title: App Shells
docs.text: These whole-screen layouts combine the techniques from the other pages. Each root fills the screen and is split with flexbox: fixed parts take a length or their content's size, and the part that fills takes fill(1). When that part holds more than fits, such as a log, a transcript or a long document, make it a scroll container with overflow_y_scroll, so its content scrolls inside it while the fixed parts stay put. Splitting space shows the same splits with grid, and Choosing a layout model builds a whole shell both ways.

docs.title: Hiding a pane
docs.text:
A pane that comes and goes, such as a sidebar the user can collapse, can be hidden two ways, and they differ in what happens to its components. display_none takes an element out of the layout, as CSS's display: none does: it takes no space and draws nothing, and its siblings fill in where it was. Its components stay mounted, so they keep their state and their effects keep running. Leaving the pane out of its parent's children instead, as React's conditional rendering does, unmounts its components, which start afresh, with new state, when it comes back.

Here each side pane shows how long it has been mounted. h hides the left one with display_none, and l leaves the right one out:

@component
def pane(name: str) -> Text:
    mounted_for = use_clock(timedelta(seconds=1)).since_mount
    return Text(
        style=length(18) | border,
        content=f"{name}\n\nmounted for\n{mounted_for // timedelta(seconds=1)} s",
    )


@component
def hiding() -> Div:
    is_hidden, set_hidden = use_state(False)
    is_left_out, set_left_out = use_state(False)

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, _: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key="h"):
                set_hidden(toggle)
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key="l"):
                set_left_out(toggle)
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col,
        on_input=on_input,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | fill(1),
                children=(
                    # Hidden, the pane takes no space and draws nothing, but stays mounted.
                    Div(style=display_none if is_hidden else default, children=(pane("display_none"),)),
                    Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="main: fill(1)"),
                    # Left out, the pane unmounts, and mounts afresh when it comes back.
                    *(() if is_left_out else (pane("left out"),)),
                ),
            ),
            Text(style=text_bg("slate", 700), content=" h: hide the left pane   l: leave out the right pane"),
        ),
    )

With both gone, the main pane fills the row:

Hide a pane with display_none when what's in it should survive being hidden, such as a half-typed draft or a scroll position, and leave it out when it should start over, or when it's expensive to keep running.

docs.title: A dialog over the app
docs.text: See A dialog centered over the app.

docs.title: Choosing a Layout Model
docs.text: The other pages in this section show how to get each effect with flexbox and with grid. This one helps you decide which of the two to use for a container.

docs.title: Who owns the sizes
docs.text:
Flexbox and grid can build most of the same layouts. What differs is where the sizes are written. In a grid, the parent lists them as track templates, and the children fill the tracks in order. In flexbox, each child carries its own size, and the parent only sets the direction. In short, grid is top-down and flexbox is bottom-up.

Here is one app shell built both ways, with the same result:

FlexboxGrid 
@component
def shell_flex() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | fill(1),
                children=(
                    Text(style=length(20) | border, content="sidebar:\nlength(20)"),
                    Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="main:\nfill(1)"),
                ),
            ),
            Text(style=length(1) | text_bg("slate", 700), content=" status: length(1)"),
        ),
    )

@component
def shell_grid() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(20, fr(1)) | grid_template_rows(fr(1), 1),
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="sidebar:\n20"),
            Text(style=border, content="main:\nfr(1)"),
            Text(style=grid_column(1, span(2)) | text_bg("slate", 700), content=" status: 1"),

So choose by which should own the sizes: the container, or each child.

docs.title: Flexbox or grid?
docs.text:
Use grid when the container owns the arrangement: a fixed set of slots known up front, such as an app shell or a dashboard, or columns that must line up across rows.

Grid costs locality. A child's size lives on its parent, away from the component that draws it, and children fill the tracks in order, so a child the template didn't plan for starts a new implicit row, and the rows split the height between them. A flexbox row takes the same extra child as one more column. Auto flow shows how grid adds the tracks.

GridFlexbox 
@component
def extra_child_grid() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1)),
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="fr(1)"),
            Text(style=border, content="fr(1)"),
            Text(style=border, content="a third child"),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText

└─────────────────────┘└────────────────────┘
┌─────────────────────┐                      
│a third child        │                      
└─────────────────────┘                      

@component
def extra_child_flex() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=(
            Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1)"),
            Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1)"),
            Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1)"),
        ),
    )

┌─────────────┐┌─────────────┐┌─────────────┐
│fill(1)      ││fill(1)      ││fill(1)      │
│             ││             ││             │
│             ││             ││             │
│             ││             ││             │

Use flexbox when each child owns its size: a variable number of children (lists, toolbars, tags), content-sized items, wrapping, or a component that keeps its size wherever it's placed, such as a sidebar that's always length(24).

Flexbox costs alignment across rows: two rows' columns line up only if each child in them repeats the same size. In a grid they line up for free, as in Dashboard tiles.

docs.title: Mixing them
docs.text:
The choice is per container, not per app. Any child of a grid can be a flexbox container, and any flexbox child can be a grid. A common split for a terminal app is a grid for the screen, whose panes are a fixed set known up front, and flexbox inside each pane, for the lists, toolbars and status items whose number varies. Here the grid places the panes, the sidebar is a col of items, and the status bar is a row that pushes its items to either end:

@component
def mixed() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(20, fr(1)) | grid_template_rows(fr(1), 1),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | border,
                children=(Text(content="inbox"), Text(content="drafts"), Text(content="sent")),
            ),
            Text(style=border, content="main: fr(1)"),
            Div(
                style=row | justify_children_space_between | grid_column(1, span(2)),
                children=(
                    Text(style=text_bg("slate", 700), content=" status: row"),
                    Text(style=text_bg("slate", 700), content="justify_children_space_between "),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )
