docs.title: Coming from ratatui?
docs.text:
Ratatui splits an area by a list of constraints on the parent, and never lets content push back: it hands each widget a rectangle to draw into. Grid with fr tracks has the same structure, and the constraint utilities give the same sizes in flexbox, with each child holding its own constraint. A few things behave differently.

Conflicts overflow instead of giving way. Ratatui shrinks lower-priority constraints until the areas fit inside the parent, so Length(30) twice in 40 cells comes out 20 and 20. Flexbox has no priorities, and the constraint utilities don't shrink, so length(30) twice overflows, as in the top row below. Decide which child gives way and say so: shrink(1) lets a length shrink below its basis, as on both children in the bottom row, and fill(1) takes whatever is left, or nothing.

@component
def conflict() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | width(42) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=length(30) | border, content="length(30)"),
                    Text(style=length(30) | border, content="length(30)"),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | width(42) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=length(30) | shrink(1) | border, content="length(30)\n| shrink(1)"),
                    Text(style=length(30) | shrink(1) | border, content="length(30)\n| shrink(1)"),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

┃└────────────────────────────┘└────────────────────────────┘

┃┌──────────────────┐┌──────────────────┐┃

┃│| shrink(1)       ││| shrink(1)       │┃                   
┃└──────────────────┘└──────────────────┘┃

Percentages don't subtract gaps. Ratatui takes spacing out of the area first; a CSS percentage is a share of the whole parent, so two halves and a gap overflow. Use fill(1) for equal shares.

Flex::Legacy, which gives leftover space to the last constraint, has no counterpart. Put grow(1) on the child that should take it. The other Flex modes are the justify_children_* utilities of the same names, and ratatui's full-size cross axis is flexbox's default stretch (see Alignment and distribution).

docs.title: Clipping
docs.text: A box's content can be larger than the box. Its overflow, as in CSS's overflow, decides whether what doesn't fit is drawn anyway or cut off. This page covers cutting it off, how a box draws on its parent's border when its parent cuts things off, and how a box such as a dropdown escapes the clip altogether.

docs.title: Hiding overflow
docs.text:
By default a box's overflow is visible: children that don't fit are drawn past its padding box, over its border and whatever lies beyond. overflow_hidden clips them to its padding box instead, so nothing inside the box is drawn outside its border. overflow_scroll clips them the same way, and lets them scroll. A Text's lines overflow its box the same way, and overflow_hidden on the Text clips them to its own padding box (see Text in layout).

@component
def hidden() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=col,
                children=(
                    Div(
                        style=col | border | height(4) | width(20) | overflow,
                        children=tuple(Text(content=f"line {i}") for i in range(1, 7)),
                    ),
                    Text(content="below"),
                ),
            )
            for overflow in (overflow_visible, overflow_hidden)
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
│line 1            │  │line 1            │
│line 2            │  │line 2            │
└line 3            ┘  └──────────────────┘
below                 below               
 line 5                                   
 line 6

Layout doesn't change: the clipped children are just as large, and only the part inside the box is drawn. The constraint utilities, length, percentage, ratio and fill, hide their box's overflow, so a constrained box always clips its children.

overflow_clip clips the same way. The two differ in layout, as they do in CSS: a flex item with overflow_hidden can shrink below its content's size, while one with overflow_clip keeps the content's size as its minimum, as a visible one does (see Content sets a minimum size).

docs.title: Clipping one axis
docs.text:
overflow_x_hidden clips only at the left and right of the padding box, and overflow_y_hidden only at the top and bottom. The overflow_x_* and overflow_y_* utilities each set one axis, so they combine with each other, as overflow_x_hidden | overflow_y_clip.

@component
def one_axis() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(8),
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=border | height(4) | width(16) | overflow,
                children=(Text(content=LINES, style=height(6)),),
            )
            for overflow in (overflow_x_hidden, overflow_y_hidden)
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText

│line 2 of a lo│        │line 2 of a lon

docs.title: Clipping applies whatever the z
docs.text:
A clip cuts off everything inside the box, wherever it's positioned and however high its z, as on the web: a raised menu inside a box that hides its overflow is cut off at the box's padding box, unless it escapes every clip.

@component
def raised() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | border | size(30, 5) | overflow_hidden,
                children=(
                    Text(content="File  Edit  View"),
                    Text(
                        content="Open…\nSave\nSave As…\nQuit",
                        style=z(1) | position_absolute | inset_top(1) | inset_left(0) | border | border_heavy,
                    ),
                ),
            ),
            Text(content="The menu is cut off inside the box's border,\nhowever high its z."),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌────────────────────────────┐                  
│File  Edit  View            │                  
│┏━━━━━━━━┓                  │                  
│┃Open…   ┃                  │                  
└────────────────────────────┘                  
The menu is cut off inside the box's border,    
however high its z.

Nested boxes that clip combine: a box inside two of them is drawn only where both let it.

docs.title: Drawing on the parent's border
docs.text:
A border title is positioned on its parent's border, outside the padding box, so a parent that hides its overflow clips it away. clip_to_border clips a box to its parent's border box instead, so it can draw on the border and is still cut off at the border's outer edge. clip_to_padding is the default.

@component
def clip_to() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | border | pad_x(1),
                children=(
                    Text(content=f" {name} ", style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip),
                    Text(content="fill(1) hides its overflow"),
                ),
            )
            for name, clip in (("clip_to_padding", clip_to_padding), ("clip_to_border", clip_to_border))
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌────────────────────────────┐┌─ clip_to_border ───────────┐
│ fill(1) hides its overflow ││ fill(1) hides its overflow │
└────────────────────────────┘└────────────────────────────┘

A parent whose overflow is visible clips nothing, so the two agree there, but a title that sets clip_to_border keeps working when its parent starts to clip. CSS has no equivalent property: its overflow-clip-margin widens the clip for every child of the box that sets it, where clip_to is set on the child, so a title can reach the border while the rest of the content stops at the padding box.

docs.title: Escaping every clip
docs.text:
A dropdown or an autocomplete list has to reach past the box it opens from, even when that box, or one around it, clips. clip_to_screen makes a box unclipped: no ancestor clips it, so only the edge of the screen cuts it off.

@component
def unclipped() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | border | size(30, 5) | overflow_hidden,
                children=(
                    Text(content="File  Edit  View"),
                    Text(
                        content="Open…\nSave\nSave As…\nQuit",
                        style=z(1)
                        | position_absolute
                        | inset_top(1)
                        | inset_left(0)
                        | clip_to_screen
                        | border
                        | border_heavy,
                    ),
                ),
            ),
            Text(content="With clip_to_screen, the menu\nreaches past the box.", style=pad_left(11)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌────────────────────────────┐                  
│File  Edit  View            │                  
│┏━━━━━━━━┓                  │                  
│┃Open…   ┃                  │                  
└┃Save    ┃──────────────────┘                  
 ┃Save As…┃With clip_to_screen, the menu        
 ┃Quit    ┃reaches past the box.

Everything else about an unclipped box is as usual. It's positioned against its parent, so the menu stays under its menu bar. It's drawn in the usual order, so it needs a z to draw over what follows it, and a box elsewhere with a higher z still covers it. Its own overflow still clips its children, whose clips start from the screen. It receives the mouse wherever it's drawn, including outside its ancestors.

On the web, a dropdown escapes a clip with position: fixed, which positions it against the viewport, so the page then has to work out where its anchor is, in script or with anchor positioning. An unclipped box keeps its parent as the box it's positioned against, so it's anchored already. The autocomplete recipe builds a complete one.

A scroll container clips to its padding box too, so in a list of titled panels that scrolls, a panel scrolled partly out of view loses the same part of its title as of its border. A title clipped to the screen would be drawn past the scroll container's edge instead.

PANELS = ElementHandle()


@component
def scrolled_panels() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | size(24, 6) | overflow_y_scroll,
        handle=PANELS,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=border | border_lightrounded | height(3) | shrink(0),
                children=(
                    Text(
                        content=f" {title} ", style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border
                    ),
                    Text(content=body),
                ),
            )
            for title, body in (("web", "3 replicas"), ("worker", "8 replicas"), ("cron", "1 replica"))
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText

╰──────────────────────╯
╭─ worker ─────────────╮
│8 replicas            │
╰──────────────────────╯
╭─ cron ───────────────╮

docs.title: Percentage insets and borders
docs.text:
Insets on an absolutely positioned box are measured from its parent's padding box, as in CSS, so inset_top=Percent(1.0) puts the box's top edge at the bottom of the padding box, which is the bottom border's row when the parent has a border.

below_parent = Style(layout=waxy.Style(position=waxy.Position.Absolute, inset_top=waxy.Percent(1.0)))


@component
def percent_inset() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=border | width(30) | pad_x(1),
        children=(
            Text(content="inset_top=Percent(1.0)"),
            Text(content=" on the border row ", style=below_parent | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌────────────────────────────┐
│ inset_top=Percent(1.0)     │
└─ on the border row ────────┘

docs.title: Clipping and the mouse
docs.text:
A box receives the mouse only where it's drawn. Over a part of a box that's clipped away, mouse events go to whatever is drawn there instead, use_hovered reports the mouse outside the box, and on_click doesn't click it.

use_rects still reports each box whole, since a box that's partly clipped is still where layout put it. Its clip is the region the box's ancestors let it draw in, and its visible is the part of its border box inside that region, or None when none of it is.

docs.title: Grids and Wrapping
docs.text: display_grid lays a container's children out in rows and columns at once. The container lists its tracks with grid_template_columns and grid_template_rows, and each child fills the next free cell, or the cells it asks for. The examples on this page size every track with fr(1), one share of the grid's free space.

docs.title: Dashboard tiles
docs.text:
Equal tracks on both axes give a grid of equal tiles, and gap separates them.

@component
def tiles() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)) | grid_template_rows(fr(1), fr(1)) | gap(1),
        children=tuple(Text(style=border, content=f"tile {n}") for n in range(1, 7)),
    )

docs.title: Cells spanning tracks
docs.text:
grid_column and grid_row place a child by grid line, counted from 1, and span(n) stretches it across n tracks. Children without a placement fill the cells that are left, in order.

Place a spanning child on both axes, as both are here. A child placed on rows alone is placed before one placed on columns alone, whatever their order among the children, so mixing the two can push a child into an extra row below the template.

@component
def spans() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)) | grid_template_rows(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)),
        children=(
            Text(
                style=grid_row(1) | grid_column(1, span(2)) | border | border_heavy,
                content="grid_row(1)\ngrid_column(1, span(2))",
            ),
            Text(
                style=grid_row(1, span(3)) | grid_column(3) | border | border_heavy,
                content="grid_row(\n  1, span(3),\n)\ngrid_column(3)",
            ),
            Text(style=border, content="auto"),
            Text(style=border, content="auto"),
            Text(style=border, content="auto"),
            Text(style=border, content="auto"),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Auto flow
docs.text:
Children beyond the template's cells get new tracks, which the grid adds as it needs them. By default, children fill each row in turn and the grid adds rows, like the seventh child on the left. grid_auto_flow_column fills each column in turn and adds columns instead.

@component
def auto_flow() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)) | fill(1) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(
                        content=" grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)) ",
                        style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border,
                    ),
                    *(Text(style=border, content=str(n)) for n in range(1, 8)),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=display_grid
                | grid_template_rows(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1))
                | grid_auto_flow_column
                | fill(1)
                | border
                | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(
                        content=" grid_template_rows(fr(1), fr(1), fr(1)) ",
                        style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border,
                    ),
                    Text(
                        content=" grid_auto_flow_column ",
                        style=position_absolute | inset_bottom(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border,
                    ),
                    *(Text(style=border, content=str(n)) for n in range(1, 8)),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.text:
When children have different sizes and there's no grid for them to line up in, flex_wrap lets a row start a new line when the next child doesn't fit. gap_width spaces the children within a line.

@component
def wrap() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | flex_wrap | align_children_start | gap_width(1),
        children=tuple(Text(style=border | pad_x(1), content=tag) for tag in TAGS),
    )

docs.title: How Layout Sizes Things
docs.text:
Counterweight lays out elements with Taffy, which implements CSS flexbox and grid with their CSS defaults:

  • flex_direction is row.
  • flex_grow is 0, so children don't grow into free space on the main axis.
  • flex_shrink is 1, so children shrink when they don't fit.
  • align_items is stretch, so children fill their parent on the cross axis.
  • Sizes are border-box: a width includes the border and padding.

Together, these mean a child takes its content's size along its parent's direction, and its parent's full size across it.

docs.title: Children take their content size along the main axis
docs.text:
In a row, each child is as wide as its content and as tall as the row:

@component
def row_defaults() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="one"),
            Text(style=border, content="two two"),
            Text(style=border, content="three three three"),
        ),
    )

The space to the right is free space that no child claimed. Splitting space shows how to hand it out.

docs.title: Children stretch across the cross axis
docs.text:
In a col, the axes swap: each child is as tall as its content and as wide as the column.

@component
def col_defaults() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="one"),
            Text(style=border, content="two two"),
            Text(style=border, content="three three three"),
        ),
    )

docs.title: The root fills the screen
docs.text:
The app places the root component in a grid cell the size of the terminal, and the root stretches to fill it, whatever its content. Content wider than the terminal can't widen the root: the wide line overflows the root, drawing over its border, and the edge of the screen cuts it off. overflow_hidden on the root would clip it at the root's padding box instead.

@component
def root_fills_screen() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_heavy,
        children=(Text(content="root: col | border | border_heavy"), Text(content=WIDE)),
    )

docs.title: Content sets a minimum size
docs.text:
A flex item can't shrink below its content's minimum size, which CSS calls the automatic minimum size. For a Text that doesn't wrap, that minimum is the whole line; for one that wraps, it's the widest word. In the top row below, two grow(1) children with long lines can't take half the row each, so they overflow it.

fill(1) has no automatic minimum, so in the bottom row the same two children split the row evenly. It hides the child's overflow, and CSS gives a box that hides its overflow a minimum size of zero. Hiding its overflow also clips each Text's line at its own padding box. min_width(0) (or min_height(0) in a col) lowers the minimum the same way on its own axis, but leaves the overflow visible, so each line would run past its box.

@component
def automatic_minimum() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=grow(1) | border, content=LONG),
                    Text(style=grow(1) | border, content=LONG),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=fill(1) | border, content=LONG),
                    Text(style=fill(1) | border, content=LONG),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Text doesn't wrap unless asked to
docs.text:
A Text renders each line of its content on one row. A line wider than the box overflows it, as text does in CSS, drawing over the box's border and past it, as in the top box below. overflow_hidden clips the line at the box's padding box, as in the middle one, and a wrap mode such as text_wrap_stable breaks lines to fit the box's width instead, as in the bottom one. Text in layout shows how wrapping text sizes itself, and Text wrapping compares the wrap modes.

@component
def wrapping() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=width(24) | border, content=PARAGRAPH),
            Text(style=width(24) | border | overflow_hidden, content=PARAGRAPH),
            Text(style=width(24) | border | text_wrap_stable, content=PARAGRAPH),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Layering
docs.text: Most boxes sit where layout puts them, side by side. Positioning moves a box off that spot, so it can overlap others, and z decides which of the overlapping boxes is drawn on top.

docs.title: Relative positioning
docs.text:
position_relative with insets moves a box from where layout placed it, without moving anything else: its siblings keep the space it would have taken. Insets are measured in cells, and inset_top(2) moves the box down two rows.

@component
def relative() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | align_children_start | gap(3),
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="first"),
            Text(
                style=position_relative | inset_top(2) | inset_left(2) | border | border_heavy,
                content="position_relative\ninset_top(2)\ninset_left(2)",
            ),
            Text(style=border, content="third"),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Controlling overlap with z
docs.text:
Where boxes overlap, the one with the higher z is drawn on top. Boxes with equal z are drawn in the order they appear in the tree, each parent before its children, and a box that sets no z counts as 0.

def root() -> Div:

        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(
                style=z(1)

                | margin(1)
                | margin_color("purple", 600),
                content="z = +1",

                | position_absolute
                | inset_left(4)
                | inset_top(3)
                | border
                | border_lightrounded
                | margin(1)

                content="z =  0",

                | border
                | border_lightrounded

                | margin_color("red", 600),

docs.title: Stacking contexts
docs.text:
z only orders boxes within a stacking context, as CSS's z-index does. A box that sets z, z(0) included, forms one: it and everything inside it are drawn together, as one layer at its z, and the z of a box inside it orders that box only among the others inside it. A box that sets no z forms none, so the boxes inside it are layered alongside it, among the boxes of the nearest stacking context around it. The app's root always forms one.

So a box is always drawn beneath the boxes inside it, whatever z they set. A negative z puts a box beneath the other boxes of its stacking context, but still over the box that forms the context.

A z(1) dropdown inside a toolbar that sets no z joins the stacking context around the toolbar, so it's drawn over the content below the toolbar:

def menu_bar(toolbar_style: Style) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=toolbar_style | row | gap(2) | border | pad_x(1),
                children=(
                    Text(content="file"),
                    Text(content="edit"),
                    Text(
                        style=z(1) | position_absolute | inset_top(2) | inset_left(0) | border | border_heavy,
                        content="new\nopen\nsave\nquit",
                    ),
                ),
            ),
            Text(style=border, content="The page's content"),
        ),
    )


@component
def dropdown_escapes() -> Div:
    return menu_bar(toolbar_style=Style())


@component
def dropdown_scoped() -> Div:
    return menu_bar(toolbar_style=z(0))

The whole toolbar is drawn at 0, and the page's content, which comes after it in the tree, is drawn over the dropdown, leaving only the part of the dropdown that hangs below the page visible.

docs.title: A dialog centered over the app
docs.text:
To center a box over its parent, as CSS does, position it absolutely with insets of 0, auto margins, and a fit-content size. The insets make its whole parent the space to place it in, the fit-content size keeps it as small as its content, and the auto margins split the space left over evenly on each side, whether or not the parent centers its children. A margin paints nothing unless its element sets margin_color, so the app's content shows around the dialog. The dialog is drawn over the content because it comes after it; a dialog that comes earlier in the tree needs a higher z.

An absolutely positioned box is always placed in its own parent, never a more distant ancestor or the screen, so a dialog centers over the whole app only when it's a child of an element that fills the screen, such as the root component's element here. A dialog rendered deeper in the tree centers over its own parent.

dialog_box = position_absolute | inset(0) | margin_auto | fit_content_width | fit_content_height


@component
def dialog() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="header"),
            Text(
                style=fill(1) | border | text_wrap_stable,
                content="The app's content stays where it is, and the dialog draws over it. " * 4,
            ),
            Text(
                style=dialog_box | border | border_double | pad_x(2) | pad_y(1),
                content="a dialog centered over the app",
            ),
        ),
    )

Known issue: parents with a border, and grids

The layout engine, Taffy, mismeasures auto margins on an absolutely positioned box in two kinds of parent. In a flex parent with a border, the dialog lands one cell right of and below center, because the space its margins split includes the parent's border. In a grid parent, the auto margins are ignored, so the dialog sits at the parent's top-left corner. A parent with padding and no border centers it correctly.

docs.title: A badge pinned to a corner
docs.text:
Negative insets reach past the parent's padding box onto its border. inset_top(-1) puts a box on the top border, and inset_right(-1) on the right border. clip_to_border keeps the badges visible if the parent hides its overflow.

@component
def badge() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | align_children_start | gap(2),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=border | pad_x(1),
                children=(
                    Text(content="inbox"),
                    Text(
                        style=position_absolute
                        | inset_top(-1)
                        | inset_right(1)
                        | clip_to_border
                        | text_color("red", 500),
                        content="3",
                    ),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=border | pad_x(1),
                children=(
                    Text(content="alerts"),
                    Text(
                        style=position_absolute
                        | inset_top(-1)
                        | inset_right(-1)
                        | clip_to_border
                        | text_bg("red", 600),
                        content="!",

docs.title: Scrolling
docs.text: A box whose overflow is Scroll is a scroll container: its content can be larger than it, and it shows the part its offset scrolls into view. This page covers making one, scrolling it with the wheel, the keyboard and from handlers, scrolling an element into view, and reading how far it's scrolled. Clipping covers how a scroll container cuts off what's outside its padding box, which it does as a box with hidden overflow does.

docs.title: Scroll areas
docs.text:
Most scrolling boxes want the same things: the wheel and the keys scroll them, Tab and a click focus them, as browsers make a scroll container focusable, and a style that scrolls even beside a constraint utility that hides overflow. use_scroll_area gives a component all of those, and leaves drawing it to the component, and scroll_area is a bordered box built on it:

SOURCE = (
    "def deploy(image: str, steps: tuple[int, ...] = (10, 50, 100)) -> None:",
    "    for percent in steps:",
    "        shift_traffic(image, percent)",
)


@component
def panes() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(1),
        on_input=tab_focus,
        children=(
            scroll_area(
                tuple(Text(content=event) for event in EVENTS),
                style=size(24, 6),
                auto_focus=True,
            ),
            scroll_area(
                tuple(Text(content=line) for line in SOURCE),
                axis="x",
                style=size(24, 6),
            ),
        ),
    )

╭──────────────────────╮ ╭──────────────────────╮
│ deploy started       │ │ def deploy(image: str│
│ pulled image web:4.2.│ │     for percent in st│
│ migrations applied   │ │         shift_traffic│
│ health check passed  │ │                      │

The rest of this page covers the pieces they're built from, for a box that needs something they don't do.

docs.title: Scroll containers
docs.text:
overflow_scroll makes a box a scroll container on both axes, and overflow_x_scroll and overflow_y_scroll on one, as CSS's overflow: scroll does. On an axis it scrolls, the box clips its children to its padding box, and moves them up and left by its offset.

Counterweight holds each scroll container's offset, as a browser holds an element's scrollTop, so a box scrolls without any state in the component that renders it. It starts at 0, the start of the content. After every layout, it moves to keep the content in view where it was (see Keeping the content in view), and is clamped to how far the content reaches, so when the content shrinks, the box scrolls back as far as it has to. A scroll container that unmounts or is hidden loses its offset, and starts at 0 again when it comes back.

How far a box can scroll is how far its content reaches past its padding box, as on the web. That includes its absolutely positioned descendants, so a dropdown that opens past the bottom of a scrolling form lets the form scroll down to show it (see the autocomplete recipe).

A scroll container's automatic minimum size is 0, as one with hidden overflow's is (see Content sets a minimum size), so a flex item that scrolls shrinks to fit beside its siblings instead of growing to fit its content. That's usually what a scrolling pane wants; give it a size, or shrink(0), when it should be as large as its content up to some limit.

A Text doesn't scroll its own text, nor a Canvas what it draws, so either one whose overflow is Scroll raises ValueError: put a long Text or a large Canvas in a Div that scrolls.

docs.title: Scrolling with the wheel
docs.text:
Nothing scrolls unless a handler scrolls it, as with every other input, so a scroll container that the wheel should scroll composes scroll_on_wheel into its on_input. A titled pane puts its border and title on a box around the part that scrolls, so they stay put while the content moves:

@component
def pane() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(30, 6),
        children=(
            Text(content=" Deploy log ", style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border),
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | col | overflow_y_scroll,
                on_input=scroll_on_wheel(),
                children=tuple(Text(content=f"{i:>2} {event}") for i, event in enumerate(EVENTS, start=1)),
            ),
        ),
    )

│ 1 deploy started           │
│ 2 pulled image web:4.2.0   │
│ 3 migrations applied       │
│ 4 health check passed      │

│ 8 latency p99 within budget│

│10 old replicas drained     │

A wheel event goes to the element under the pointer and bubbles from there, so of nested scroll containers, the innermost under the pointer scrolls. scroll_on_wheel lets an event that would move its container past either end of its range bubble on, so once the inner one reaches its end, the wheel scrolls the one around it, as the web chains scrolling from one container to the next.

With Shift held, scroll_on_wheel scrolls sideways for the vertical wheel, as browsers on Windows and Linux do, so a mouse without a sideways wheel can scroll a container that only scrolls sideways, such as a wide code block. The wheel event still says which way the wheel turned and that Shift was held, as Firefox's does, rather than reporting a sideways turn, as Chrome's does, so a handler before scroll_on_wheel can give Shift with the wheel a meaning of its own. Some terminals keep Shift with the wheel for their own scrollback and never report it, so a sideways wheel or a trackpad's sideways swipe is the only way to scroll sideways there.

docs.title: Scrolling with the keyboard
docs.text:
scroll_on_keys scrolls for the keys that scroll a page in a browser: the arrow keys by a row or a column, PageUp and PageDown by a page, and Home and End to the start and the end. A key press goes to the focused element and bubbles from there, so a container the keys scroll is usually a focusable component's top-level element, and the keys scroll it while it, or anything inside it, is focused. Like scroll_on_wheel, it lets a key that would move its container past either end of its range bubble on, to the next container out.

A page is 87.5% of the height of the view, rounded down, as in Chrome, so the last lines of one page stay in view at the top of the next, to read on from. page_down and page_up return the ScrollBy for a page of any size, for apps that bind paging to other keys, such as less's Space for a whole page and d and u for half of one:

def less_keys(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    # Receiver.scroll is None only off a scroll container, and this handler is only on one.
    if receiver.scroll is None:
        return None
    match event:
        case KeyPressed(key=" "):
            return page_down(receiver.subtree, receiver.scroll, fraction=1.0)
        case KeyPressed(key="d"):
            return page_down(receiver.subtree, receiver.scroll, fraction=0.5)
        case KeyPressed(key="u"):
            return page_up(receiver.subtree, receiver.scroll, fraction=0.5)
        case _:
            return None


@component
def pager() -> Div:
    focus = use_focus(auto_focus=True)

    return Div(
        style=col
        | border
        | border_lightrounded
        | size(30, 8)
        | overflow_y_scroll
        | (border_color("sky", 400) if focus.is_focused else border_color("slate", 600)),
        on_input=first(less_keys, scroll_on_keys(), scroll_on_wheel()),
        children=tuple(Text(content=f"{i:>2} {EVENTS[i % len(EVENTS)]}") for i in range(30)),
    )

docs.title: Scrolling from a handler
docs.text:
The ScrollTo and ScrollBy controls scroll a container to an offset, or by an amount, clamped to its range. A handler on the scroll container itself names it by its receiver's subtree, as scroll_on_wheel does. A handler anywhere else names it by an element handle, an ElementHandle, as a React component reaches a DOM node through a ref: create one with use_state(ElementHandle), and pass it to the element's handle.

@component
def controlled() -> Div:
    log, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)

    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | gap(2),
                children=(
                    Text(content="[ Top ]", on_input=on_click(lambda: ScrollTo(log, y=0))),
                    Text(content="[ Bottom ]", on_input=on_click(lambda: ScrollTo(log, y=len(EVENTS)))),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(30, 5) | overflow_y_scroll,
                handle=log,
                children=tuple(Text(content=f"{i:>2} {event}") for i, event in enumerate(EVENTS, start=1)),
            ),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

[ Top ]  [ Bottom ]           

╭────────────────────────────╮
│ 9 traffic shifted to 100%  │
│10 old replicas drained     │
│11 deploy finished          │
╰────────────────────────────╯

Two mounted elements given the same element handle raise DuplicateElementHandle, and a control whose handle names no mounted scroll container does nothing.

Scroll controls apply to the layout of the render after the handler that returns them, before that render paints, in the order they were returned, and after anchoring and sticking to the end have placed the content, so each moves the view from where those left it. So a handler that adds a line to a log and returns ScrollBy(log, y=1) beside the state change scrolls by a row of the log that has the new line, in the same frame. That's where Counterweight differs from the web: a browser's scrollBy scrolls the page as it stands while the handler runs, before React renders the state change, and a React app that wants to scroll the content that change lays out calls it from useLayoutEffect instead, which is what scroll controls do. A handler that runs later in the same batch of input sees the controls returned before it: its receiver's scroll is moved by each ScrollTo and ScrollBy since the last render, clamped to the range as of that render, so scroll_on_keys passes a key on once an earlier key has scrolled its container to the end.

docs.title: Scrolling an element into view
docs.text:
ScrollIntoView scrolls to an element rather than to an offset, as the web's scrollIntoView does: it scrolls each scroll container above the element, from the innermost out, until the element is in view. Its block says where the element goes vertically: "start", the default, puts its top at the top of the view, "center" in the middle, "end" at the bottom, and "nearest" scrolls as little as it takes, and not at all if the element is already in view. inline says the same horizontally, and is "nearest" by default. It stops at an element with clip_to_screen, since no container above that element clips it, so none has to scroll to show it.

A table of contents scrolls each section's heading to the top of the pane it's in:

SECTIONS = (
    ("Install", "Add counterweight to your project with uv."),
    ("Components", "A component is a function that returns an element."),
    ("Hooks", "Hooks keep state and run effects for a component."),
    ("Styles", "Styles are merged from small utilities with |."),
)


@component
def contents() -> Div:
    headings, _ = use_state(lambda: tuple(ElementHandle() for _ in SECTIONS))

    return Div(
        style=row | size(40, 6),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | width(14) | border_right | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1),
                children=tuple(
                    Text(
                        content=title,
                        style=text_color("sky", 300),
                        on_input=on_click(partial(ScrollIntoView, heading)),
                    )
                    for (title, _), heading in zip(SECTIONS, headings, strict=True)
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | col | gap(1) | pad_x(1) | overflow_y_scroll,
                on_input=scroll_on_wheel(1),
                children=tuple(
                    Div(
                        style=col,
                        children=(
                            Text(content=title, style=text_color("amber", 400), handle=heading),
                            Text(content=body, style=text_wrap_pretty),
                        ),
                    )
                    for (title, body), heading in zip(SECTIONS, headings, strict=True)
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

Like the other scroll controls, it applies to the layout of the render after the handler that returns it, as React's useLayoutEffect would call scrollIntoView after the DOM updates and before the browser paints. So a handler that changes state and returns ScrollIntoView beside it shows both in the same frame, and the handle names the element that has it in that render, not the one before. A list that moves a highlight with Down puts one element handle on whichever item is highlighted, and returns ScrollIntoView(handle, block="nearest") beside the state change that moves it: the handle has moved to the new item by the time the control applies (see the autocomplete recipe). use_text_area does the same for its cursor: it returns a cursor_row element handle for the element the cursor's row is drawn in, and its handler returns ScrollIntoView for it with block="nearest" beside each edit, so a text area in a scroll container keeps the cursor in view as it moves between rows.

Moving focus scrolls the newly focused element into view with block="nearest", as browsers do, so Tab never leaves focus on something out of sight. That includes a component that takes focus with auto_focus as it mounts.

ScrollIntoView scrolls in one step. The web's behavior: "smooth" animates the scroll across frames, which Counterweight has no design for yet: a fixed number of frames and a fixed duration are both plausible.

docs.title: Reading the scroll
docs.text:
use_scroll returns a Scroll: how far the calling component's top-level element is scrolled, how far it can be, and the size of its padding box, the part of the content in view. Given an ElementHandle, it reports on the element with that handle instead, as a React component reads another element's scrollTop through a ref (see Jumping to the end). A handler's Receiver carries the same for a receiving element that's a scroll container, which is how scroll_on_wheel knows whether its container can move any further.

Like use_rects, use_scroll reports the previous frame's scroll, and a component that calls it renders again as soon as it changes. A list too long to render whole can render only the rows in view, with empty boxes above and below them so the content is as tall as every row would make it, as React's windowing libraries do:

ROWS = 100_000


@component
def windowed_row(i: int) -> Text:
    return Text(content=f"row {i:,} of {ROWS:,}")


@component
def windowed() -> Div:
    scroll = use_scroll()

    # Render the rows in view, with a screen's worth of rows on each side
    # so a scroll shows rows, not blank space, before this re-renders,
    # and an empty box above and below for the rest, so the content is as tall as every row.
    overscan = scroll.view_height
    first = max(0, scroll.offset.y - overscan)
    last = min(ROWS, scroll.offset.y + scroll.view_height + overscan)

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(30, 6) | overflow_y_scroll,
        on_input=scroll_on_wheel(),
        children=(
            Div(style=height(first) | shrink(0)),
            # Keyed, so a row keeps its node as the window moves, and scroll anchoring follows the row.
            *(windowed_row(i).with_key(str(i)) for i in range(first, last)),
            Div(style=height(ROWS - last) | shrink(0)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────╮
│row 6 of 100,000            │
│row 7 of 100,000            │
│row 8 of 100,000            │
│row 9 of 100,000            │
╰────────────────────────────╯

The rows on each side of the view cover the frame between a scroll and the render that follows it, which would otherwise show the empty boxes. The rows are keyed components, so each keeps its place as the window moves (see Keeping the content in view).

docs.title: Keeping the content in view
docs.text:
When content changes above what's in view, an offset that stayed put would show different content: a message dropped from the top of a transcript would pull everything up by its height. So a scroll container keeps what's in view where it is, as browsers do with scroll anchoring. Before each layout, it picks an anchor: the first node in view, or, for a node only partly in view, the first of its descendants in view. After the layout, it moves its offset so the anchor's top edge is as far from the top of the view as it was. Content that changes below the anchor, or inside it, doesn't move the view; content that changes above it moves the view with it.

These two feeds show the same alerts, newest first, and a new one arrives at the top every two seconds. The wheel scrolls both together, a row a notch. The left one anchors, as every scroll container does unless told otherwise; the right one has overflow_anchor_none, so its offset stays where it was:

ALERTS = (
    "disk 91% on db-2",
    "p99 latency 840ms",
    "pod web-7 restarted",
    "cert expiring",
    "queue depth 12k",
)


@component
def alert(number: int) -> Text:
    return Text(content=f"{number:>2} {ALERTS[number % len(ALERTS)]}")


@component
def alert_feed(title: str, viewport: ElementHandle, anchor: Style, newest: int) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(26, 6),
        children=(
            Text(content=f" {title} ", style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border),
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | col | overflow_y_scroll | anchor,
                handle=viewport,
                # Newest first, keyed, so each alert keeps its node, which anchoring follows, as new ones arrive above.
                children=tuple(alert(n).with_key(str(n)) for n in range(newest, 0, -1)),
            ),
        ),
    )


@component
def anchoring() -> Div:
    feeds, _ = use_state(lambda: (ElementHandle(), ElementHandle()))
    tick = use_clock(timedelta(seconds=2))
    # A new alert every two seconds, at the top.
    newest = 8 + int(tick.since_mount / timedelta(seconds=2))

    def scroll_both(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case MouseScrolledDown() | MouseScrolledUp():
                return tuple(ScrollBy(feed, y=event.direction) for feed in feeds)
            case _:
                return None

    anchored, unanchored = feeds
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(1),
        on_input=scroll_both,
        children=(
            alert_feed("Anchored", anchored, overflow_anchor_auto, newest),
            alert_feed("overflow_anchor_none", unanchored, overflow_anchor_none, newest),
        ),
    )

While they're scrolled to the top, new alerts push the rest down in both, since a container at the top doesn't anchor. Once they're scrolled down, the anchored feed keeps showing the alerts it was showing, with the new ones arriving out of view above, while the other's offset stays put, so each new alert pushes what it shows down a row. Scrolling the anchored feed back up reaches the new ones:

The anchor is a node, so it follows what each node shows from one render to the next. Siblings without keys continue the sibling at the same index, so when items drop off the front of an unkeyed list, every node shows the item after the one it did, and the view lurches forward by however far that moved the anchor. Give each item of a list whose front changes its own key, as React asks of a list (see When position isn't identity).

As on the web:

  • A container scrolled to the top doesn't anchor, so content added above the top pushes the rest down into view.
  • Anchoring moves only the vertical offset.
  • overflow_anchor_none turns it off: on a scroll container, its offset only gets clamped, and on an element inside one, neither it nor anything inside it is picked as the anchor. An element with clip_to_screen is never picked either.
  • A container whose anchor unmounted or was hidden only clamps its offset.

docs.title: Following the end
docs.text:
A log or a transcript should stay scrolled to its end as lines arrive, so the newest is always in view, until the reader scrolls back to read something earlier. stick_to_end_y does that: a container that's scrolled to its end before a layout is scrolled to its end after it, and one that isn't is anchored as usual. stick_to_end_x does the same horizontally, stick_to_end on both axes, and unstick turns it off. A container whose content fits is at its end, so a log that starts short follows its end from its first line, and one that mounts already overflowing starts at its end.

This log keeps its newest eight lines, adds one a second, and sticks to its end:

KEPT_LINES = 8


@component
def request_line(number: int) -> Text:
    return Text(content=f"{number:>3} GET /items/{number} 200")


@component
def tail() -> Div:
    tick = use_clock(timedelta(seconds=1))
    # A line a second, keeping the newest few.
    newest = 4 + int(tick.since_mount.total_seconds())

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(30, 6) | overflow_y_scroll | stick_to_end_y,
        on_input=scroll_on_wheel(1),
        # Keyed, so a line keeps its node, which anchoring follows, as older lines drop off the top.
        children=tuple(request_line(n).with_key(str(n)) for n in range(max(0, newest - KEPT_LINES), newest)),
    )

docs.title: Jumping to the end
docs.text:
Counterweight doesn't draw scrollbars (#417), as most terminal apps don't, so a reader scrolled back through a log has no sign of how far the end is. A button over the last line that appears once the log is scrolled back, and jumps to the end, gives them one:

@component
def jump_to_end() -> Div:
    log, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)
    scroll = use_scroll(log)

    return Div(
        style=col | border | border_lightrounded | size(30, 6),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=fill(1) | col | overflow_y_scroll | stick_to_end_y,
                handle=log,
                on_input=scroll_on_wheel(1),
                children=tuple(Text(content=f"{i:>2} {event}") for i, event in enumerate(EVENTS, start=1)),
            ),
            # A sibling of the log, not a child, so it stays over the last line as the log scrolls.
            *(
                ()
                if scroll.offset.y == scroll.max_offset.y
                else (
                    Text(
                        content=" ↓ Jump to end ",
                        style=position_absolute
                        | inset_bottom(0)
                        | inset_x(0)
                        | margin_x_auto
                        | fit_content_width
                        | text_bg("sky", 800),
                        on_input=on_click(lambda: ScrollTo(log, y=scroll.max_offset.y)),
                    ),
                )
            ),
        ),
    )

│ 7 traffic shifted to 50%   │

Scrolling back, then clicking the button:

The button is a sibling of the log in a box around it, not a child of the log, because a scroll container moves everything inside it by its offset, absolutely positioned elements included, so a button inside the log would scroll away with the lines. Being outside the log, it reads the log's scroll with use_scroll(log). That's the previous frame's scroll, so the button appears a frame after the scroll that should show it, which nobody notices for a button that comes and goes. A wheel event over the button goes to the box around the log, not the log, so the wheel doesn't scroll it there. use_scroll_area puts its handler on the box around the part that scrolls, so its is_at_end and to_end make the same button from inside the component, and the wheel scrolls the log from over the button too.

docs.title: Where scrolled boxes are
docs.text: Scrolling moves boxes, so everything that reports where a box is reports where it's painted: use_rects, a receiver's rects, the element the mouse is over, and use_hovered. A box scrolled partly out of view is still whole there, with its visible region the part in view, as for any box that's clipped.

docs.title: counterweight.focus.ElementHandle dataclass
docs.text:
ElementHandle()

An opaque token that names one element, as a React ref names a DOM node: a scroll container for ScrollTo, ScrollBy and use_scroll, or an element to bring into view with ScrollIntoView, such as the cursor's row a text area draws with its cursor_row.

It's an identity token, equal only to itself, so it can exist before the element it names has mounted: a component creates one with use_state(ElementHandle) and passes it to an element's handle. Two mounted elements given the same handle raise DuplicateElementHandle.

docs.title: __repr__
docs.text:
__repr__() -> str

Names the handle by its identity, since that's all that tells two handles apart.

docs.title: counterweight.focus.DuplicateElementHandle
docs.text: Raised when two mounted elements are given the same ElementHandle, which leaves it naming neither.

docs.title: Sizing One Box
docs.text: A box that doesn't set its own size takes its content size along its parent's main axis, and stretches across it (see How layout sizes things). The utilities on this page override either.

docs.title: A fixed size
docs.text:
width, height and size set a box's size in cells. An axis left unset keeps its default: the height(4) box below still stretches across the column.

@component
def fixed() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=size(24, 4) | border, content="size(24, 4)"),
            Text(style=width(36) | border, content="width(36)"),
            Text(style=height(4) | border, content="height(4)"),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Fit to content
docs.text:
Along the main axis, a box already fits its content. Across it, a box stretches unless its alignment says otherwise: align_self_start (or any alignment except stretch) shrinks it to its content.

@component
def fit() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="stretched by its col"),
            Text(style=align_self_start | border, content="align_self_start"),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Sizing keywords
docs.text:
The sizing keywords set a box's width or height from its content, whichever axis it is on:

  • min_content_width is as narrow as the content goes without breaking a word: for wrapping text, its widest word.
  • max_content_width is as wide as the content is unwrapped.
  • fit_content_width is the max-content width, capped at the space available (but never below the min-content width), as a wrapping paragraph is in CSS. It differs from max_content_width only when the content doesn't fit.
  • stretch_width fills the space available, after the box's margins.

Each has a _height counterpart. Here each box is the only child of a row:

KEYWORDS = {
    "min_content_width": min_content_width,
    "max_content_width": max_content_width,
    "fit_content_width": fit_content_width,
    "stretch_width": stretch_width,
}


@component
def content_keywords() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=row,
                children=(Text(style=keyword | border | text_wrap_stable, content=f"{name} sizes this"),),
            )
            for name, keyword in KEYWORDS.items()
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

┌─────────────────┐                     
│min_content_width│                     
│sizes this       │                     
└─────────────────┘                     
┌────────────────────────────┐          
│max_content_width sizes this│          
└────────────────────────────┘          
┌────────────────────────────┐          
│fit_content_width sizes this│          
└────────────────────────────┘          
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│stretch_width sizes this              │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘

In a col, a width keyword doesn't size wrapping text correctly: taffy measures the box's height at the column's full width, before applying the keyword, and doesn't measure it again. Below, min_content_width keeps the one row its text takes at full width, so sizes this, wrapped onto a second row, overflows the box and is drawn over its bottom border. A max_content_width box wider than the column keeps extra rows for the same reason. Put the box in a row, as above, or in a grid.

@component
def content_keywords_col() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=tuple(
            Text(style=keyword | border | text_wrap_stable, content=f"{name} sizes this")
            for name, keyword in KEYWORDS.items()
        ),
    )

docs.title: Fill the parent
docs.text:
fill(1) fills the free space along the main axis, after the other children take theirs. full_width and full_height (the same as stretch_width and stretch_height) fill the parent, after the box's margins, whatever the other children need.

@component
def filling() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=border, content="content height"),
            Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1): the rest of the col"),
            Div(
                style=row,
                children=(Text(style=full_width | border, content="full_width: the whole row"),),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Clamped with minimum and maximum sizes
docs.text:
max_width and max_height cap a box that would otherwise grow; min_width and min_height stop one shrinking. In the top row, the first box would take half the row but stops at 20 cells. In the bottom row, two 30-cell boxes don't fit in 40 cells, so both shrink, but the first stops at 24 cells and the second gives up the rest.

@component
def clamped() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row,
                children=(
                    Text(style=fill(1) | max_width(20) | border, content="fill(1)\nmax_width(20)"),
                    Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1)"),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | width(40) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=width(30) | min_width(24) | border, content="width(30)\nmin_width(24)"),
                    Text(style=width(30) | border, content="width(30)"),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Aspect ratio
docs.text:
aspect_ratio sets a box's width divided by its height, so a box with a width and an aspect ratio gets its height from them. Terminal cells are about twice as tall as they are wide, so aspect_ratio(1) looks tall, and aspect_ratio(2) is the one that looks square. The parent here sets align_children_start: a box stretched across a row has its height from the row, and its aspect ratio has nothing to set.

@component
def aspect() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | align_children_start,
        children=(
            Text(style=width(18) | aspect_ratio(1) | border, content="width(18)\naspect_ratio(1)"),
            Text(style=width(18) | aspect_ratio(2) | border, content="width(18)\naspect_ratio(2)"),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Border box and content box
docs.text:
Sizes include the border and padding by default, so a width(24) box is 24 cells wide overall. With content_box, the size applies to the content alone, and the border and padding are added outside it: here 24 cells of content, 4 of padding and 2 of border.

@component
def box_sizing() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | align_children_start,
        children=(
            Text(style=width(24) | pad_x(2) | border, content="width(24)"),
            Text(style=content_box | width(24) | pad_x(2) | border, content="content_box | width(24)"),
        ),
    )

docs.title: The box model
docs.text:
Counterweight's layout follows the CSS box model. Every element's box is four nested rectangles:

  • Content: where the element's content goes. A Div's content is its children, and a Text's content is its text.
  • Padding: space between the content and the border.
  • Border: the box-drawing characters around the padding.
  • Margin: space between the border and the element's neighbors.

The example below colors each rectangle:

@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=fill(1)
                | content_color("green", 500)
                | padding_color("orange", 500)
                | pad_x(2)
                | pad_y(1)
                | border
                | border_lightrounded
                | border_bg("blue", 500)
                | margin_color("red", 500)
                | margin_x(2)
                | margin_y(1)
            ),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

  ╭────────────────────────╮  
  │                        │  
  │                        │  
  │                        │  
  │                        │  
  │                        │  
  │                        │  
  ╰────────────────────────╯

Terminal cells are not square

Terminal cells are about twice as tall as they are wide, so one row of vertical padding or margin looks about as big as two columns of horizontal. The example above uses twice as much horizontal spacing as vertical for that reason, and horizontal spacing alone is often enough.

docs.title: Gap, margin and padding
docs.text:
All three put space around children, but they belong to different elements:

  • gap is set on the parent, and puts space between its children only.
  • margin is set on a child, and puts space all around it, including at the ends of the row. Margins don't collapse into each other, so two children with margin_x(1) are two cells apart.
  • pad is set on the parent, and puts space between its border and all of its children.

margin_sides and pad_sides set each side separately, in the order of CSS's four-value shorthands: top, right, bottom, left.

margin_color and padding_color color the margin and padding, in red and blue here. As on the web, a margin is painted only where its element sets margin_color, and content_color fills the box inside the margin, so a margin otherwise leaves whatever lies beneath it visible.

@component
def gap_margin_pad() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | gap(2) | border | border_heavy,
                children=tuple(Text(style=border, content=f"gap(2) on the row {n}") for n in range(2)),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | border | border_heavy,
                children=tuple(
                    Text(style=margin_x(1) | margin_color("red", 600) | border, content=f"margin_x(1) {n}")
                    for n in range(2)
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | pad_x(2) | padding_color("blue", 600) | border | border_heavy,
                children=tuple(Text(style=border, content=f"pad_x(2) on the row {n}") for n in range(2)),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Sharing borders between neighbors
docs.text:
border_collapse on a parent overlaps its children's borders by one cell, so neighbors share a border instead of drawing two side by side. Where the shared borders meet, border healing joins them with the right junction characters.

@component
def collapse() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row,
                children=tuple(Text(style=border, content="side by side") for _ in range(3)),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | border_collapse,
                children=tuple(Text(style=border, content="border_collapse") for _ in range(3)),
            ),
        ),
    )

└────────────┘└────────────┘└────────────┘

docs.title: Borders on some sides
docs.text:
Borders work as they do in Tailwind. A side is drawn where its border width is 1, and layout reserves a cell for it. border sets all four sides, border_top, border_bottom, border_left and border_right set one, and border_x and border_y set a pair. Each has a _0 form, such as border_right_0, that takes its sides away. Sides start at 0, so border_top | border_left draws just those two.

Merging is ordered, as it is for every style: the right side wins. border | border_right_0 leaves the right side off, but border_right_0 | border turns it back on.

The border kind only chooses the characters, and defaults to BorderKind.Light, so border alone draws a light border and border | border_heavy a heavy one. A kind with no widths draws nothing. border_none removes the border along with its space. border_sides sets all four sides at once from a set of side names.

@component
def sides() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | align_children_start | gap(2),
        children=(
            Text(style=border_y, content="border_y"),
            Text(style=border_top | border_left, content="border_top\n| border_left"),
            Text(style=border | border_right_0, content="border\n| border_right_0"),
            Text(style=border_right_0 | border, content="border_right_0\n| border"),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

────────  ┌─────────────  ┌────────────────  ┌──────────────┐
border_y  │border_top     │border            │border_right_0│
────────  │| border_left  │| border_right_0  │| border      │
                          └────────────────  └──────────────┘

docs.title: Shortening edges next to missing sides
docs.text:
border_contract(n) stops each edge n cells short at an end next to a side that isn't drawn.

@component
def contract() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | align_children_start | gap(2),
        children=(
            Text(
                style=border_top | border_left | pad_x(1),
                content="top and left\nsides",
            ),
            Text(
                style=border_top | border_left | border_contract(2) | pad_x(1),
                content="top and left\nsides\nborder_contract(2)",

│ sides            sides

docs.title: Splitting Space
docs.text:
Each split on this page can be built two ways. With flexbox, each child carries its own share. With grid, the parent lists the shares as track sizes, and children fill the tracks in order. Both give the same screenshot.

The flexbox versions use the constraint utilities, named after the constraints ratatui splits an area with:

Utility The child takes length(n) n cells percentage(p) p percent of the parent ratio(a, b) a / b of the parent fill(n) n shares of the space the others leave

Each acts along its parent's main axis, so the same utility works in a row and in a col, and none of them lets content push a child past its share. They are ordinary Styles, so you can override one part and keep the rest: length(20) | grow(1) takes 20 cells and then a share of whatever is left, and fill(1) | min_width(15) fills but never gets narrower than 15 cells.

The grid versions list the same constraints as track sizes: a plain int is that many cells, and fr(n) is n shares of the space the others leave.

docs.title: Nested splits
docs.text:
With flexbox, a split inside a split is a container inside a container: here a col that fills the rest of the row, split in turn between two children. fill works on the column's vertical axis just as it does on the row's horizontal one. With grid, one parent can hold both axes, and a child spans tracks to cover the space a nested container would have.

def nested_flex() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=(
            Text(style=length(20) | border, content="length(20)"),
            Div(
                style=col | fill(1),
                children=(
                    Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1)"),
                    Text(style=fill(1) | border, content="fill(1)"),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Content wider than its share
docs.text:
A bare waxy.Fraction track has the same floor as a flex item: it is never narrower than its content's minimum size. In the top grid below, two lines of unwrapped text push their columns past the grid's edge. fr(1) is CSS's minmax(0, 1fr), which lowers the floor to zero, so in the middle grid the columns split the space. Each line is still wider than its column, so it overflows the column, as text does in CSS, over the next column and the grid's border. In the bottom grid, overflow_hidden on each Text clips its line at its own padding box.

@component
def overflow_grid() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(waxy.Fraction(1), waxy.Fraction(1)) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=border, content=LONG),
                    Text(style=border, content=LONG),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1)) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=border, content=LONG),
                    Text(style=border, content=LONG),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=display_grid | grid_template_columns(fr(1), fr(1)) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=border | overflow_hidden, content=LONG),
                    Text(style=border | overflow_hidden, content=LONG),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Percentages and gaps
docs.text:
A percentage is a share of the parent's whole content box, and gaps aren't subtracted first, so two halves and a gap don't fit. percentage doesn't shrink, so in the bottom row the halves keep their size and overflow the row by the width of the gap. With shrink(1), as in the top row, each half gives up one cell to the gap instead. To split a row with gaps into equal shares, use fill as in Equal shares.

@component
def percent_gap() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | gap(2) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=percentage(50) | shrink(1) | border, content="percentage(50) | shrink(1)"),
                    Text(style=percentage(50) | shrink(1) | border, content="percentage(50) | shrink(1)"),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | gap(2) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(
                    Text(style=percentage(50) | border, content="percentage(50)"),
                    Text(style=percentage(50) | border, content="percentage(50)"),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Text in Layout
docs.text: A Text is sized by measuring its content: unwrapped, it is as wide as its longest line; with a wrap mode, its height is the number of lines its content wraps to at the width it gets. Content that doesn't fit overflows the Text's box and is drawn past it, as text is in CSS, unless the Text or one of its ancestors clips it. Text wrapping compares the wrap modes themselves.

docs.title: Wrapping inside a pane
docs.text:
A wrapping Text in a column is stretched to the column's width, and wraps to fit it, taking as many rows as it needs.

@component
def wrap_in_pane() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row,
        children=(
            Text(style=length(16) | border, content="length(16)"),
            Div(
                style=col | fill(1) | border | pad_x(1),
                children=(Text(style=text_wrap_stable, content=PARAGRAPH),),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Wrapping beside other text
docs.text:
Wrapping Texts side by side in a row shrink to share it, and each wraps to its share. A flex item can't shrink below its automatic minimum size, and a wrapping Text's is the width of its widest word, so neither needs anything set to give up the space its unwrapped line would take.

@component
def wrap_in_row() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2) | border | border_heavy,
        children=(
            Text(style=text_wrap_stable | border, content=PARAGRAPH),
            Text(style=text_wrap_stable | border, content=PARAGRAPH),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Justification needs room
docs.text:
text_justify_center and text_justify_right align each line within the Text's own width. A Text stretched across its parent has room to move its lines, but one sized to its content, like the align_self_start one below, has none. With a wrap mode, each line is aligned separately.

@component
def justify() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(style=text_justify_center | border, content="text_justify_center, stretched"),
            Text(
                style=text_justify_center | align_self_start | border,
                content="text_justify_center | align_self_start",
            ),
            Text(
                style=text_justify_center | text_wrap_balance | border,
                content="text_justify_center | text_wrap_balance centers each line of a paragraph "
                "within the width of the box",
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Long unwrapped text in a narrow pane
docs.text:
In the top panes below, a line too long for its pane overflows it, as unwrapped text does in CSS, drawing over the pane's border and past it. In a col, the Text is stretched to the column's width, however long its content, so its box fits the column and only its line overflows. In a row, a Text can't shrink below its content's width, so its whole box overflows the row (see Content sets a minimum size).

In the bottom panes, overflow_hidden on the Text fixes both: it clips the line at the Text's own padding box, and, as for any box that hides its overflow, lowers its minimum width to zero, so it shrinks to fit the row. A wrap mode breaks the lines to fit instead. overflow_hidden on the pane clips the Text at the pane's padding box (see Clipping), which in a row cuts off the Text's own right border with its line. overflow_x_scroll on the pane makes it a scroll container the reader can scroll along the line, in a col or a row alike.

@component
def narrow_panes(text_style: Style) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(8),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col | width(20) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(Text(style=text_style, content="unwrapped text in a col"),),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | width(20) | border | border_heavy,
                children=(Text(style=text_style, content="unwrapped text in a row"),),
            ),
        ),
    )


@component
def narrow() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(narrow_panes(border), narrow_panes(border | overflow_hidden)),
    )

docs.title: Hyperlinks
docs.text:
Any text can be a hyperlink that the terminal opens when it's clicked: merge in text_link(uri), which sets link on the text_style. On a Chunk's style, that makes the chunk a link; on a Text's style, it makes all of its text one.

LINK = text_underline | text_color("sky", 300)


@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1) | pad_x(1),
        children=(
            Text(
                content=(
                    Chunk(content="Counterweight is on "),
                    Chunk(content="GitHub", style=LINK | text_link("https://github.com/JoshKarpel/counterweight")),
                    Chunk(content=", and its docs are at "),
                    Chunk(content="counterweight.dev", style=LINK | text_link("https://www.counterweight.dev")),
                    Chunk(content="."),
                ),
                style=text_wrap_pretty,
            ),
            Text(
                content="This whole Text is one link.",
                style=pad_x(1) | border | border_lightrounded | text_link("https://pygments.org"),
            ),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText

 counterweight.dev.                               

 ╭──────────────────────────────────────────────╮ 
 │ This whole Text is one link.                 │ 
 ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────╯

A link changes how nothing looks, so style it to look like one, as the example does with an underline and a color. It merges like any other field, so a Chunk inside a linked Text can link elsewhere, or merge in text_link(None) to not be a link at all.

docs.title: How terminals handle them
docs.text:
Counterweight writes links as OSC 8 escape sequences, which most modern terminals support, including iTerm2, kitty, WezTerm, Ghostty, foot, GNOME Terminal and Windows Terminal. A terminal that doesn't ignores them, and shows the text as if it weren't a link.

Clicking a link is handled by the terminal, not the app, and the app never sees the click. Counterweight turns on mouse reporting, so some terminals only open a link with a modifier held, such as Shift, Ctrl or Cmd, depending on the terminal.

A link's URI must be printable ASCII, so CellStyle raises ValueError for anything else: a control character could end the escape sequence and start another. Percent-encode anything outside ASCII, as urllib.parse.quote does.

docs.title: Markdown
docs.text:
markdown_document renders a Markdown document as a component, which goes anywhere a component does. It handles GitHub Flavored Markdown, and YAML front matter at the top of a document.

README = """\
# Peaks

The *fourteen* peaks above **8000 m** are all in Asia;
see [the list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander).

> Because it's there.

- Himalayas
  - Everest
  - Kangchenjunga
- Karakoram
  - K2

| Peak | Height (m) |
|:-----|-----------:|
| Everest | 8849 |
| K2 | 8611 |

```python
tallest = max(peaks, key=lambda p: p.height)
```
"""


@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(style=col | pad_x(1), children=(markdown_document(README),))

  • Links, bare URLs, and images are hyperlinks to their destinations. An image is shown as its alt text, since a terminal can't show the image.
  • Fenced code blocks are highlighted as the language their info string names, or shown as written if it names none, or one Pygments doesn't know. Code blocks and tables too wide for the space they're given scroll sideways.
  • Math, between $s within a line or $$s on lines of their own, is shown as written, since a terminal can't typeset it. A dollar sign starts math only by Pandoc's rule, with no space just inside it and no digit right after the closing one, so $5 and $10 stays text.
  • Raw HTML is shown as written.

GitHub's extensions to CommonMark draw like this:

EXPEDITION = """\

peak: K2
---

- [x] Reach base camp
- [ ] Summit, weather permitting[^window]

> [!WARNING]

Forecasts are at www.mountain-forecast.com.

"""


@component
def github() -> Div:
