  • A task list item's box takes the place of its bullet, or follows its number.
  • An alert is a block quote with a title, colored by its kind.
  • Footnotes are numbered in the order they're referenced, and their definitions follow the rest of the document.

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text:
markdown_document is a memo component, so it parses its document again only when its arguments change, and keeps what it rendered while it stays mounted, freed when it unmounts. A transcript that renders each message with one parses only the message that changed, however many messages there are, as React apps wrap a Markdown component in React.memo.

The function it calls, markdown, returns the document's Div of elements, and parses the document each time it's called. Call it to put the elements together with others yourself, under use_memo in a component that renders often.

docs.title: Scrolling
docs.text:
A document is as tall as its content, so one longer than the space it's given runs past the bottom of it. Put it in a scroll container, as a browser puts a page in a scrolling viewport, with scroll_on_keys and scroll_on_wheel to scroll it:

@component
def scrolling() -> Div:
    # Focused, so the keys reach scroll_on_keys.
    use_focus(auto_focus=True)
    return Div(
        style=col | full | border | border_lightrounded | pad_x(1) | overflow_y_scroll,
        on_input=first(scroll_on_keys(), scroll_on_wheel()),
        children=(markdown_document(README),),
    )

docs.title: Wide code and tables
docs.text:
A code block with lines wider than the space it's given scrolls sideways rather than wrapping them, as GitHub's styles give a pre overflow: auto. markdown puts it in a box with overflow_x_scroll and scroll_on_wheel, so the wheel scrolls it under the pointer:

INSTALL = """\
Install it with:

```bash
uv add counterweight markdown-it-py mdit-py-plugins pygments
```
"""


@component
def wide() -> Div:
    return Div(style=col | pad_x(1), children=(markdown_document(INSTALL),))
BeforeAfter four wheel notches to the right ScreenshotText 

 Install it with:                       

  uv add counterweight markdown-it-py m
ScreenshotText 

 Install it with:                       

 terweight markdown-it-py mdit-py-plugi

A table scrolls the same way once its cells have wrapped as narrow as their words allow, as GitHub's styles make a table a block with overflow: auto. Only a sideways wheel scrolls them, such as a tilting wheel or a trackpad's sideways swipe, or the wheel with Shift held, as in a browser. An up or down notch without Shift over one passes on to the scroll container around the document, so the document scrolls as it does anywhere else. Some terminals keep Shift with the wheel for their own scrollback and never report it, so there only a sideways wheel scrolls them.

Browsers also let Tab focus a scroll container with nothing focusable inside, and the arrow keys scroll it. A code block here isn't focusable, since markdown returns elements, not components that could call use_focus, so only the wheel scrolls it.

To wrap long lines instead, pass MarkdownStyles(code_block_text=text_wrap_stable).

docs.title: Line breaks
docs.text:
CommonMark joins the lines of a paragraph with a space, so a document's source can wrap wherever its author likes. What people type into a chat is different: GitHub's comments and chat apps keep each line break they type. Pass keeps_line_breaks=True to break the line wherever the source does, as the chat example does for your messages. Here the same message is rendered both ways:

MESSAGE = """\
on my way
running ten minutes late
save me a seat
"""


@component
def line_breaks() -> Div:
    return Div(

docs.title: Styles
docs.text:
MarkdownStyles holds a Style for each kind of block and a CellStyle for each kind of inline span. A code block and a table are each a box around what they show: code_block and table style the box, which scrolls, and code_block_text and table_grid what's inside it. Pass the fields you want to change, and the rest keep their defaults. A field you pass replaces its default whole, so merge over the default's value to change only part of it, as this document does to recolor its heading, block quote and table without losing their bold, border or wrapping:

DEFAULTS = MarkdownStyles()

# Each field replaces its default, so these merge over the defaults to change only their colors.
WARM = MarkdownStyles(
    heading_1=DEFAULTS.heading_1 | text_color("amber", 300),
    block_quote=DEFAULTS.block_quote | border_color("amber", 500),
    block_quote_text=DEFAULTS.block_quote_text | text_color("amber", 200).text_style,
    list_marker=text_color("amber", 400),
    table_cell=DEFAULTS.table_cell | border_color("stone", 500),
    code_theme="monokai",
    block_gap=0,
)


@component
def styled() -> Div:
    return Div(style=col | pad_x(1), children=(markdown_document(README, WARM),))

docs.title: counterweight.markdown.markdown

markdown(
    source: str,
    styles: MarkdownStyles = MarkdownStyles(),
    keeps_line_breaks: bool = False,
) -> Div

source, a Markdown document, as a Div of its blocks, drawn with styles.

Links, bare URLs, and images are hyperlinks to their destinations. Fenced code blocks are highlighted as the language their info string names, or shown as written if it names none or one Pygments doesn't know. Code blocks and tables wider than the space they're given scroll sideways with the wheel. Math and raw HTML are shown as written, too.

It parses source each time it's called. In a component that renders often, use markdown_document, or call it under use_memo.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION keeps_line_breaks

Whether a line break inside a paragraph breaks the line where it's drawn, as GitHub's comments and chat apps draw what people type, rather than joining the lines with a space, as CommonMark does.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

SOURCE = '''\

def greeting(name: str) -> Text:
    """Say hello."""
    return Text(content=f"Hello, {name}!")
'''


@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1),
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=col,
                children=(
                    Text(content=f" {theme} ", style=text_color("slate", 400)),
                    code_block(SOURCE.rstrip("\n"), "python", theme=theme, style=pad(1)),
                ),
            )
            for theme in ("github-dark", "monokai", "solarized-light")

A theme is the name of any Pygments style, or a pygments.style.Style subclass, which is how to define your own.

code_block is as wide as its longest line, as an HTML pre is. To scroll lines wider than the space it's given, put it in a scroll container with overflow_x_scroll and scroll_on_wheel, as markdown does, so a sideways wheel, or the wheel with Shift held, scrolls it:

Div(style=overflow_x_scroll, on_input=scroll_on_wheel(), children=(code_block(source, "python"),))

Highlighting is cached by its arguments, so a component can highlight the same code on every render without lexing it again. Tabs are expanded, to four columns unless tab_size says otherwise.

docs.title: Laying the code out yourself
docs.text:
To lay the code out yourself, highlight returns its chunks, to put in a Text with whatever else you like, and code_style the background and text color to draw them on. Here the chunks are split into lines, each in a row beside its number, and one line is marked, as an editor marks the line its cursor is on:

PATCHED = """\
def mean(values: list[float]) -> float:
    if not values:
        return 0.0

    return sum(values) / len(values)
"""


def lines_of(chunks: tuple[Chunk, ...]) -> list[tuple[Chunk, ...]]:
    """The chunks on each line, split where a chunk holds a line break."""
    lines: list[list[Chunk]] = [[]]
    for chunk in chunks:
        first, *rest = chunk.content.split("\n")
        lines[-1].append(Chunk(content=first, style=chunk.style))
        lines.extend([Chunk(content=part, style=chunk.style)] for part in rest)
    return [tuple(chunk for chunk in line if chunk.content) for line in lines]


@component
def numbered(code: str, marked: int, theme: str = "github-dark") -> Div:
    base = code_style(theme)
    mark = text_bg("slate", 700) | content_color("slate", 700)
    return Div(
        style=col | pad_y(1) | base | fit_content_width,
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=row,
                children=(
                    Text(
                        content=f" {number:>2} ",
                        style=base
                        | (text_color("amber", 400) | mark if number == marked else text_color("slate", 500)),
                    ),
                    Text(
                        content=line,
                        style=base | grow(1) | pad_right(2) | (mark if number == marked else default),
                    ),
                ),
            )
            for number, line in enumerate(lines_of(highlight(code.rstrip("\n"), "python", theme)), start=1)
        ),
    )


@component
def lines() -> Div:
    return Div(children=(numbered(PATCHED, marked=3),))

docs.title: Styles
docs.text: Every element takes a style, a Style that says how it's laid out and drawn. Rather than build one field by field, most code merges utilities, small styles that each set a few fields, as Tailwind's classes do.

docs.title: Merging
docs.text:
Styles are merged using the | operator: left | right. Every field starts out unset (the counterweight.styles.UNSET sentinel), and the result takes right's value for every field right sets, and left's value otherwise.

A field set to its default value is still set, so it overrides left. CellStyle(bold=True) | CellStyle(bold=False) is CellStyle(bold=False), border | border_none draws no border, and text_justify_center | text_justify_left justifies left. Utilities set only the fields they are about, so they layer without clearing each other: text_color("red", 500) | text_bg("slate", 900) is red text on a slate background.

merge does the same for any number of Styles: merge(a, b, c) is a | b | c. It skips None wherever it appears, so a style that only sometimes applies can be passed inline, as in merge(base, hover_style if hovered else None), and merge() is an empty Style().

Nested styles merge field by field too: Style(text_style=CellStyle(bold=True)) | Style(text_style=CellStyle(italic=True)) is both bold and italic. layout follows the same rule, field by field.

Each Text below is styled by the expression it shows:

MERGES: tuple[tuple[str, Style], ...] = (
    ('text_color("red", 500) | text_bg("slate", 800)', text_color("red", 500) | text_bg("slate", 800)),
    ('text_color("red", 500) | text_color("sky", 400)', text_color("red", 500) | text_color("sky", 400)),
    (
        "Style(text_style=CellStyle(bold=True)) | Style(text_style=CellStyle(italic=True))",
        Style(text_style=CellStyle(bold=True)) | Style(text_style=CellStyle(italic=True)),
    ),
    ("border | border_heavy", border | border_heavy),
    ("border | border_heavy | border_double", border | border_heavy | border_double),
    ("border | border_heavy | border_none", border | border_heavy | border_none),
)


@component
def layering() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | align_children_start | gap(1),
        children=tuple(Text(style=style, content=expression) for expression, style in MERGES),
    )

┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓                                                           
┃border | border_heavy┃                                                           
┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛                                                           

╔═════════════════════════════════════╗                                           
║border | border_heavy | border_double║                                           
╚═════════════════════════════════════╝                                           

border | border_heavy | border_none
  • The first line is red on slate, since each utility sets a different field.
  • The second is sky, since both set the text's foreground and the right one wins.
  • The third is bold and italic, since the two text_styles merge field by field.
  • border_double replaces border_heavy's characters, and border_none takes the border away entirely.

A component usually builds its style from a base and a few variants that apply only sometimes. Below, every button starts from BUTTON; the selected one merges in SELECTED, which overrides its border kind and color and sets a text color, and the one under the mouse (use_hovered) merges in HOVERED, which only adds a background, so it layers over a selected button as well as an unselected one.

BUTTON = border | border_lightrounded | border_color("slate", 500) | pad_x(1)
SELECTED = border_heavy | border_color("amber", 400) | text_color("amber", 300)
HOVERED = text_bg("slate", 700) | padding_color("slate", 700)


@component
def button(label: str, is_selected: bool, select: Callable[[str], None]) -> Text:
    hovered = use_hovered()

    return Text(
        content=label,
        style=merge(BUTTON, SELECTED if is_selected else None, HOVERED if hovered.border else None),
        on_input=on_click(lambda: select(label)),
    )


@component
def toolbar() -> Div:
    selected, set_selected = use_state("Edit")

    return Div(
        style=row | gap(1),

docs.title: Text in a filled box
docs.text:
A Text's characters are drawn on its text_style's background, and where that's unset, on the Text's own content_color, as a Canvas's painter's cells are. They don't take the color of a box the Text lies in: an unset background is the default, black, not transparent as a CSS background-color starts out. Layouts here put elements side by side, or lay a modal over the rest with a fill of its own, rather than stacking partly painted elements, so each cell's color is decided by the element that draws it. A Div with a content_color therefore shows it around a Text inside it, but not under the text, and there are two ways to color text inside a filled box:

Div(style=content_color("slate", 800), children=(Text(content="hi", style=content_color("slate", 800)),))
Div(style=content_color("slate", 800), children=(Text(content="hi", style=text_bg("slate", 800)),))

The first colors the Text's whole content box, under its text and below its last line, and the second colors only its lines of text, each across the content box's width. Padding takes its padding_color either way. What isn't painted at all still shows what lies beneath it: a margin without a margin_color, and an element with no border, padding, text or content_color.

docs.title: counterweight.styles.Style dataclass
docs.text:
Style(
    *,
    layout: Style = Style(),
    z: int | UNSET = UNSET,
    clip_to: ClipTo | UNSET = UNSET,
    overflow_anchor: OverflowAnchor | UNSET = UNSET,
    stick_to_end_x: bool | UNSET = UNSET,
    stick_to_end_y: bool | UNSET = UNSET,
    margin_color: AnyColor | Gradient | UNSET = UNSET,
    padding_color: AnyColor | Gradient | UNSET = UNSET,
    content_color: AnyColor | Gradient | UNSET = UNSET,
    border_kind: BorderKind | UNSET | None = UNSET,
    border_style: CellStyle = _DEFAULT_CELL_STYLE,
    border_contract: int | UNSET = UNSET,
    text_style: CellStyle = _DEFAULT_CELL_STYLE,
    text_justify: TextJustify | UNSET = UNSET,
    text_wrap: TextWrap | UNSET = UNSET,
    text_overflow: TextOverflow | UNSET = UNSET,
)

How an element is laid out and drawn.

Every field except layout starts UNSET, and the nested border_style and text_style start as empty CellStyles. Merging with | takes the right side's value wherever it is set, including when it is set to the default, so border | border_none has no border. layout merges the same way, field by field. Unset fields resolve to the defaults in STYLE_DEFAULTS.

Each color, margin_color, padding_color and content_color and the colors of border_style and text_style, can be a gradient, which maps over the box its color paints unless the gradient's box names another: the margin box for margin_color, the padding box for padding_color, the border box for content_color and border_style, and the content box for text_style (and the chunks of a Text).

A border side is drawn where its width in layout (border_top, ...) is 1, and border_kind chooses the characters it's drawn with. A border_kind of None removes the border, along with the space reserved for it. Each side is one cell, so a Style whose layout sets a border width other than Length(0) or Length(1) raises ValueError.

clip_to chooses what clips the element. With "padding", the default, or "border", it's its parent's padding or border box, on each axis where the parent's overflow is Hidden, Clip or Scroll, and every clip above the parent clips the element too; "border" lets a title be drawn on its parent's border. With "screen", the element is unclipped: no ancestor clips it, so a popup can reach past them, though its own overflow still clips its descendants.

overflow_anchor and stick_to_end_x and stick_to_end_y choose how a scroll container's offset follows its content when the content changes. With overflow_anchor "auto", the default, a scroll container keeps the content in view where it was, as CSS's overflow-anchor does; with "none", a scroll container keeps its offset, and nothing inside an element that sets it is an anchor for the scroll container around it. A scroll container that sticks to its end on an axis and is scrolled to its end there stays scrolled to its end when its content grows.

text_overflow chooses how a Text ends a line wider than its content box. With "clip", the default, the line is drawn whole, past the box unless something clips it; with "ellipsis", it keeps the graphemes that fit before the box's last cell, which … takes, in the Text's own style, as CSS draws the ellipsis in its block's. A two-cell grapheme the cut runs through is left out, with a space in its style in its place. It changes only what's painted, never the size of any element.

docs.title: Gradients
docs.text:
A gradient is a color that changes across a box. Every place a style holds a color can hold one instead: margin_color, padding_color and content_color, and the foreground and background of border_style, text_style, and a Text's chunks. This page covers making gradients, where they map, and what drawing them in cells changes. It doesn't cover transparency or layering one gradient over another, since colors have no alpha.

Counterweight takes gradients from CSS: a gradient is CSS's linear-gradient, radial-gradient or conic-gradient, built by a function of the same name with the same parts. CSS paints a gradient as an image, so only backgrounds and borders take one; here, as in SVG's fill and stroke, a gradient goes anywhere a color does, text included, without CSS's background-clip: text.

docs.title: Linear gradients
docs.text:
linear_gradient takes its colors in order, and points down unless it's given a side or corner to point to, or an angle. An angle is in degrees clockwise from up, so 90 points right, as in CSS. A corner points the way that puts the gradient's halfway line through the other two corners, so the corner itself takes the last color whatever the box's shape (CSS's "magic corners").

@component
def linear() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=(
            labeled("to right", Div(style=SWATCH | content_gradient(linear_gradient(rose_500, sky_500, to="right")))),
            labeled("angle=45", Div(style=SWATCH | content_gradient(linear_gradient(rose_500, sky_500, angle=45)))),
            labeled(
                "to top right",
                Div(style=SWATCH | content_gradient(linear_gradient(rose_500, sky_500, to="top right"))),
            ),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

to right          angle=45          to top right

docs.title: Radial and conic gradients
docs.text:
radial_gradient spreads its colors outward from a center, at, to an ending shape: an ellipse, or a circle, sized by the side or corner of the box it reaches ("farthest-corner" unless it's given another), or by its radius. conic_gradient turns its colors around a center, clockwise from its start angle. A center is a fraction of the way across the box on each axis, so (0.5, 0.5), the default, is its middle, or a number of cells from its top left cell, as a waxy.Length.

@component
def shapes() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=(
            labeled("ellipse", Div(style=SWATCH | content_gradient(radial_gradient(amber_300, violet_900)))),
            labeled(
                "circle at a corner",
                Div(
                    style=SWATCH | content_gradient(radial_gradient(amber_300, violet_900, shape="circle", at=(0, 0))),
                ),
            ),
            labeled(
                "conic",
                Div(

docs.title: Stops
docs.text:
Each color is a stop, which goes wherever the gradient's other stops leave room for it, or at a position given with it as (color, position), a fraction of the way along the gradient, or from one position to another as (color, start, end). Two stops at one position make a hard edge between them. A Hint between two stops moves the point where their colors mix half and half, and a repeating gradient repeats its stops for as long as the box goes on. Stops are fixed up as CSS fixes them up: a position smaller than one before it is moved up to it, and stops without positions are spaced evenly between the ones around them.

@component
def stops() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=(
            labeled(
                "a hint at 0.2",
                Div(style=SWATCH | content_gradient(linear_gradient(gray_950, Hint(0.2), gray_100, to="right"))),
            ),
            labeled(
                "hard stops",
                Div(
                    style=SWATCH
                    | content_gradient(
                        linear_gradient(
                            (rose_500, 0, 1 / 3), (amber_300, 1 / 3, 2 / 3), (teal_500, 2 / 3, 1), to="right"
                        )
                    ),
                ),
            ),
            labeled(
                "repeating",
                Div(
                    style=SWATCH
                    | content_gradient(
                        linear_gradient((sky_500, 0), (gray_950, 0.2), (sky_500, 0.4), angle=120, repeating=True)
                    ),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

A stop is a Color, not an IndexedColor or TERMINAL_DEFAULT, since the terminal decides what those look like, so there's no color to mix them from.

docs.title: Mixing colors
docs.text:
A gradient mixes its colors in Oklab unless it's given another color space as its interpolation, as CSS does, which keeps the colors between two stops about as bright as the stops, rather than going muddy. "srgb" mixes them as CSS does colors given in hex, and a polar space such as "oklch" goes around the hue circle the shorter way, or the way its hue says.

@component
def interpolation() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | gap(0),
        children=tuple(
            Div(
                style=row,
                children=(
                    Text(content=space, style=width(8)),
                    Div(
                        style=size(40, 1)
                        | content_gradient(linear_gradient(blue_600, yellow_300, to="right", interpolation=space)),
                    ),
                ),
            )
            for space in ("srgb", "oklab", "oklch")
        ),
    )

docs.title: Where a gradient goes
docs.text:
The utilities put a gradient in each place a color goes. Each place maps its gradient over the box it paints:

Utility Field Maps over margin_gradient margin_color the margin box content_gradient content_color the border box, under the border and padding padding_gradient padding_color the padding box border_gradient, border_bg_gradient border_style the border box text_gradient, text_bg_gradient text_style, and a chunk's style the content box 
SUNRISE = linear_gradient(amber_300, rose_500, to="right")


@component
def slots() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=size(20, 5) | border | border_heavy | border_gradient(SUNRISE),
                children=(Text(content="gradient border", style=pad_x(1)),),
            ),
            Div(
                style=size(24, 5) | pad_x(1),
                children=(
                    Text(
                        content=(
                            Chunk(content="Gradient text, "),
                            Chunk(content="with a highlight", style=text_bold),
                            Chunk(content=" that continues it"),
                        ),
                        style=text_wrap_pretty | text_gradient(SUNRISE),
                    ),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=size(20, 5)
                | pad(1)
                | padding_gradient(linear_gradient(teal_500, sky_700))
                | content_gradient(radial_gradient(gray_100, gray_400)),

DUSK = linear_gradient(violet_500, sky_400, to="right")
DUSK_OVER_THE_MARGIN = linear_gradient(violet_500, sky_400, to="right", box="margin")

def boxes() -> Div:

        style=col,
        children=(
            Text(content="each over its own box"),
            Div(style=size(12, 2) | margin_x(4) | margin_gradient(DUSK) | content_gradient(DUSK)),
            Text(content="both over the margin box"),

                | margin_x(4)

docs.title: What cells change
docs.text:
A cell is about twice as tall as it is wide, so a gradient computes its angles and circles as if each row were two columns tall, which makes 45 degrees look like 45 degrees, and a circle look round. The ratio is app's cell_aspect_ratio parameter, which a font with other proportions can change. A circle or ellipse given radii in cells keeps them: a circle of radius 10 reaches 10 columns across, and 5 rows down.

A browser colors each pixel by its center, and so does a terminal each cell, but a gradient spans from the center of its box's first cell to the center of its last, so the cells at the ends take the end colors exactly: a box 3 cells tall shows its first color, the color halfway between, and its last, where a browser would show neither end.

docs.title: On a canvas
docs.text:
A Canvas is drawn by its painter, which has no places for a gradient, so HalfBlockGradient is a painter that fills it with one, two pixels to a cell, as HalfBlocks draws a picture, which shows a gradient at twice the vertical resolution of a content_gradient. Pixels.from_gradient is a picture of a gradient, for a picture that draws more on top of it.

ARC = conic_gradient(rose_500, amber_300, teal_500, violet_600, rose_500)


@component
def on_a_canvas() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=(
            labeled("content_gradient", Div(style=SWATCH | content_gradient(ARC))),
            labeled("HalfBlockGradient", Canvas(painter=HalfBlockGradient(ARC), style=SWATCH)),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Sampling a gradient's colors
docs.text:
To color something a gradient can't fill, such as one character of a Text or a pixel a painter computes, read the gradient's colors yourself from its ramp, which paint draws it from:

colors = ramp(linear_gradient(Color.from_name("red"), Color.from_name("blue")))
halfway = colors.color(colors.index(0.5))

field_indices gives the entry of the ramp each cell of a box takes, as paint maps the gradient over it, for drawing a whole gradient cell by cell.

docs.title: Animating a gradient
docs.text:
A gradient is a value, so animating one means building a new one each frame from the time, which use_clock reads. Each of these turns its gradient's angle, or slides its stops along, once every three seconds:

LOOP = timedelta(seconds=3)


@component
def turning() -> Div:
    start = 360 * use_loop(LOOP)
    return Div(style=SWATCH | content_gradient(conic_gradient(rose_500, amber_300, teal_500, rose_500, start=start)))


@component
def orbiting_border() -> Div:
    angle = 360 * use_loop(LOOP)
    return Div(
        style=SWATCH | border | border_heavy | border_gradient(linear_gradient(amber_300, violet_600, angle=angle)),
        children=(Text(content="orbiting", style=pad_x(1)),),
    )


@component
def shimmer(content: str) -> Text:
    # The highlight starts off the left end and finishes off the right one, so the loop starts over unseen.
    at = 1.6 * use_loop(LOOP) - 0.3
    return Text(
        content=content,
        style=text_gradient(
            linear_gradient((slate_500, at - 0.25), (slate_50, at), (slate_500, at + 0.25), to="right")
        ),
    )


@component
def animated() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=(
            labeled("turning", turning()),
            labeled("orbiting border", orbiting_border()),
            labeled("shimmer", Div(style=SWATCH, children=(shimmer("Thinking…"),))),
        ),
    )

Browsers don't animate one gradient into another, so a page animates a gradient by sliding an oversized background with background-position, or by registering an angle or a stop position with @property so that it can transition. Here a gradient's angle, center, stops and colors are arguments like any other, so any of them can change from one frame to the next. A stop's position can be outside the gradient, as the shimmer's are when its highlight is off either end. Each animated component reads the clock itself, so a frame re-runs only them, though each frame draws their gradients again (see Performance).

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Paint keeps what it builds for each element's gradients from frame to frame, so a gradient that doesn't change costs about what a solid color does once it's drawn. What costs is drawing one again: a gradient whose stops or geometry change, as in an animation, or that scrolls, or whose box changes size, is drawn again in every frame it changes, at roughly half a millisecond per thousand cells, and all of its cells' colors are sent to the terminal again too.

    hue: HueMethod = "shorter",

Colors that change along a line through the middle of the box, as CSS's linear-gradient does.

ramp(gradient: Gradient) -> Ramp

The ramp of gradient's colors, which paint draws it from, so ramp(gradient).color(ramp(gradient).index(position)) is its color at position along it, where its first stop is at 0 and its last at 1, unless they name other positions. docs.title: Text Wrapping
docs.text: By default, Text elements render their content on a single line. When the content is wider than the available space, it overflows rather than wrapping. Use the text_wrap_* style utilities to control how long text is broken across lines.

docs.title: Wrap Modes
docs.text:
Counterweight supports four wrap modes, illustrated below with the same paragraph of Markdown, whose paragraphs wrap with the paragraph style of MarkdownStyles:

SAMPLE = """\
It was the *best of times*, it was the *worst of times*,
it was the age of **wisdom**, it was the age of **foolishness**.
"""

WRAP_STYLE: dict[TextWrap, Style] = {
    "none": text_wrap_none | overflow_hidden,
    "stable": text_wrap_stable,
    "pretty": text_wrap_pretty,
    "balance": text_wrap_balance,
}


@component
def wrap_pane(mode: TextWrap) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=fill(1) | col | border | pad_x(1),
        children=(
            Text(
                content=f" {mode} ",
                style=position_absolute | inset_top(-1) | inset_left(1) | clip_to_border,
            ),
            markdown_document(SAMPLE, MarkdownStyles(paragraph=WRAP_STYLE[mode])),
        ),
    )


@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | fill(1),
                children=tuple(wrap_pane(mode) for mode in WRAP_STYLE),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: text_wrap_none (default)
docs.text: No wrapping. The text renders as a single line regardless of the available width. A line wider than its box overflows it and is drawn past it, as text is in CSS, unless the Text or one of its ancestors clips it. The comparison above gives the none paragraph overflow_hidden, which clips its line at the paragraph's own padding box.

docs.title: text_wrap_stable
docs.text: Greedy line-breaking — fills each line as much as possible before starting the next. This is the fastest algorithm and produces consistent, deterministic output. Use it when performance matters or when you want predictable line breaks.

docs.title: text_wrap_balance
docs.text: Attempts to make all lines roughly equal in length by binary-searching for the narrowest target width that doesn't increase the total line count. Useful for headings and short paragraphs where visual balance is more important than filling lines to the edge.

docs.title: text_wrap_pretty
docs.text: Dynamic-programming line-breaking (Knuth–Plass style) that minimises the sum of squared slack on non-final lines. This produces typographically "nicer" output than greedy wrapping — shorter lines near the end of a paragraph are avoided — at the cost of slightly higher CPU usage for very long texts.

docs.title: Ending a Line with an Ellipsis
docs.text:
A line that doesn't wrap can be wider than its Text's content box. text_overflow_clip, the default, draws it whole, for a clip to cut; text_overflow_ellipsis keeps what fits before the box's last cell and draws … there, as CSS's text-overflow: ellipsis does:

PATHS = (
    "README.md",
    "src/counterweight/_layout.py",
    "docs/styles/text-wrapping.md",
    "tests/日本語/e2eテスト.py",
)

STATUS = content_color("slate", 800)


def files(title: str, overflow: Style) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | width(20) | border | border_light | overflow_hidden,
        children=(
            Text(content=title, style=text_bold),
            *(Text(content=path, style=overflow) for path in PATHS),
        ),
    )


@component
def root() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1) | pad_x(1),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=row | gap(2),
                children=(files("clip", text_overflow_clip), files("ellipsis", text_overflow_ellipsis)),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | width(42),
                children=(
                    Text(
                        content="~/projects/counterweight/src/counterweight/styles/_styles.py",
                        style=grow(1) | overflow_x_hidden | text_overflow_ellipsis | STATUS,
                    ),
                    Text(content=" Ln 12, Col 4 ", style=STATUS | text_color("sky", 300)),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

The cut is measured in cells, as layout measures text, so a wide character the box's edge runs through is left out, with a space in its place, as テ is in the last path. The … is drawn in the Text's own style, rather than its chunks', as CSS draws it in its block's style.

It changes only what's painted, not any element's size, so it shows only where the Text's content box is narrower than its line. A Text in a column stretches across it, as the paths do. In a row, a Text keeps the width of its line, and only shrinks below it with overflow_x_hidden, as a flex item with overflow: hidden does in CSS, so the status bar's path sets both, and grow(1) to take the room the position leaves it.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: A wrapping Text wraps to the width layout gives it, inside its border and padding. In a column that width comes from the column, since children stretch across it by default. Side by side in a row, wrapping Texts shrink to share it, down to the width of their widest word. Text in layout shows both cases.

docs.title: Long Words and Hyphenation
docs.text: Words longer than the available width are broken with a hyphen (-) inserted at the break point. This applies to all three wrapping modes. Words are measured in terminal cells and broken between grapheme clusters, never inside one, so a line of wide characters may end a cell short, and a wide character in a box one cell wide sticks out past it rather than widening the box.

docs.title: Multi-paragraph Text
docs.text: Newline characters (\n) in the content string are treated as paragraph separators. Each paragraph is wrapped independently, so explicit line breaks in your content are always preserved.

docs.title: Utilities
docs.text:
To avoid the tedium of writing out styles explicitly over and over, Counterweight provides a variety of Tailwind-inspired "utility styles". These utilities are pre-defined styles that can be combined to form more complex styles.

The utilities can be imported from the counterweight.styles.utilities module. We recommend a * import for ease of use:

from counterweight.styles.utilities import *

That brings in the utilities, the palette's colors, and the ColorName, Shade and Side types the utility functions take, but not Style, Color or anything else the module itself imports, which come from counterweight.styles.

Each utility is a Style that sets just a small set of properties. Some are constants (e.g., border_heavy, justify_children_center), and the rest are functions that return one (e.g., gap(n), margin_x(n), pad(n)). Color utilities take a color name and shade, or any color. For example, border_color("rose", 200) returns a Style that sets the border color to rose-200, as does border_color(rose_200), with the palette's constant for that color: 

from counterweight.styles import Style, CellStyle, Color

border_color("rose", 200) == Style(border_style=CellStyle(foreground=Color.from_hex("#fecdd3")))
border_color(rose_200) == border_color("rose", 200)

Since they are normal Styles, they can be combined to form more complex styles using the | operator. Here we make a new Style for a rose_200-colored heavy border on the top and bottom sides:

from counterweight.styles.utilities import *

border_heavy_top_bottom_rose_200 = border_y | border_heavy | border_color("rose", 200)

Actually giving a name to the new style is optional. We can also use the expression directly in our component:

from counterweight.styles.utilities import *
from counterweight.components import component
from counterweight.elements import Text


@component
def my_component() -> Text:
    return Text(
        content="Hello, world!",
        style=border_y | border_heavy | border_color("rose", 200),
    )

Performance Considerations

If you have an expression like border_y | border_heavy | border_color("rose", 200) in your component, it will be evaluated every time the component is rendered. Merging styles with | does take some time, though it is aggressively cached inside the framework. If you find that this is causing performance issues, you should create the style just once, ideally outside your component (i.e., at module scope), so that it runs only once.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Each table below is built from the utilities module when the docs are built. The constants' tables list every field each one sets. Fields not listed are left unset, so merging the utility into another style leaves them alone (see Merging). The functions' tables give their signatures, since what they set depends on their arguments.

default is the empty style, a starting point that sets nothing.

Utility Sets default Nothing

docs.title: Colors
docs.text:
The color utilities draw from Tailwind's color palette when given a ColorName such as "rose" and a Shade from 50 (lightest) to 950 (darkest). Given one color instead, they use it, as Tailwind's arbitrary values such as text-[#fbbf24] do: a Color, such as a palette constant or Color.from_hex("#fbbf24"), one of the terminal colors, or a gradient. text_white and text_black are outside the palette.

Each utility colors one part of a box. In the box below, every part has its own color, matched by the swatch beside the utility that paints it:

    ("padding_color", "teal", 700),
    ("content_color", "rose", 900),
    ("text_color", "lime", 300),
    ("text_bg", "sky", 800),
)


def legend_line(utility: str, color: ColorName, shade: Shade) -> Text:
    return Text(
        content=(
            Chunk(content="██ ", style=text_color(color, shade).text_style),
            Chunk(content=f'{utility}("{color}", {shade})'),
        )
    )


@component
def places() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2) | align_children_center,
        children=(
            Div(
                style=width(26)
                | height(7)
                | center_children
                | margin(1)
                | margin_color("indigo", 900)
                | border
                | border_heavy
                | border_color("amber", 400)
                | border_bg("slate", 600)
                | pad_x(2)
                | pad_y(1)
                | padding_color("teal", 700)
                | content_color("rose", 900),
                children=(Text(style=text_color("lime", 300) | text_bg("sky", 800), content="Some text"),),
            ),
            Div(style=col, children=tuple(legend_line(*place) for place in PLACES)),
        ),
    )

docs.title: Terminal colors
docs.text:
A Color looks the same in every terminal. The terminal's own colors follow the user's theme instead, as the colors of a program run in it do: an IndexedColor is an entry of the terminal's 256-color palette, whose first 16 are the black, red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan and white that themes set, then their bright forms, and TERMINAL_DEFAULT is the terminal's default foreground where it colors text, and its default background where it fills one. These utilities set them in each place the color utilities above do, the *_indexed ones taking a palette index from 0 to 255. Screenshots draw them in DEFAULT_PALETTE, and the defaults as white on black, as the first 16 indexed colors and the defaults are drawn below. In a terminal, they take whatever colors its theme gives them.

def swatch(index: int) -> Text:
    return Text(style=text_bg_indexed(index) | width(6) | text_justify_center, content=str(index))


@component
def terminal_colors() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col,
        children=(
            Div(style=row, children=tuple(swatch(index) for index in range(8))),
            Div(style=row, children=tuple(swatch(index) for index in range(8, 16))),
            Text(
                style=text_terminal_default | text_bg_terminal_default | margin_top(1) | pad_x(1),
                content="text_terminal_default | text_bg_terminal_default",
            ),
        ),
    )

A gradient in a color place maps over the box that place paints unless the gradient names its own box. The color utilities above take one, and these put one in each place too.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
The text_* attributes draw the text bold, dim, italic, underlined or struck through, and the border_* ones draw the border characters that way. Each has a not_ form that turns it off when merged over a style that turns it on, such as a style for a selected row that isn't bold, merged over a table's bold one. text_link(uri) makes the text a hyperlink that the terminal opens when it's clicked, and text_link(None) makes it not a link, inside text that is one. They're CSS's font-weight: bold, font-style: italic and text-decoration, with dim, which a terminal draws faint, in place of CSS's lighter weights.

TEXT_ATTRIBUTES: tuple[tuple[str, Style], ...] = (
    ("text_bold", text_bold),
    ("text_dim", text_dim),
    ("text_italic", text_italic),
    ("text_underline", text_underline),
    ("text_strikethrough", text_strikethrough),
)

EMPHASIS = text_bold | text_italic | text_underline | text_color("amber", 300)


def bordered(utility: str, style: Style) -> Text:
    return Text(content=utility, style=border | border_heavy | border_color("sky", 400) | pad_x(1) | style)


@component
def attributes() -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1),
        children=(
            Div(
                style=col,
                children=tuple(Text(content=utility, style=style) for utility, style in TEXT_ATTRIBUTES),
            ),
            Div(
                style=col,
                children=(
                    Text(content="EMPHASIS", style=EMPHASIS),
                    Text(content="EMPHASIS | text_not_italic", style=EMPHASIS | text_not_italic),
                    Text(content="EMPHASIS | text_not_underline", style=EMPHASIS | text_not_underline),
                ),
            ),
            Div(
                style=row | gap(1),
                children=(
                    bordered("border_bold", border_bold),
                    bordered("border_dim", border_dim),
                    bordered("border_dim | border_not_dim", border_dim | border_not_dim),
                ),
            ),
        ),
    )

docs.title: One-Shot Commands
docs.text:
A one-shot command runs a program that's expected to exit, though not necessarily to succeed, and shows everything it printed, colors and all, as a terminal would have shown it. A slide can run an example command when it's shown, and an editor can run the code in a text area and show what it printed.

This page covers running a command, how its output is sized, the terminal it runs on, cancelling and timing out a run, and showing output recorded ahead of time.

docs.title: Running a command
docs.text:
use_command runs a program when its run is called, and returns the latest run, a CommandRun value holding the program's argv, everything it printed so far as output, and its outcome. command_output shows a run: its output in a scroll_area that sticks to its end, so it follows the output while the program runs, with a line beneath that says how the run is going, or how it ended.

A slide that runs its command when it's shown calls run from an effect:

@component
def slide(title: str, argv: tuple[str, ...]) -> Div:
    # The box the output is shown in, which sets how wide the program's terminal is.
    viewport, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)
    command = use_command(columns=use_rects(viewport).content.width)

    async def start() -> None:
        command.run(argv)

    # Runs the command when the slide is shown, and again if it's shown with another one.
    use_effect(start, deps=(argv,))

    return Div(
        style=col | full | gap(1) | pad(1),
        children=(
            Text(content=title, style=text_color("sky", 300)),
            command_output(command.latest, viewport, style=fill(1)),
        ),
    )
A run that succeededA run that failed ScreenshotText

A code runner runs its code on a key press instead:

@component
def code_runner() -> Div:
    code, set_code = use_state('for n in range(3):\n    print(f"{n} squared is {n * n}")')
    viewport, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)
    command = use_command(columns=use_rects(viewport).content.width, timeout=timedelta(seconds=10))

    def on_input(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
        match event:
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.F5):
                command.run((sys.executable, "-c", code))
                return ()
            case KeyPressed(key=Key.Escape):
                command.cancel()
                return ()
            case _:
                return None

    return Div(
        style=col | full,
        on_input=first(on_input, tab_focus),
        children=(
            text_area(code, set_code, enter_inserts_newline=True, auto_focus=True, style=max_height(10)),
            command_output(command.latest, viewport, style=fill(1)),
            Text(content="F5 runs the code, Escape stops it, Tab moves to the output", style=text_color("slate", 500)),
        ),
    )

This follows React Query's hooks for a fetch. useMutation runs on an event, through its mutate(), and exposes the latest run's status and result, which is run and latest here, and useQuery runs when its component mounts and again when its key changes, which is the slide's effect. A run differs from a fetch in two ways: its output streams, so latest shows what the program has printed so far while it runs, updating at most once a frame, and a program that exits with a failing status is a result like any other, not an error.

This recording shows a build's run as it streams in:

Notice that the progress bar redraws its line rather than adding one, that the box follows the output once it fills, and that the line beneath says running until the program exits. The recording replays a build's output written ahead of time into a run rather than running a build (see Recorded output), so it comes out the same on every run.

A run is a value that outlives its program, so a component can keep finished runs in state, show one again, or show it beside the next. Calling run again starts another run, even with the same argv, and hangs up the run in progress.

docs.title: How a run is sized
docs.text:
A run has two sizes, and only the first comes from its box.

  • The terminal's size is what the program formats its output for (wrapping, tables, progress bars). Its width is use_command's columns, which the slide and the runner read from the box their output is shown in, by passing command_output the same viewport handle they measure with use_rects(viewport). It's read when the run starts, and a run waits to start until it's positive, since use_rects reports zero on the first render. A later change doesn't rewrap a run's output: columns past the box's edge are cut off, and running again at the new width is up to the caller. Its height is rows, 24 by default, as a fresh xterm's is, which a program drawing a live display sizes it to. It doesn't come from the box, since the box scrolls rather than being the program's screen.
  • The output's size is how much the program printed: the run's columns wide, and as tall as the lines it printed, which grow while it runs. Its canvas takes that height, and the scroll area shows as many lines as fit.

Size the box from its parent

The output's width is the run's columns, which comes from the box, so the box has to take its width from its parent, by stretching, fill, or a styled width. A box sized by its content stays zero wide, and its run never starts.

docs.title: The terminal it runs on
docs.text:
A run gets a pseudo-terminal rather than pipes, so it prints what it would in a terminal:

  • Colors. Most programs color their output only when their output is a terminal.
  • Cursor movement. A progress bar that rewrites its line with \r, or a live display that moves the cursor up and redraws, leaves its last frame in the output, rather than every frame run together.

Its standard output and standard error arrive together, as they do in a terminal. A program that has to tell them apart is better run with asyncio's subprocess functions, which need no terminal.

The program sees a terminal, so it acts as it would on one:

  • Its standard input is /dev/null, so a program that reads input gets end of file rather than waiting for keys. A program that has to talk to its terminal can still open /dev/tty.
  • PAGER and GIT_PAGER are cat, so git log and other commands that start a pager print instead. Other tools read their own variables, such as MANPAGER, which env can set.
  • A program that asks its terminal something, such as where its cursor is, gets an answer from the emulator.
  • Its environment is the app's, under the terminal's variables (TERM=xterm-256color, COLORTERM=truecolor) and the pager defaults, under env, as for run_pty. clear_env=True leaves out the app's, which keeps a run's output from depending on who runs it.

docs.title: Cancelling and timing out
docs.text:
cancel hangs up the run in progress and makes its outcome Cancelled, keeping what it printed:

ScreenshotText 

╭──────────────────────────────────────╮
│ ===== test session starts =====      │
│ tests/test_slow.py ....              │
╰──────────────────────────────────────╯
cancelled

Starting another run and unmounting the component hang it up too. Hanging up sends the program's process group SIGHUP, as closing a terminal window does, and SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to whatever is still running a second apart, so nothing a run started outlives it. That goes on in the background, so a program slow to exit doesn't hold up the app, which waits for it when it stops (see Hanging up in the background).

A program never gets the keys the app reads, so it can't be interrupted with Ctrl+C: bind a key to cancel, as the runner does with Escape. Ctrl+C reaches the app as a key press, so an app can bind it to cancel, as a shell does, rather than leaving it to quit the app. timeout bounds a run: a program still running when it runs out is hung up, and its outcome is TimedOut. Only the program's own run counts against it: one that exits in time has exited, even if a background job it left keeps its terminal open past the timeout.

A run keeps the last max_lines lines of its output, 10,000 by default, dropping the oldest, so a program that never stops printing can't grow it without bound.

docs.title: Recorded output
docs.text:
Transcript.of turns output recorded ahead of time, such as with script, into the same output a run has, with no program run, so a slide can show a command's output without running it. That's how the screenshots on this page are drawn:

BUILD = (
    b"\x1b[1mBuilding\x1b[0m web v4.2.0\r\n"
    b"[####......] 40%\r[##########] 100%\r\n"
    b"\x1b[32m\xe2\x9c\x93\x1b[0m compiled 42 modules\r\n"
    b"\x1b[33m!\x1b[0m 2 warnings in \x1b[4msrc/app.ts\x1b[0m\r\n"
    b"\x1b[32m\xe2\x9c\x93\x1b[0m wrote \x1b[36mdist/web.js\x1b[0m (184 kB)\r\n"
)


@component
def recorded_build() -> Div:
    viewport, _ = use_state(ElementHandle)
    # Recorded at the width of the box's content: 40 columns, less its border and padding.
    run = CommandRun(argv=("./build.sh",), output=Transcript.of(BUILD, columns=36), outcome=Exited(status=0))
    return Div(children=(command_output(run, viewport, style=size(40, 8)),))

The recording of a streaming run feeds its output to an emulator in chunks instead, taking the transcript after each with followed_by, as a run does while its program prints. A Transcript is a Canvas painter, so a canvas can show it without command_output.

docs.title: counterweight.commands.use_command
docs.text:
use_command(
    columns: int,
    rows: int = 24,
    env: Mapping[str, str] = frozendict(),
    clear_env: bool = False,
    cwd: Path | None = None,
    timeout: timedelta | None = None,
    max_lines: int = MAX_LINES,
    hangup_grace: timedelta = HANGUP_GRACE,
) -> Command

Runs a program, when its run is called, on a pseudo-terminal columns by rows, with its standard input on /dev/null, so a program that reads input gets end of file rather than waiting, and returns the latest run, with everything it printed so far, which updates at most once a frame while it runs. Starting another run, cancelling, and unmounting the component each hang the program up (see run_pty) in the background, so a program slow to exit doesn't hold up the app's rendering, and an app that stops waits for it.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION columns

How wide the program's terminal is, which it formats its output for, such as the content width that use_rects reports for the box the output is shown in. It's read when the run starts, and a run waits to start until it's positive, since use_rects reports zero on the first render. A later change doesn't rewrap a run's output: running it again at the new width does.

TYPE: int

rows

How tall the program's terminal is, which a program that draws a live display sizes it to. It doesn't bound the output, which grows with what the program prints.

TYPE: int DEFAULT: 24

env

Variables to set in the program's environment. It gets PAGER=cat and GIT_PAGER=cat, so a command such as git log prints rather than paging, over the environment run_pty gives it, and env over those.

TYPE: Mapping[str, str] DEFAULT: frozendict()

clear_env

Leave out the app's environment (see run_pty).

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

cwd

The directory to run the program in, or None for the app's working directory. It's read when a run starts, as columns is.

TYPE: Path | None DEFAULT: None

timeout

How long the program may run before it's hung up and its outcome is TimedOut, or None for no limit (see run_pty).

TYPE: timedelta | None DEFAULT: None

max_lines

How many lines of output a run keeps, dropping the oldest, at most MAX_SCROLLBACK.

TYPE: int DEFAULT: MAX_LINES

hangup_grace

How long the program has to exit after each signal that hangs it up (see run_pty).

TYPE: timedelta DEFAULT: HANGUP_GRACE

docs.title: Embedded Terminals
docs.text:
An embedded terminal runs an interactive program, such as a shell, an editor or htop, in a box, shows its screen as the program draws it, and sends it the keys, pastes and mouse events the box receives, as a terminal window or a multiplexer's pane does. It's enough to build a terminal multiplexer: the multiplexer example runs shells side by side, with direct hotkeys as zellij has.

This page covers the widget, the hook it's built on, a multiplexer built from it, how input reaches the program, and how the terminal is sized. For a program that's expected to exit, whose output is read rather than used, see One-Shot Commands. Pseudo-terminals need Linux or macOS.

docs.title: A terminal widget
docs.text:
terminal is a bordered box that runs a program in a terminal the size of its content:

SHELL = (os.environ.get("SHELL", "/bin/sh"),)


def quit_on_ctrl_q(event: InputEvent, receiver: Receiver) -> InputResponse:
    match event:
        case KeyPressed(key=Key.ControlQ):
            return Quit()
        case _:
            return None


@component
def shell(command: tuple[str, ...] = SHELL) -> Div:
    return Div(
        style=col | full,
        children=(
            # Ctrl+] bubbles past the shell, so an app that embeds this one, such as the examples' gallery, gets it.
            terminal(
                command,
                style=fill(1),
                intercept=quit_on_ctrl_q,
                auto_focus=True,
                skips={Key.ControlRightBracket},
            ),
            Text(content="Ctrl+Q quits", style=text_color("slate", 500)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

╭──────────────────────────────────────╮
│~/project $ ls --color                │
│docs  src  tests  README.md  build.sh │
│~/project $ git status --short        │
│ M src/app.py                         │
│A  tests/test_app.py                  │
│~/project $                           │
╰──────────────────────────────────────╯

The screenshot feeds shell output written ahead of time to an emulator rather than running a shell, so it comes out the same on every run.

The box takes no size from the program, since the program draws whatever fits the terminal it's given, so size the box with style, as fill(1) does here. The program starts once the box has room, and its terminal resizes with the box.

While the box is focused, the program gets every key, Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z included, so an app that embeds a terminal needs some other way out. intercept is a handler that sees each event before the terminal does, and keeps it from the program by claiming it, as quit_on_ctrl_q does for Ctrl+Q.

docs.title: The hook
docs.text:
use_terminal runs the program, emulates its terminal, and makes the calling component focusable, leaving how it's drawn to the component, which returns a Canvas with the hook's view and on_input. This pane puts a prefix handler before the terminal's, as a tmux-style multiplexer would:

@component
def pane(argv: tuple[str, ...], prefix: InputHandler) -> Canvas:
    # The terminal is the canvas's content box, so it resizes with the pane.
    content = use_rects().content
    embedded = use_terminal(argv, content.width, content.height, auto_focus=True)

    return Canvas(
        painter=embedded.view,
        style=fill(1) | border | border_heavy | (border_color("amber", 400) if embedded.focus.is_focused else default),
        on_input=first(prefix, embedded.on_input),
    )

The hook returns the program's Screen as of the last snapshot, with its title and the modes it set, and its status: starting, running, exited with its status, or the reason it failed to start. The component's view is a ScreenView that draws the cursor while the component is focused.

docs.title: A multiplexer
docs.text:
Panes like that one, side by side, with keys that open, close and move focus between them, make a multiplexer. The multiplexer example puts its keys before each pane's terminal, so Alt+N, Alt+X and Alt+Left and Right reach it rather than the shell:

ScreenshotText 

╭─ Pane #1 ────────────────────────────╮╭─ Pane #2 ────────────────────────────╮
│$ echo hello from the first pane      ││$ echo $((6 * 7))                     │
│hello from the first pane             ││42                                    │
│$                                     ││$                                     │
│                                      ││                                      │
│                                      ││                                      │
│                                      ││                                      │
│                                      ││                                      │
│                                      ││                                      │
│                                      ││                                      │
╰──────────────────────────────────────╯╰──────────────────────────────────────╯
 <Alt n> NEW PANE   <Alt ←/→> FOCUS   <Alt x> CLOSE

Each pane's title is the title its program set, from its Screen, after the pane's number, and a pane closes when its program exits, since its status is then Exited.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Keys, pastes and mouse events reach the program re-encoded, as tmux sends them, rather than passed through, since the app has already parsed the bytes its terminal sent into events. Each is encoded as xterm sends it, since the program is told TERM=xterm-256color, and for the modes the program set:

  • Keys go to the program while the component is focused and the program is running, and are claimed, so they don't bubble. Cursor keys switch to their application form (ESC O A) for a program that set DECCKM, as vim does.
  • Pastes are wrapped in bracketed paste's markers for a program that set ?2004, with any end marker in the text removed, so a paste can't end itself early.
  • Mouse events on the program's screen go to it only if it asked for them, at the level it asked for: presses, releases and the wheel, motion while a button is held, or all motion. A press focuses the component wherever it lands, and one on the border or padding only focuses it. Once the terminal has claimed a press, the drag and release that follow come to it wherever the pointer goes, and are clamped to the screen's edges. A wheel the program didn't ask for passes on, so a scroll container around the terminal still scrolls.
  • Focus events, ESC [ I and ESC [ O, go to a program that set ?1004 as the component gains and loses focus.

Once the program has exited, keys and pastes pass on, so the app's own keys work again.

docs.title: Keys before the program
docs.text:
A handler put before the terminal's with first sees each key first, as a multiplexer's prefix key does: it claims the keys it binds, and passes on the rest to the program. The DOM would intercept with a capture-phase listener on an ancestor, but composing handlers on the terminal's own element does the same. A prefix and its key often arrive in one read, so keep whether the prefix is waiting in a ref, as the Prefix Keys cookbook page does.

To let a key past the program to a handler around the terminal instead, name it in skips: the terminal doesn't send its program a key in skips, and its handler returns None for one, so it bubbles, as VS Code's terminal skips the keys bound to its own commands. The multiplexer skips Ctrl+], so it still reaches the examples' gallery around it.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text: Programs ask their terminal things, such as where the cursor is or what kind of terminal it is, and wait for the answer. The emulator answers from its own state, as tmux does, and the answer goes to the program as its input.

docs.title: Output and size
docs.text:
The emulator is fed as the program writes, and snapshotted at most once a frame, so a program that writes as fast as it can (cat of a large file) costs one snapshot a frame. When the app falls behind, the pseudo-terminal's buffer fills and the program waits, which is the backpressure a terminal gives.

A component that sizes the terminal from its own box, with use_rects().content, resizes the program's terminal along with it, which sends the program SIGWINCH. use_rects reports the box as of the last frame, so for one frame after a resize the old screen shows, cropped or padded, until the program redraws, as in tmux.

A program's colors reach the app's terminal as the program chose them (see Colors).

use_terminal(
    argv: Sequence[str],
    columns: int,
    rows: int,

It makes the component focusable, and leaves drawing the terminal to it: the component returns a Canvas with the hook's view and on_input.

The emulator is fed as the program writes, and snapshotted at most once a frame, which renders the component again. The emulator answers the program's queries, such as for the cursor's position, from its own state. A component that sizes the terminal from its own box, with use_rects().content, resizes the program's terminal along with it, which sends the program SIGWINCH; until the program redraws, the old screen shows, cropped or padded. While the component is focused and the program set ?1004, it's sent focus events as the component gains and loses focus.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION argv

The program and its arguments. A change hangs the program up and starts the new one, as a change to env, clear_env or cwd does.

TYPE: Sequence[str]

env

Passed to use_pty, as are clear_env, cwd and hangup_grace.

TYPE: Mapping[str, str] DEFAULT: frozendict()

foreground

What the program's default colors stand for wherever a cell has to name them, as for Emulator, as background is. A change to either recolors the program's terminal, keeping what it shows.

TYPE: Color DEFAULT: foreground

auto_focus

Passed to use_focus, as are handle, is_focusable and in_focus_order.

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

skips

Keys the program isn't sent, which on_input returns None for, so they bubble up to the app's handlers, as VS Code's terminal skips the keys bound to its own commands. An app that embeds a terminal and binds keys on an element around it, rather than before it, such as an app that embeds the whole app this terminal is in, skips those keys.

docs.title: Emulators and Pseudo-Terminals
docs.text:
One-shot commands and embedded terminals are built from two lower layers, which this page covers for code that needs them directly: a pseudo-terminal, which runs a program as a terminal window does and hands back the bytes it writes, and a terminal emulator, which turns those bytes into what the terminal shows. Neither knows about the other, so output recorded ahead of time can be fed to an emulator with no program run, and a program's output can go somewhere other than an emulator.

Pseudo-terminals need Linux or macOS.

docs.title: Pseudo-terminals
docs.text:
run_pty runs a program on a new pseudo-terminal until it exits, in its own session with the terminal as its controlling terminal, calling on_output with what the program writes, standard output and standard error together. It returns how the program exited (Exited), why it couldn't start (FailedToStart), or that it outran its timeout (TimedOut), and hands out a PtyConnection that writes to the program without blocking and resizes its terminal. Cancelling it hangs the program up, as closing a terminal window does.

This component runs a short Python script with run_pty in an effect, keeping every byte it writes, and shows them twice: as a Text, which draws the escape and carriage return characters among them as ␛ and ␍, and as the Screen an emulator makes of them:

SCRIPT = """
for done in range(4):
    print(f"\\r[{'#' * done}{'.' * (3 - done)}]", end="")
print(" \\x1b[32mdone\\x1b[0m")
print("\\x1b[1mbold\\x1b[0m and \\x1b[31mred\\x1b[0m")
"""

COLUMNS, ROWS = 36, 3


@cache
def emulated(output: bytes) -> Screen:
    """
    What a terminal shows once a program has written `output` to it,
    the same `Screen` every time it's asked, since each emulator's snapshots are its own.
    """
    with Emulator(COLUMNS, ROWS, on_reply=lambda reply: None) as emulator:
        emulator.feed(output)
        return emulator.snapshot()


def describe(outcome: Exited | FailedToStart | None) -> str:
    match outcome:
        case None:
            return "Running..."
        case Exited(status=status):
            return f"Exited with status {status}"
        case FailedToStart(reason=reason):
            return f"Failed to start: {reason}"
        case _ as unreachable:
            assert_never(unreachable)


@component
def program(argv: tuple[str, ...] = (sys.executable, "-c", SCRIPT)) -> Div:
    output, set_output = use_state(b"")
    not_yet: Exited | FailedToStart | None = None
    outcome, set_outcome = use_state(not_yet)

    async def run() -> None:
        def on_output(chunk: bytes) -> None:
            set_output(lambda written: written + chunk)

        set_output(b"")
        set_outcome(None)
        set_outcome(await run_pty(argv, COLUMNS, ROWS, on_output=on_output))

    use_effect(run, deps=(argv,))

    def panel(title: str, content: Text | Canvas) -> Div:
        return Div(
            style=col | border | border_lightrounded | border_color("slate", 600) | pad_x(1),
            children=(Text(content=title, style=text_color("sky", 300)), content),
        )

    return Div(
        style=col | gap(1) | fit_content_width,
        children=(
            # A Text draws the control characters it holds as symbols, such as ␛ for escape and ␍ for carriage return.
            panel("What the program wrote", Text(content=output.decode(errors="replace"))),
            panel("What a terminal shows", Canvas(painter=ScreenView(emulated(output)), style=size(COLUMNS, ROWS))),
            Text(content=describe(outcome), style=text_color("slate", 500)),
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

╭────────────────────────────────────────╮  
│ What the program wrote                 │  
│ ␍[...]␍[#..]␍[##.]␍[###] ␛[32mdone␛[0m │  
│ ␛[1mbold␛[0m and ␛[31mred␛[0m          │  
│                                        │  
╰────────────────────────────────────────╯  

╭────────────────────────────────────────╮  
│ What a terminal shows                  │  
│ [###] done                             │  
│ bold and red                           │  
│                                        │  
╰────────────────────────────────────────╯  

Exited with status 0

Notice that the bytes hold every step of the progress bar, each redrawn after a carriage return, and the escape sequences that color the text, while the terminal shows only where the bar ended and the colors. The program printed line feeds, and the pseudo-terminal turned each into a carriage return and a line feed, as a terminal's line discipline does.

use_pty runs a program while its component is mounted, as a terminal window or a multiplexer's pane does: it starts once its size is positive, resizes the terminal as its size changes, and starts the program again when its argv or environment change. It hangs the program up in the background, so a program slow to exit doesn't hold up the app's rendering.

docs.title: Hanging up in the background
docs.text:
The render loop waits for a cancelled effect to finish before it renders again, and hanging up a program that ignores SIGHUP takes up to two hangup_graces. So use_pty, and use_command for each run, call run_pty in a task of the app's task group and await that task through asyncio.shield, which keeps their effect's cancellation from waiting for it:

sequenceDiagram
    participant L as Render loop
    participant E as Effect
    participant R as run_pty, in the app's task group

    L->>E: Start the effect
    E->>R: Start run_pty and await it through shield
    alt The program exits, or outruns its timeout
        R->>R: Hang up whatever it left running
        R-->>E: Exited or TimedOut
        E->>E: Set the status, or report the run's outcome
    else Cancelled, by cancel, another run or argv, or unmounting
        L->>E: Cancel, then wait for it to finish
        E->>R: Cancel
        E-->>L: Finished at once
        Note over L: Renders again
        R->>R: Hang up the program, for up to two hangup_graces
        R-->>R: Ends cancelled, with no outcome to return
    end
    Note over L,R: An app that stops waits for every hangup still going

A program that ends by itself returns its outcome through the effect as usual, but only once run_pty has hung up what it left running. Only that effect waits for it, not the render loop, but a program that exits leaving a background job that ignores SIGHUP reads as running until that job is gone. A cancelled run has no outcome to return: cancel has already made it Cancelled, and another run or argv reports its own.

docs.title: Emulators
docs.text:
An Emulator is fed the bytes a program writes, answers the program's queries through on_reply, and snapshot turns what its terminal shows into an immutable Screen. A snapshot of a terminal that didn't change is the same Screen as before, and rows that didn't change are shared between snapshots, so a canvas drawing one redraws only when it changed. scrolled_off returns the rows that scrolled off the top of the screen since it was last called, for an emulator given a scrollback.

ScreenView is the Canvas painter that draws a Screen, with its cursor when asked, and Transcript the one that draws everything a program printed.

docs.title: Replaying recorded output
docs.text:
An emulator needs no program, only bytes, so output recorded ahead of time replays into one. Feeding it in the chunks the program wrote, with a snapshot after each, gives the screens the program showed, which a component reading the clock shows in turn:

type RecordedOutput = Sequence[tuple[timedelta, bytes]]
"""What a program wrote, in chunks, each with how long after the program started it wrote it."""


def replay(output: RecordedOutput, columns: int, rows: int) -> tuple[tuple[timedelta, Screen], ...]:
    """What the terminal showed after each chunk of `output`, with when it was written."""
    with Emulator(columns, rows, on_reply=lambda reply: None) as emulator:
        screens = []
        for at, chunk in output:
            emulator.feed(chunk)
            screens.append((at, emulator.snapshot()))
        return tuple(screens)


TICK = timedelta(milliseconds=100)


@component
def replayed(screens: tuple[tuple[timedelta, Screen], ...], style: Style = default) -> Canvas:
    elapsed = use_clock(TICK).since_mount
    screen = last((screen for at, screen in screens if at <= elapsed), screens[0][1])
    return Canvas(painter=ScreenView(screen, show_cursor=True), style=style)

Snapshots are values, so the screens are taken once, the first time they're needed, rather than in every render, and the component only picks the latest one whose time has come. This recording replays output in the style of vim's, written by hand rather than recorded from vim, as it opens a line, types into it, and saves:

Notice that the emulator applies the cursor movement, colors and alternate screen in the output, so the replay shows the editor's screen rather than the bytes that draw it. The embedded terminals and one-shot commands pages replay output the same way for their screenshots and recordings, since a real program's output isn't the same on every run.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text:
A program's colors reach the app's terminal as the program chose them, so they follow the user's theme as they would had the program run there: a palette color (ESC [ 31 m, or ESC [ 38 ; 5 ; n m) stays an IndexedColor, and an RGB color a Color. A palette entry the program changed (with OSC 4) is the RGB color it changed it to, since the user's terminal doesn't know it.

A cell in the program's default colors leaves them unset, so it follows the text_style of the canvas showing it. To have those follow the user's theme too, give the canvas the terminal's default colors, as text_terminal_default | text_bg_terminal_default | content_terminal_default (see Terminal colors). A cell whose colors the program swapped (inverse video) or hid (invisible text) has to name its default colors, so it takes the emulator's foreground and background instead, which are white and black unless the program changes them (with OSC 10 and 11). set_default_colors changes them on a running emulator, as the user changing their terminal's theme does, though a color the program set stays what it set.

Here the same output, with palette, 256-color and RGB backgrounds, plain text and inverse video, is shown on a light theme twice: once from an emulator left at its defaults, and once from one given the theme's colors:

@cache
def snapshot(output: bytes, foreground: Color, background: Color) -> Screen:
    with Emulator(26, 6, on_reply=lambda reply: None, foreground=foreground, background=background) as emulator:
        emulator.feed(output)
        return emulator.snapshot()


@component
def themed_output(screen: Screen) -> Canvas:
    # The theme's colors again, for the cells in the program's default colors.
    theme = text_color("slate", 900) | text_bg("slate", 100) | content_color("slate", 100)
    return Canvas(painter=ScreenView(screen), style=size(28, 6) | pad_x(1) | theme)


@component
def colors() -> Div:
    untold = snapshot(COLORS, foreground=Color.from_name("white"), background=Color.from_name("black"))
    # Told the theme's colors, for the cells whose colors the program swapped.
    themed = snapshot(COLORS, foreground=slate_900, background=slate_100)
    return Div(
        style=row | gap(2),
        children=tuple(
            Div(style=col, children=(Text(content=label, style=text_color("slate", 400)), themed_output(screen)))
            for label, screen in (("The emulator's defaults", untold), ("The theme's colors", themed))
        ),
    )
ScreenshotText 

The emulator's defaults       The theme's colors          
 palette                       palette                    
 bright                        bright                     
 256                           256                        
 rgb                           rgb                        
 default plain text            default plain text         
 inverse  swapped              inverse  swapped

The palette, 256-color and RGB rows and the plain text match, since none of them names a default color. Only the inverse cell differs: on the left it swaps the emulator's white and black, which reads as no swap at all on a light theme, and on the right it swaps the theme's colors.

        [PtyConnection], None
    ] = lambda connection: None,
